text: The first part introduces the basic objects and the scaling predictions. The model is Bernoulli percolation, but the guiding comparison is with branching processes and branching random walk. This comparison explains the mean-field exponents, the upper critical dimension six, and the reason that intrinsic and extrinsic geometry should be kept separate. The scaling and hyperscaling chapter then records the exponent relations predicted by the finite-box picture, while also identifying where this picture is expected to fail in high dimensions.

The second part develops inequalities that hold with little or no Euclidean input. Sharpness and the correlation inequalities give the foundational finite-volume estimates. The triangle condition then supplies a sufficient condition for mean-field critical behaviour by turning diagrammatic control into a reverse differential inequality for the susceptibility. Entropy, decision trees, OSSS, and universal tightness provide complementary ways to convert information about one observable into information about another. These chapters should be read as a toolkit: each method is robust, but each sees a different part of the geometry.

The third part turns to geometry below the upper critical dimension. In two dimensions, RSW estimates and arm-gluing replace the triangle condition as the basic source of control. The continuum \(k\)-point discussion is deliberately more conditional: it explains what sort of multiplicative geometry is forced once the relevant power laws and gluing inputs are available, rather than claiming that all such inputs are presently known for every planar model.

The fourth part concerns long-range percolation. Long-range models are useful because the decay exponent \(\alpha\) acts as a continuously variable dimension-like parameter. They also force one to separate several notions that coincide in simpler settings: high-dimensional volume exponents, stable versus Brownian spatial scaling, effectively long-range versus effectively short-range behaviour, and mean-field powers versus logarithmic critical-dimensional corrections. The intended order of ideas is the one used in the original course plan: first identify the critical two-point function, then use it to control high-dimensional cluster moments, then extract the scaling limits, and only afterwards discuss critical-dimensional logarithms and low-effective-dimensional hyperscaling. The cutoff-renormalization chapter gives a worked account of the main differential inequalities and records the more technical tightness and convergence inputs as quoted theorems.

Let us start from a high vantage point. A \emph{phase transition} is a qualitative change in the behaviour of a system as a parameter is varied continuously through a special value. In probabilistic lattice models, the parameter might be a density, a temperature, or an inverse temperature, and the special value is usually called the \emph{critical point}. The main interest of these notes is not merely whether a phase transition occurs, but what the system looks like at and near the point where it occurs.

It is useful to separate two phenomena that are sometimes conflated. A phase transition can be discontinuous: water boiling at fixed pressure has a sharp qualitative change, but it is not the kind of critical point at which one sees clusters at all scales. The transitions emphasized here are continuous critical phenomena. At the critical point there is no characteristic finite length scale. The system looks complicated no matter how far one zooms out, and many observables have polynomial rather than exponential behaviour.

Examples of this broad phenomenon appear throughout probability and statistical mechanics. In epidemic models, one tunes the infection rate and asks whether an infection dies out or persists. In traffic models, one tunes a density and asks whether large-scale flow jams. In average-case questions in theoretical computer science, one tunes constraint density and asks whether a random instance is typically satisfiable, connected, or searchable. Percolation is the cleanest model for isolating the geometric part of this story: edges or sites are independently retained, and the question is whether the retained set contains large connected components.

Universality should not be interpreted as saying that everything is independent of microscopic details. The critical point itself is usually not universal: bond percolation on the square lattice, site percolation on the triangular lattice, and spread-out percolation on $\Z^d$ have different numerical critical probabilities. The expectation is rather that, after one tunes to the critical point and looks at large scales, the exponents and scaling limits depend only on coarse features. In two dimensions this principle is closely connected to conformal invariance. In high dimensions it is connected to the emergence of branching random walk and mean-field behaviour.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected, locally finite graph. In Bernoulli bond percolation on $G$ with parameter $p\in[0,1]$, each edge of $G$ is declared \emph{open} with probability $p$ and \emph{closed} otherwise, independently of all other edges. The connected components of the random subgraph of open edges are called \emph{clusters}. We write $K_v$ for the cluster of a vertex $v$, and write $x\leftrightarrow y$ for the event that $x$ and $y$ belong to the same open cluster.

More formally, the configuration space is $\{0,1\}^E$, where $\omega(e)=1$ means that $e$ is open. The percolation measure $\Pp$ is the product measure for which
\[
  \Pp(\omega(e)=1)=p
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \Pp(\omega(e)=0)=1-p
\]
for every edge $e$. Events depending on finitely many edges are called cylinder events. Infinite-volume events are generated by countable combinations of cylinder events; most of the events in these notes, such as $\{|K_0|=\infty\}$ or $\{0\leftrightarrow \partial\Lambda_r\}$, are obtained as limits of finite events.

The main example is nearest-neighbour percolation on $\Z^d$, where $x,y\in\Z^d$ are adjacent when $\norm{x-y}_1=1$. We write
\[
  \Lambda_r=[-r,r]^d\cap\Z^d
\]
and let $\partial\Lambda_r$ denote a convenient vertex boundary, for instance the set of vertices in $\Lambda_r$ adjacent to a vertex outside $\Lambda_r$. None of the exponent-level statements below depends on the particular equivalent convention for boxes and boundaries.

When $G$ is infinite, the basic qualitative question is whether there exists an infinite cluster. We define
\[
  p_c(G)=\inf\{p\in[0,1]: \Pp(\text{there exists an infinite cluster})=1\}.
\]
Equivalently, one often writes the infimum with the condition that the probability is positive. The event that there exists an infinite cluster is a tail event, so Kolmogorov's zero-one law implies that its probability is either zero or one. On a transitive graph the event that a fixed vertex lies in an infinite cluster is also independent of the vertex, and the percolation probability
\[
  \theta(p)=\Pp(|K_0|=\infty)
\]
is the natural order parameter.

The monotonicity in $p$ can be made completely explicit. Let $(U_e)_{e\in E}$ be independent uniform random variables on $[0,1]$, and define
\[
  \omega_p(e)=\1_{\{U_e\leq p\}}.
\]
Then $\omega_p$ has law $\Pp$, and $\omega_p\leq \omega_q$ edgewise whenever $p\leq q$. This is the \emph{standard monotone coupling}. It implies that every increasing event has probability nondecreasing in $p$, and in particular that the set of supercritical parameters is an interval.

On $\Z^d$ with nearest-neighbour edges, the phase transition is non-trivial for $d\geq 2$: one has
\[
  0<p_c(\Z^d)<1.
\]
We include the elementary proof because it is the first example of the two complementary methods that recur throughout the subject: exploration by paths for lower bounds, and dual or separating surfaces for upper bounds.

\begin{proof}
The lower bound is valid on any bounded-degree graph. Suppose $G$ has maximum degree $\Delta$. If $K_0$ is infinite, then for every $n$ there exists an open simple path of length $n$ starting from $0$. Equivalently, the finite tree of open simple paths from $0$ has vertices at every depth; by König's lemma, or just by the compactness of the product of the finite choice sets along the path, this is the same as the existence of an infinite open simple path. The number of simple paths of length $n$ starting from $0$ is at most
\[
  \Delta(\Delta-1)^{n-1},
\]
since after the first step there are at most $\Delta-1$ choices if the path is not to immediately traverse the edge it just used. Hence
\[
  \Pp(0\leftrightarrow \partial B(n))
  \leq
  \Delta(\Delta-1)^{n-1}p^n,
\]
where $B(n)$ denotes the graph-distance ball of radius $n$. If $p<1/(\Delta-1)$, the right-hand side tends to zero with $n$. Therefore $\Pp(|K_0|=\infty)=0$, and $p_c(G)\geq 1/(\Delta-1)$. For $\Z^d$, $\Delta=2d$, so this gives a positive lower bound.

For the upper bound it suffices to work in $\Z^2$, since $\Z^2$ embeds as a subgraph of $\Z^d$ for every $d\geq 2$. Consider bond percolation on the square lattice and its planar dual lattice. If the open cluster of the origin is finite, take the union of the unit squares centred at vertices of this finite cluster. Its outer boundary is a finite collection of dual circuits. The outermost component surrounds the origin, and every dual edge in this circuit crosses a primal edge that is closed: if such a primal edge were open, the cluster would continue across the boundary. Thus finiteness of the origin cluster forces the existence of a closed dual circuit surrounding the origin. Consequently
\[
  \Pp(0\not\leftrightarrow \infty)
  \leq
  \sum_{\gamma}\Pp(\gamma\text{ is a closed dual circuit surrounding }0),
\]
where the sum is over dual circuits surrounding the origin. A circuit of length $n$ can be encoded by its first intersection with a fixed ray and by its subsequent steps. A crude bound of the form $n\,3^n$ suffices. Thus
\[
  \Pp(0\not\leftrightarrow \infty)
  \leq
  \sum_{n\geq 1} n\,3^n(1-p)^n,
\]
up to an irrelevant constant depending on the precise ray convention. This sum can be made smaller than one by taking $p$ sufficiently close to one. For such $p$, the origin has positive probability to lie in an infinite open cluster, so $p_c(\Z^2)<1$ and hence $p_c(\Z^d)<1$ for all $d\geq 2$.
\end{proof}

This theorem proves only that there is a non-trivial transition. It says almost nothing about the critical point itself. In one dimension, $p_c(\Z)=1$. In two dimensions, planar self-duality identifies $p=1/2$ as the candidate critical point for square-lattice bond percolation, and Kesten's theorem proves that indeed $p_c(\Z^2)=1/2$; Harris and Kesten also prove that there is no infinite cluster at criticality. In sufficiently high dimensions, absence of an infinite cluster at criticality follows from the lace expansion and the triangle condition. For nearest-neighbour percolation on $\Z^d$, the problem remains open in dimensions $3,4,5,$ and $6$.

We will focus primarily on quantitative critical behaviour. The most basic objects are the \emph{two-point function}
\[
  \tau_p(x,y)=\Pp(x\leftrightarrow y),
\]
the \emph{susceptibility}
\[
  \chi(p)=\Ep |K_0|=\sum_{x\in V}\tau_p(0,x),
\]
the \emph{percolation probability}
\[
  \theta(p)=\Pp(|K_0|=\infty),
\]
the \emph{volume tail} $\Pp(|K_0|\geq n)$, and the \emph{one-arm probability}
\[
  \Pp(0\leftrightarrow \partial \Lambda_r),
\]
where $\Lambda_r$ is a box or ball of radius $r$ around the origin. At criticality these quantities are expected to obey power laws whenever the model is sufficiently homogeneous.

One should think of these observables as measuring different views of the same random object. The two-point function asks for the probability that a cluster reaches a specified location. The susceptibility is the expected cluster volume and is equal to the spatial sum of the two-point function by Fubini:
\[
  \Ep |K_0|
  =
  \sum_{x\in V}\Pp(0\leftrightarrow x).
\]
The one-arm probability asks for large spatial diameter. The volume tail asks for many vertices. In low-dimensional models, large volume and large diameter are strongly tied by geometry; in high-dimensional or tree-like models, they decouple more strongly because clusters can be spatially diffuse.

On $\Z^d$, one traditionally writes the critical exponents by the asymptotic relations
\begin{align*}
  \theta(p) &\as (p-p_c)^\beta, && p\downarrow p_c,\ p>p_c,\\
  \chi(p) &\as (p_c-p)^{-\gamma}, && p\uparrow p_c,\ p<p_c,\\
  \P_{p_c}(|K_0|\geq n) &\as n^{-1/\delta}, && n\to\infty,\\
  \P_{p_c}(0\leftrightarrow \partial\Lambda_r) &\as r^{-1/\rho}, && r\to\infty,\\
  \tau_{p_c}(0,x) &\as \norm{x}^{-d+2-\eta}, && \norm{x}\to\infty.
\end{align*}
These relations are not definitions unless the corresponding limits exist, and the notation hides several possible logarithmic corrections at marginal dimensions. Nevertheless, the exponent language is extremely useful. It allows us to state the predictions of scaling theory and to compare rigorous inequalities with the expected picture.

The exponent $\beta$ describes how the infinite cluster is born above criticality. The exponent $\gamma$ describes the divergence of the expected finite cluster below criticality. The exponent $\delta$ describes the critical cluster-volume tail. The exponent $\rho$ describes the critical one-arm probability in Euclidean distance. The exponent $\eta$ describes the anomalous dimension of the two-point function. Later we will also use the correlation-length exponent $\nu$ and the gap exponent $\Delta$.

There is a small but important convention issue here. Some authors write the one-arm exponent as $\rho$ and some write it as its reciprocal. In these notes the displayed relation
\[
  \Pc(0\leftrightarrow \partial\Lambda_r)\as r^{-1/\rho}
\]
means that the Euclidean mean-field value is $\rho=1/2$, because the high-dimensional one-arm probability decays like $r^{-2}$. Intrinsic one-arm probabilities, measured in graph distance inside the cluster, have the tree-like decay $r^{-1}$ and will be denoted separately when needed.

The mean-field values for percolation are
\[
  \beta=1,\qquad \gamma=1,\qquad \delta=2,\qquad \rho=\frac12,\qquad \eta=0
\]
These are the values one obtains on regular trees, in branching processes, and in high-dimensional percolation once the triangle condition is known. The central dimensional prediction is that nearest-neighbour percolation has upper critical dimension $6$: above six dimensions the mean-field exponents hold, at six dimensions they hold with logarithmic corrections, and below six dimensions the exponents are different and hyperscaling relations become visible.

In two dimensions, the exactly predicted and in several cases rigorously proved exponents are very different. For site percolation on the triangular lattice one has
\[
  \beta=\frac{5}{36},\qquad
  \gamma=\frac{43}{18},\qquad
  \delta=\frac{91}{5},\qquad
  \rho=\frac{48}{5},\qquad
  \eta=\frac{5}{24}.
\]
These rational values are special to two dimensions and are tied to conformal invariance, SLE, and representation-theoretic structures that are not available in the same form in dimensions three, four, and five. The intermediate dimensions are expected to have non-rational exponents with no simple exact formula.

At the upper critical dimension $d=6$, one expects mean-field powers multiplied by logarithmic corrections. The standard physics predictions include
\[
  \Pc(|K_0|\geq n)
  \as
  n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{2/7},
\]
\[
  \chi(p)
  \as
  (p_c-p)^{-1}\bigl(\log(1/(p_c-p))\bigr)^{2/7},
\]
and
\[
  \tau_{p_c}(0,x)
  \as
  \norm{x}^{-4}(\log \norm{x})^{1/21}.
\]
The exponents $2/7$ and $1/21$ are related to the first terms in the $\eps$-expansion around $d=6$. These logarithmic predictions remain far beyond current rigorous techniques for nearest-neighbour six-dimensional percolation.
There are three different levels at which one can try to understand the above predictions.

First, one can seek \emph{qualitative} theorems: existence of a phase transition, absence of infinite clusters at criticality, sharpness of the phase transition, and so on. These results are foundational but do not by themselves identify critical exponents.

Second, one can seek \emph{conditional} theorems. The most important example is the triangle condition, which implies mean-field critical behaviour. Conditional theorems are valuable because they separate robust probabilistic mechanisms from the model-specific analysis needed to verify their hypotheses.

It is also worth identifying what a satisfactory proof should \emph{not} hide. A proof of an exponent should explain which estimates are truly geometric and which are consequences of general inequalities. A proof of mean-field behaviour should explain why intersections of different branches are negligible. A proof of a low-dimensional hyperscaling relation should explain how finite-volume clusters fill space and why the largest clusters are not wildly uneven after normalization. A proof in a long-range model should explain how the spatial scale induced by the step distribution interacts with the intrinsic tree-like structure of critical clusters.

section_title: Long-range models as a running test case
text:
Although the detailed treatment of long-range percolation comes later, it is useful to keep the model in mind from the beginning. Long-range percolation replaces the nearest-neighbour lattice by a weighted complete graph whose edge weights decay like
\[
  J(x,y)\asymp \norm{x-y}^{-d-\alpha}.
\]
The parameter \(\alpha\) then acts as a continuously variable dimension-like parameter. By changing \(\alpha\), one can move through mean-field behaviour, critical-dimensional logarithms, low-dimensional hyperscaling, stable spatial scaling, Brownian spatial scaling, and the crossover between genuinely long-range and effectively short-range behaviour. This makes long-range percolation a useful testing ground for the general theory: the same inequalities appear, but the geometry changes visibly as the exponent \(\alpha\) is varied.

Consider a Galton-Watson branching process $(Z_n)_{n\geq 0}$ with $Z_0=1$ and offspring distribution of mean $\mu$. There is a phase transition at $\mu=1$: if $\mu\leq 1$ the process dies out almost surely, while if $\mu>1$ it survives with positive probability. At criticality, assuming finite non-zero offspring variance, classical branching-process theory gives
\[
  \P\left(\sum_{n\geq 0} Z_n\geq N\right)\as N^{-1/2},
  \qquad
  \P(Z_n>0)\as n^{-1}.
\]
Near criticality, the expected total progeny is of order $(1-\mu)^{-1}$ as $\mu\uparrow 1$.

Let us recall the elementary generating-function derivation. Let $\xi$ be the offspring distribution and let
\[
  \phi(s)=\E s^\xi
\]
be its generating function. The extinction probability $q$ is the smallest solution of
\[
  q=\phi(q).
\]
Indeed, the process dies out if and only if all child sub-processes die out. When $\mu=\phi'(1)\leq 1$, convexity implies that the only solution in $[0,1]$ is $q=1$. When $\mu>1$, the graph of $\phi$ crosses the diagonal at a second point $q<1$, and the survival probability is $1-q$.

Near criticality, suppose for simplicity that the offspring distribution has finite second moment and that $\mu=1+\eps$ with $\eps>0$ small. Expanding $\phi(1-a)$ around $1$ gives
\[
  \phi(1-a)
  =
  1-\mu a+\frac{\E[\xi(\xi-1)]}{2}a^2+O(a^3)
\]
under a corresponding moment assumption. The equation $1-a=\phi(1-a)$ then gives
\[
  a
  =
  \frac{2(\mu-1)}{\E[\xi(\xi-1)]}+o(\mu-1).
\]
Thus the survival probability grows linearly above criticality, giving the mean-field value $\beta=1$.

For the total progeny
\[
  T=\sum_{n\geq 0}Z_n,
\]
the generating function $F(s)=\E s^T$ satisfies
\[
  F(s)=s\,\phi(F(s)).
\]
At criticality, $\phi'(1)=1$. Writing $F(s)=1-u$ and $s=1-t$, and expanding again, one obtains
\[
  1-u
  =
  (1-t)\left(1-u+\frac{\sigma^2}{2}u^2+o(u^2)\right),
\]
where $\sigma^2=\Var(\xi)$ in the critical case. The leading balance is
\[
  t\as u^2,
\]
so
\[
  1-F(s)\as (1-s)^{1/2}
\]
as $s\uparrow 1$. Tauberian theorems convert this square-root singularity into
\[
  \P(T\geq n)\as n^{-1/2}
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  \P(T=n)\as n^{-3/2}.
\]
This is the branching-process origin of the critical volume-tail exponent $\delta=2$.

Finally, below criticality the expected total progeny is immediate from summing expected generation sizes:
\[
  \E T=\sum_{n\geq 0}\E Z_n=\sum_{n\geq 0}\mu^n=\frac1{1-\mu}.
\]
Thus the susceptibility exponent is $\gamma=1$. These three calculations are deliberately elementary. Much of high-dimensional percolation consists of proving that, after enough diagrammatic or renormalization work, the same balances survive despite spatial self-interaction.

section_title: Critical percolation on the binary tree
text:
Let $T$ be the rooted binary tree in which each vertex has two children. Critical Bernoulli percolation on $T$ has parameter $p_c=1/2$. Let $K$ be the open cluster of the root. If $Q_n=\P_{1/2}(|K|=n)$, then the recursive structure of the tree implies a Catalan-number formula for $Q_n$. In particular,
\[
  \P_{1/2}(|K|\geq n)\as n^{-1/2}.
\]
Similarly, the intrinsic one-arm probability satisfies
\[
  \P_{1/2}(0\leftrightarrow \partial B_{\mathrm{int}}(r))\as r^{-1}.
\]
Here $B_{\mathrm{int}}(r)$ denotes the intrinsic ball of radius $r$, i.e. vertices within graph distance $r$ inside the tree.

section_title: Critical percolation on the binary tree
text:
The two-point function is completely explicit. There is a unique path between any two vertices $x$ and $y$, so
\[
  \tau_p(x,y)=p^{d(x,y)}.
\]
This is not the Euclidean power law that one expects on $\Z^d$; a tree has exponential volume growth and no Euclidean embedding compatible with the later geometry. The value of the tree is instead that the cluster-volume and intrinsic-distance exponents can be computed exactly.

section_title: Critical percolation on the binary tree
text:
Let $C_n$ be the number of rooted connected subtrees of the binary tree with $n$ vertices. If $K$ has $n$ vertices, then it contains $n-1$ open edges and has $n+1$ boundary edges leading from the cluster to children not in the cluster. Therefore
\[
  \Pp(|K|=n)=C_n p^{n-1}(1-p)^{n+1}.
\]
The numbers $C_n$ are Catalan numbers:
\[
  C_n=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
One way to see this is to decompose a rooted subtree into its left and right child subtrees. If
\[
  C(z)=\sum_{n\geq 1}C_n z^n,
\]
then the recursive decomposition gives
\[
  C(z)=z(1+C(z))^2,
\]
after allowing either child subtree to be empty. Solving the quadratic and extracting coefficients gives the Catalan formula. Stirling's approximation yields
\[
  C_n\sim \frac{4^n}{\sqrt{\pi}n^{3/2}}.
\]
At $p=1/2$ this becomes
\[
  \P_{1/2}(|K|=n)
  \sim
  \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}}n^{-3/2}.
\]
This is an exact asymptotic for the rooted full-binary-tree convention just described. Summing over $m\geq n$ gives
\[
  \P_{1/2}(|K|\geq n)\as n^{-1/2}.
\]

section_title: Critical percolation on the binary tree
text:
The intrinsic one-arm probability has an equally useful recurrence. Let
\[
  q_r=\P_{1/2}(0\leftrightarrow \partial B_{\mathrm{int}}(r)),
\]
where on the tree this is the probability that the open cluster reaches generation $r$. The cluster reaches generation $r$ if at least one of the two child edges is open and the corresponding child subtree reaches generation $r-1$. Hence, at $p=1/2$,
\[
  q_r=1-\left(1-\frac12 q_{r-1}\right)^2
  =
  q_{r-1}-\frac14 q_{r-1}^2.
\]
Since $q_r\downarrow 0$, this recurrence is asymptotic to the differential equation $q'=-q^2/4$, whose solution behaves like $4/r$. A short discrete argument makes this precise:
\[
  \frac1{q_r}-\frac1{q_{r-1}}
  =
  \frac{q_{r-1}-q_r}{q_rq_{r-1}}
  =
  \frac14\frac{q_{r-1}}{q_r}
  \longrightarrow \frac14.
\]
Thus
\[
  q_r\sim \frac4r.
\]
This is the intrinsic one-arm exponent of the critical tree.

section_title: Critical percolation on the binary tree
text:
The Catalan formula also shows how the critical distribution is cut off away from criticality. If $p=1/2+\eps$, then
\[
  4p(1-p)=1-4\eps^2.
\]
Combining this with the Catalan asymptotic gives, for large $n$ and small $\eps$ in the appropriate joint regime,
\[
  \Pp(|K|=n)
  \approx
  n^{-3/2}\exp(-4\eps^2 n)
\]
up to a prefactor depending smoothly on $p$. Thus the characteristic finite-cluster size is of order
\[
  |p-p_c|^{-2}.
\]
This is the tree computation of the gap exponent $\Delta=2$.

section_title: Large critical trees and the continuum random tree
text: There is a precise scaling-limit theorem behind this heuristic. A critical Galton-Watson tree with finite offspring variance, conditioned to have $n$ vertices, converges after rescaling graph distance by $n^{-1/2}$ to the Brownian continuum random tree. One way to see why Brownian objects appear is through the depth-first contour process. For a plane tree, the contour records the height of a walk as it traverses the tree. For a uniform critical tree with $n$ vertices, the contour is closely related to a simple random walk excursion of length $2n$. After diffusive rescaling, this excursion converges to the Brownian excursion. The continuum random tree is encoded by identifying times of the Brownian excursion whose intervening minimum has the appropriate height.

section_title: Branching random walk and the upper critical dimension
text:
In a branching random walk on $\Z^d$, each particle branches and its children move according to a random-walk step distribution. At criticality, the expected number of visits to a vertex $x$ by the branching random walk started at the origin is the Green function of the underlying random walk:
\[
  G(0,x)\as \norm{x}^{-d+2}
\]
when $d>2$.

section_title: Branching random walk and the upper critical dimension
text: The analogy is best understood by first recalling self-avoiding walk. A self-avoiding walk is a random-walk path conditioned, or weighted, not to visit the same vertex twice. In dimensions $d>4$, two independent random walks intersect only finitely many times, and self-avoidance becomes a perturbative effect rather than a dominant large-scale constraint. This is the intuition made rigorous by the lace expansion, which proves diffusive behaviour for high-dimensional self-avoiding walk. At the critical dimension $4$, logarithmic corrections are expected.

section_title: Branching random walk and the upper critical dimension
text:
The heuristic comparison between percolation and branching random walk suggests that high-dimensional critical percolation should have
\[
  \tau_{p_c}(0,x)\as \norm{x}^{-d+2},
\]
which is the exponent value $\eta=0$. This comparison becomes self-consistent when large critical clusters do not intersect themselves too much at macroscopic scales. The dimension at which this self-interaction changes its character is the upper critical dimension.

section_title: Branching random walk and the upper critical dimension
text:
Let us spell out the dimension count. A critical branching random walk has expected occupation density comparable to $\norm{x}^{-d+2}$. If one asks whether two independent such objects intersect, a first-moment calculation involves the sum
\[
  \sum_{x\in\Z^d} G(0,x)^2
  \as
  \sum_x \norm{x}^{-2d+4}.
\]
This sum converges when $d>4$. This threshold is the one relevant to intersections of two ordinary random-walk ranges and is the upper critical dimension for self-avoiding walk.

section_title: Branching random walk and the upper critical dimension
text:
For percolation, however, the cluster is not just a single random-walk path. It has branching structure, and the relevant diagram for the susceptibility of intersections is the triangle diagram
\[
  \sum_{x,y}\tau(0,x)\tau(x,y)\tau(y,0).
\]
If $\tau(0,x)$ is approximated by the Green function $\norm{x}^{-d+2}$, then this diagram has the same scaling as the convolution cube of the Green function at the origin. A Fourier-space calculation says that near $k=0$ the random-walk Green function behaves like $\norm{k}^{-2}$, so the triangle behaves like
\[
  \int_{\norm{k}\leq 1}\norm{k}^{-6}\,\dd k,
\]
which converges exactly when $d>6$. This is the diagrammatic source of the upper critical dimension for percolation.

section_title: Branching random walk and the upper critical dimension
text: The heuristic should be read in both directions. If $d>6$, the triangle diagram is predicted to be finite, and finiteness of the triangle diagram is precisely the robust condition that implies mean-field critical exponents. If $d<6$, the diagram is predicted to diverge, meaning that the naive branching-random-walk approximation counts too many configurations and ignores important geometric correlations. At $d=6$, the integral diverges logarithmically, leading to the expectation of logarithmic corrections.

Ghost fields give a useful way to turn cluster-size information into differentiable generating functions. Given a percolation configuration, independently declare each vertex to be green with probability $1-e^{-h}$. Write $0\leftrightarrow \mathcal G$ for the event that the cluster of the origin contains at least one green vertex, and set
\[
  M_p(h)=\P_{p,h}(0\leftrightarrow \mathcal G)
  =\E_p\left[1-e^{-h|K_0|}\right].
\]
The function $M_p(h)$ is a regularized version of the cluster-size distribution. Tauberian reasoning says that if
\[
  \P_{p_c}(|K_0|\geq n)\as n^{-1/\delta},
\]
then
\[
  M_{p_c}(h)\as h^{1/\delta}
\]
as $h\downarrow 0$, at least at the exponent level.

For the binary tree the recursion is explicit. Let $\theta(p,h)$ denote the probability that the root cluster intersects the ghost field. The root either is green, or it is not green and connects to a green vertex through at least one of its two child subtrees. Since each child edge is open with probability $p$ and the two subtrees are independent,
\[
  \theta
  =
  1-e^{-h}
  +
  e^{-h}\left[1-(1-p\theta)^2\right].
\]
Equivalently,
\[
  \theta
  =
  1-e^{-h}
  +
  e^{-h}(2p\theta-p^2\theta^2).
\]
At $h=0$, the non-zero solution appears precisely when $p>1/2$, and one obtains
\[
  \theta(p,0)=\frac{2p-1}{p^2}\,\1_{\{p>1/2\}}.
\]
Thus $\beta=1$ on the tree. At $p=1/2$, the same quadratic gives
\[
  \theta(1/2,h)\as h^{1/2},
\]
which, by Tauberian theory, is equivalent at the exponent level to
\[
  \P_{1/2}(|K|\geq n)\as n^{-1/2}.
\]

The advantage of the ghost-field formulation is that it survives when no exact recursion exists. The quantity
\[
  M_p(h)=\E_p[1-e^{-h|K_0|}]
\]
is differentiable in $h$, and in finite volume it is differentiable in $p$. Its derivatives can be written in terms of cluster moments and pivotal events. For example,
\[
  \partial_h M_p(h)=\E_p\left[|K_0|e^{-h|K_0|}\right].
\]
When $h$ is of order $1/n$, this derivative sees clusters of size about $n$. This makes ghost fields a flexible substitute for exact cluster-size enumeration.

Several arguments in these notes move between a tail estimate and a Laplace-transform estimate. The analytic language for doing this cleanly is regular variation. A positive measurable function $L$ is \emph{slowly varying} if
\[
  \frac{L(\lambda x)}{L(x)}\longrightarrow 1
  \qquad\text{as }x\to\infty
\]
for every fixed $\lambda>0$. A function of the form $x^\alpha L(x)$ is called regularly varying with index $\alpha$.

The basic examples are powers multiplied by logarithmic corrections:
\[
  x^\alpha,\qquad
  x^\alpha(\log x)^a,\qquad
  x^\alpha(\log x)^a(\log\log x)^b.
\]
Regular variation is the right class because it is stable under the integrations and moment transformations that arise in percolation.

\begin{theorem}[Karamata's Tauberian theorem; quoted analytic input, informal normalization]
Let $X$ be a nonnegative random variable and let $0<a<1$. If
\[
  \P(X\geq n)\sim n^{-a}L(n)
\]
with $L$ slowly varying, then
\[
  \E[1-e^{-hX}]
  \sim
  \Gamma(1-a) h^a L(1/h)
\]
as $h\downarrow 0$, up to the normalization convention for continuous versus lattice tails. Conversely, the corresponding Laplace-transform asymptotic implies the tail asymptotic under the usual regular-variation hypotheses.
\end{theorem}

The constant can be remembered from the elementary identity
\[
  \E[1-e^{-hX}]
  =
  h\int_0^\infty e^{-ht}\P(X>t)\,\dd t
\]
valid for nonnegative $X$. If $\P(X>t)\sim t^{-a}L(t)$, then the change of variables $u=ht$ turns the leading term into
\[
  h^aL(1/h)\int_0^\infty e^{-u}u^{-a}\,\dd u
  =
  \Gamma(1-a)h^aL(1/h).
\]

For exponent computations the constants are less important than the power. Thus
\[
  \P(X\geq n)\as n^{-a}
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \E[1-e^{-hX}]\as h^a
\]
at the level of regularly varying power laws. Applied to $X=|K_0|$, this is the bridge between the cluster-volume exponent $\delta$ and the ghost-field magnetization:
\[
  \Pc(|K_0|\geq n)\as n^{-1/\delta}
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  M_{p_c}(h)\as h^{1/\delta}.
\]

For cluster volumes, assume that below criticality
\[
  \Pp(|K_0|\geq n)
  \approx
  n^{-1/\delta} f(n/\zeta(p)),
\]
where $f$ decays rapidly at infinity and
\[
  \zeta(p)\approx |p-p_c|^{-\Delta}.
\]
The scale $\zeta(p)$ is called the \emph{gap scale}, and $\Delta$ is the \emph{gap exponent}. Under this ansatz,
\[
  \chi(p)=\Ep |K_0|
  =
  \sum_{n\geq 0}\Pp(|K_0|\geq n)
  \approx
  \sum_{n\leq \zeta(p)} n^{-1/\delta}
  \approx
  \zeta(p)^{(\delta-1)/\delta}.
\]
Comparing with $\chi(p)\approx |p-p_c|^{-\gamma}$ gives
\[
  \gamma=\frac{\delta-1}{\delta}\Delta.
\]

The same ansatz predicts the growth of higher moments:
\[
  \Ep |K_0|^m
  \approx
  \chi(p)\zeta(p)^{m-1}
  \approx
  |p-p_c|^{-\gamma-(m-1)\Delta}.
\]
This is one reason moment ratios are a natural way to define the gap scale rigorously. A common subcritical definition is
\[
  \zeta(p)=\frac{\Ep |K_0|^2}{\Ep |K_0|}.
\]
This is the expected size of $K_0$ under the size-biased cluster law
\[
  \widehat \Ep[F(K_0)]
  =
  \frac{\Ep[F(K_0)|K_0|]}{\Ep |K_0|}.
\]
Other ratios, such as $\Ep |K_0|^3/\Ep |K_0|^2$, are also plausible; proving that all such definitions have the same asymptotics is itself a nontrivial part of scaling theory.

Above criticality, if the finite-cluster distribution is cut off at the same scale, then
\[
  \theta(p)
  =
  \Pp(|K_0|=\infty)
  \approx
  \Pc(|K_0|\geq \zeta(p))
  \approx
  \zeta(p)^{-1/\delta}.
\]
Thus
\[
  \beta=\frac{\Delta}{\delta}.
\]
On the binary tree $\Delta=2$ and $\delta=2$, recovering $\beta=1$ and $\gamma=1$.

There is an analogous ansatz for the two-point function. Below criticality one expects a correlation length $\xi(p)$ such that
\[
  \tau_p(0,x)\approx \norm{x}^{-d+2-\eta} g(\norm{x}/\xi(p)),
\]
where $g$ decays rapidly at infinity. A nearest-neighbour benchmark definition is
\[
  \xi(p)
  =
  \left[
  \lim_{n\to\infty}
  -\frac1n\log \tau_p(0,(n,0,\ldots,0))
  \right]^{-1}.
\]
This definition records the exponential decay rate of the two-point function in a coordinate direction. It is not always the right definition for long-range models, but it is useful for short-range percolation. If
\[
  \xi(p)\approx |p-p_c|^{-\nu},
\]
then summing the two-point ansatz over a ball of radius $\xi(p)$ gives
\[
  \chi(p)
  =
  \sum_x \tau_p(0,x)
  \approx
  \sum_{\norm{x}\leq \xi(p)} \norm{x}^{-d+2-\eta}
  \approx
  \xi(p)^{2-\eta},
\]
and therefore
\[
  \gamma=(2-\eta)\nu.
\]
\section{The incipient infinite cluster}

Before turning to hyperscaling, it is helpful to revisit the tree from a conditioning point of view. Critical clusters are almost surely finite in the regimes where the critical point is understood, but one can still ask what a typical large critical cluster looks like. One way to do so is to condition the cluster to reach a large distance and then take a weak limit. The limiting object, when it exists, is called the \emph{incipient infinite cluster} (IIC).

On the binary tree this can be computed directly. Let $L_r$ be the set of vertices at level $r$ and let
\[
  B_r=L_0\cup L_1\cup\cdots\cup L_r.
\]
At $p_c=1/2$, the expected number of cluster vertices at each level is one, so
\[
  \E_{p_c}|K\cap B_r|=r+1.
\]
The survival probability to level $r$ is $Q_r\as r^{-1}$. Hence conditioning on survival to level $r$ makes the expected mass in the next block of $r$ levels of order
\[
  \E_{p_c}\bigl[|K\cap (B_{2r}\setminus B_r)|\mid 0\leftrightarrow L_r\bigr]
  \geq
  \frac{\E_{p_c}|K\cap (B_{2r}\setminus B_r)|}{Q_r}
  \as r^2.
\]
The inequality is crude but captures the right scale: conditioning on long survival size-biases the cluster.

More explicitly, fix $r$ and condition on survival to a much larger level $R$. If $|K\cap L_r|=k$, then there are $k$ opportunities to survive from level $r$ to level $R$. Since $Q_{R-r}/Q_R\to 1$ as $R\to\infty$, one obtains heuristically, and rigorously with a Bonferroni correction,
\[
  \P_{p_c}(|K\cap L_r|=k\mid 0\leftrightarrow L_R)
  \longrightarrow
  k\,\P_{p_c}(|K\cap L_r|=k).
\]
No extra normalization is needed because $\E_{p_c}|K\cap L_r|=1$. Thus the IIC level law is the size-biased level law. In particular,
\[
  \E_{\mathrm{IIC}}|K\cap L_r|
  =
  \E_{p_c}|K\cap L_r|^2.
\]
Computing the second moment by summing over pairs of vertices and grouping according to their most recent common ancestor gives
\[
  \E_{p_c}|K\cap L_r|^2\as r.
\]
Summing over levels yields
\[
  \E_{\mathrm{IIC}}|K\cap B_r|\as r^2.
\]
This is another manifestation of the intrinsic dimension-two picture.

Hyperscaling begins with a finite-box picture. Let
\[
  \Lambda_r=[-r,r]^d\cap\Z^d.
\]
At criticality, let $V(r)$ denote the typical volume of a large cluster in $\Lambda_r$, and let $N(r)$ denote the number of such large clusters. Write
\[
  V(r)\approx r^{d_f},
  \qquad
  N(r)\approx r^\kappa.
\]
Here $d_f$ is the fractal dimension of a typical large cluster, while $\kappa$ measures the proliferation of large clusters in the box. The low-dimensional hyperscaling regime corresponds to $\kappa=0$: only order-one many macroscopic clusters are relevant. In high dimensions one expects $\kappa>0$: the box contains a whole soup of large clusters.

This is the most useful finite-volume diagnostic for the change of dimension. In low dimensions the number of large clusters on a fixed macroscopic scale should be tight as $r\to\infty$, and this order-one picture is what makes hyperscaling plausible: two distant macroscopic clusters have a serious chance to find one another through the surrounding annulus. In high dimensions the number of large clusters grows with the scale, and the clusters behave more like independent branching-random-walk objects moving through the same box without usually coalescing. In the short-range mean-field regime this number is of order $r^{d-6}$. Thus $d=6$ is not just the dimension at which a diagram becomes marginal; it is also the unique dimension at which the mean-field exponents are compatible with the order-one large-cluster picture.

The main contribution to the $m$th moment of $|K_0\cap\Lambda_r|$ should come from the event that the origin lies in one of these typical large clusters. Since the origin is a typical point of the box, that probability is approximately
\[
  \frac{N(r)V(r)}{r^d}.
\]
Therefore
\[
  \E_{p_c}|K_0\cap\Lambda_r|^m
  \approx
  V(r)^m \frac{N(r)V(r)}{r^d}
  \approx
  r^{(m+1)d_f+\kappa-d}.
\]

Taking $m=1$ gives a relation with the two-point exponent. Indeed,
\[
  \E_{p_c}|K_0\cap\Lambda_r|
  =
  \sum_{x\in\Lambda_r}\tau_{p_c}(0,x)
  \approx
  \sum_{\norm{x}\leq r}\norm{x}^{-d+2-\eta}
  \approx
  r^{2-\eta}.
\]
On the other hand the finite-box cluster heuristic gives
\[
  \E_{p_c}|K_0\cap\Lambda_r|
  \approx
  r^{2d_f+\kappa-d}.
\]
Hence
\[
  2-\eta=2d_f+\kappa-d.
\]
In the low-dimensional regime $\kappa=0$, this becomes
\[
  2-\eta=2d_f-d.
\]

The same picture gives the volume-tail exponent. The heuristic is that the best way to have $|K_0|$ of order $V(r)$ is for the origin to lie in one of the typical large clusters in $\Lambda_r$. Thus
\[
  \Pc(|K_0|\geq V(r))
  \approx
  \frac{N(r)V(r)}{r^d}
  \approx
  r^{d_f+\kappa-d}.
\]
Since $V(r)\approx r^{d_f}$, this says
\[
  \Pc(|K_0|\geq n)
  \approx
  n^{(d_f+\kappa-d)/d_f},
\]
and therefore
\[
  \delta=\frac{d_f}{d-d_f-\kappa}.
\]
In the low-dimensional regime this reduces to
\[
  \delta=\frac{d_f}{d-d_f}.
\]
Combining this with $2-\eta=2d_f-d$ gives the familiar hyperscaling relation
\[
  2-\eta=d\frac{\delta-1}{\delta+1}.
\]

There is also a one-arm version. Suppose
\[
  \Pc(0\leftrightarrow \partial\Lambda_r)\approx r^{-1/\rho}.
\]
In low dimensions, if two points $x$ and $y$ at distance $r$ each connect to macroscopic clusters on scale $r$, those macroscopic clusters have order-one probability to merge through the surrounding annulus. This suggests
\[
  \tau_{p_c}(x,y)\approx r^{-2/\rho}.
\]
Comparing with $\tau_{p_c}(x,y)\approx r^{-d+2-\eta}$ gives
\[
  d-2+\eta=\frac2\rho.
\]
Equivalently, since a cluster reaching distance $r$ has volume about $r^{d_f}$,
\[
  d_f=d-\frac1\rho
\]
in the low-dimensional regime.

The high-dimensional contrast is sharp. The lace expansion implies in sufficiently high dimensions that the Euclidean one-arm probability decays like $r^{-2}$, so $\rho=1/2$ in our convention, while
\[
  \tau_{p_c}(0,x)\as \norm{x}^{-d+2}.
\]
If the low-dimensional one-arm hyperscaling argument were valid, it would predict $r^{-4}$ for the two-point function, which agrees with $r^{-d+2}$ only at $d=6$. Above six dimensions, connecting to the correct scale is much easier than connecting to a particular distant point, because there are many large clusters at that scale and most of them do not merge.

In high dimensions the expected values are
\[
  d_f=4,
  \qquad
  \kappa=d-6.
\]
The value $d_f=4$ comes from embedding an intrinsic critical tree, whose volume-radius relation is $n\sim r_{\mathrm{int}}^2$, by random-walk displacement, where Euclidean distance is of order $r_{\mathrm{int}}^{1/2}$. Thus Euclidean radius $r$ corresponds to intrinsic radius $r^2$ and volume $r^4$. The exponent $\kappa=d-6$ records the number of such large clusters in a box of side length $r$.

The preceding relations give a quick way to identify the upper critical dimension. If mean-field exponents hold and hyperscaling remains valid at the boundary, then plugging $\delta=2$ and $\eta=0$ into
\[
  2-\eta=d\frac{\delta-1}{\delta+1}
\]
gives
\[
  2=\frac d3,
\]
so
\[
  d_c=6.
\]
This calculation is not a proof that $6$ is the critical dimension; rather, it explains why all the independent heuristics agree. The branching-random-walk triangle diagram changes behaviour at $6$, hyperscaling with mean-field exponents is consistent only at $6$, and the high-dimensional box picture has $\kappa=d-6$.

At the critical dimension itself, one expects powers to take their mean-field values but to be modified by logarithmic factors. In the finite-box language, $N(r)$ should grow like a power of $\log r$ rather than a power of $r$. This is one reason marginal dimensions are hard: leading power counting no longer identifies the answer, and second-order terms in renormalization or diagrammatic inequalities become decisive.

section_title: Universal tightness as a rigorous substitute
text: The finite-box heuristics above rely on phrases such as ``typical large cluster'' and ``number of large clusters''. Universal tightness theorems are one rigorous way to replace these phrases by inequalities. The general setup is to choose a finite domain $\Lambda$ and a typical scale $M(\Lambda)$ for the largest critical cluster, often an $e^{-1}$-median or median-like quantity. One then proves upper-tail, lower-tail, and moment bounds showing that the largest cluster is not spread over many incomparable scales.

section_title: Universal tightness as a rigorous substitute
text:
A convenient definition, used in the later long-range references, is the following. For a finite vertex set $\Lambda$, let $K_{\max}(\Lambda)$ be the largest open cluster contained in or intersecting $\Lambda$ according to the convention at hand, and define the typical value
\[
  M_\beta(\Lambda)
  =
  \min\{m\geq 0:\Pb(|K_{\max}(\Lambda)|\geq m)\leq e^{-1}\}.
\]
This is an $e^{-1}$-median-type normalization: replacing $e^{-1}$ by any other fixed probability bounded away from $0$ and $1$ only changes constants.

section_title: Universal tightness as a rigorous substitute
text:
A schematic form of universal tightness is
\[
  \P(|K_{\max}(\Lambda)|\geq \lambda M(\Lambda))\leq C\lambda^{-a},
\]
together with lower-tail estimates saying that the largest cluster is unlikely to be much smaller than its typical scale, and moment estimates comparable to powers of $M(\Lambda)$. The exact statements require care: the right normalizing quantity is not always the expectation, and the lower-tail formulation is more delicate than the upper-tail one.

We now begin the rigorous part of the book. The first theorem says that the phase transition is sharp: below criticality, clusters have exponential volume tails, while above criticality, the infinite cluster appears at least linearly in the distance from criticality.

It is convenient to work in the weighted $\beta$ parametrization. Let $G=(V,E,J)$ be a transitive weighted graph, with $J(e)\geq 0$ and
\[
  |J|=\sum_{x\in V}J(o,x)<\infty
\]
for a fixed origin $o$. An edge $e$ is open with probability
\[
  1-e^{-\beta J(e)}.
\]
For nearest-neighbour percolation with $J\equiv 1$, this is the same as the usual parameter $p=1-e^{-\beta}$. The exponential parametrization is useful because independent configurations at intensities $\beta_1J$ and $\beta_2J$ have union distributed as intensity $(\beta_1+\beta_2)J$. The integrability assumption gives the elementary lower bound $\beta_c\geq |J|^{-1}>0$: when $\beta |J|<1$, the cluster exploration is dominated by a subcritical branching process with mean $\beta |J|$.

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness of the phase transition]
Let $G=(V,E,J)$ be a transitive integrable weighted graph, and let $K=K_o$ be the cluster of the origin.

If $\beta<\beta_c$, then there exists $c_\beta>0$ such that
\[
  \Pb(|K|\geq n)\leq e^{-c_\beta n}
\]
for every $n\geq 1$. In particular $\Eb |K|<\infty$.

If $\beta>\beta_c$, then there is a constant $c>0$ such that
\[
  \Pb(o\leftrightarrow\infty)
  \geq
  c\bigl((\beta-\beta_c)\wedge 1\bigr).
\]
In the normalization used below, the proof gives the explicit lower bound
\[
  \Pb(o\leftrightarrow\infty)\geq \frac{\beta-\beta_c}{\beta}
\]
for $\beta>\beta_c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the subcritical half]
The proof below follows the Duminil-Copin--Tassion strategy. For a finite set $S\subseteq V$ containing $o$, define
\[
  \varphi_\beta(S)
  =
  \sum_{e\in\partial_E S}
  \bigl(1-e^{-\beta J(e)}\bigr)
  \Pb(o\stackrel S\leftrightarrow e^-).
\]
Here $\partial_E S$ is the set of oriented boundary edges with $e^-\in S$ and $e^+\notin S$, and
\[
  o\stackrel S\leftrightarrow e^-
\]
means that $o$ is connected to $e^-$ by an open path using only vertices of $S$. Define
\[
  \widetilde\beta_c
  =
  \inf\{\beta:\varphi_\beta(S)\geq 1
  \text{ for every finite }S\ni o\}.
\]
The proof has two parts:
\[
  \Eb |K|<\infty\quad\text{for }\beta<\widetilde\beta_c
\]
and
\[
  \Pb(o\leftrightarrow\infty)
  \geq
  \frac{\beta-\widetilde\beta_c}{\beta}
  \quad\text{for }\beta>\widetilde\beta_c.
\]
These imply $\widetilde\beta_c=\beta_c$ and hence sharpness.

Assume first that $\beta<\widetilde\beta_c$. Then there is a finite $S\ni o$ with $\varphi_\beta(S)<1$. For $x\notin S$, if $o\leftrightarrow x$, the connection must exit $S$ through some boundary edge $e$. Revealing the cluster of $o$ inside $S$ gives
\[
  \Pb(o\leftrightarrow x)
  \leq
  \sum_{e\in\partial_E S}
  \Pb(o\stackrel S\leftrightarrow e^-)
  \Pb(e\text{ open})
  \Pb(e^+\leftrightarrow x).
\]
Summing over $x$ suggests
\[
  \Eb |K|
  \leq
  |S|+\varphi_\beta(S)\Eb |K|.
\]
If $\Eb |K|$ were already known to be finite, this would prove
\[
  \Eb |K|\leq \frac{|S|}{1-\varphi_\beta(S)}.
\]
But the argument is circular: the whole point is to prove finite susceptibility.

The repair is to introduce a ghost field. Let $\mathcal G$ be an independent random subset of vertices in which each vertex is green with probability $1-e^{-h}$. Then
\[
  \P_{\beta,h}(o\leftrightarrow\mathcal G)
  =
  \Eb[1-e^{-h|K|}]
\]
is finite and bounded by one. The same exploration argument yields
\[
  \P_{\beta,h}(o\leftrightarrow \mathcal G\setminus S)
  \leq
  \varphi_\beta(S)\P_{\beta,h}(o\leftrightarrow\mathcal G).
\]
Consequently
\[
  \P_{\beta,h}(o\leftrightarrow\mathcal G)
  \leq
  \varphi_\beta(S)\P_{\beta,h}(o\leftrightarrow\mathcal G)
  +
  \P(\mathcal G\cap S\neq\varnothing).
\]
Since $\P(\mathcal G\cap S\neq\varnothing)\leq 1-e^{-h|S|}$, we may safely rearrange:
\[
  \P_{\beta,h}(o\leftrightarrow\mathcal G)
  \leq
  \frac{1-e^{-h|S|}}{1-\varphi_\beta(S)}.
\]
Dividing by $h$ and letting $h\downarrow0$ gives
\[
  \Eb |K|
  \leq
  \frac{|S|}{1-\varphi_\beta(S)}<\infty.
\]
A sharper version replaces $|S|$ by the expected number of vertices connected to $o$ inside $S$:
\[
  \Eb |K|
  \leq
  \frac{\Eb[\#\{x\in S:o\stackrel S\leftrightarrow x\}]}
  {1-\varphi_\beta(S)}.
\]
This numerator is the finite-volume precursor of a correlation length. On $\Z^d$ one can define a subcritical length scale by the least $r$ for which $\varphi_\beta([-r,r]^d)\leq 1/2$.
\end{proof}

section_title: Russo formulae and the supercritical bound
text:
Russo's formula expresses derivatives in terms of pivotal edges. In the weighted parametrization, if $F$ depends on finitely many edges, then
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\Eb F(\omega)
  =
  \sum_e J(e)\,
  \Eb\bigl[F(\omega\cup\{e\})-F(\omega)\bigr].
\]
For an increasing event $A$ this becomes
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\Pb(A)
  =
  \sum_e J(e)\Pb(e\text{ is closed pivotal for }A).
\]
For infinite-volume events, one usually applies this in finite volume and then passes to one-sided derivatives or integrated inequalities.

section_title: Russo formulae and the supercritical bound
text:
\begin{proof}[Proof of the supercritical half of sharpness]
Let $\Lambda\subset V$ be finite and contain $o$, and consider the event $\{o\leftrightarrow\Lambda^c\}$. Define the random set
\[
  S=\{x\in\Lambda:x\not\leftrightarrow\Lambda^c\}.
\]
This is the region cut off from the exterior. Conditional on $S$, the edges with both endpoints in $S$ retain their Bernoulli product law. To see this, explore from \(\Lambda^c\) inward, revealing the open clusters touching the exterior and the closed edges on their boundary. The set \(S\) is exactly the part of \(\Lambda\) not reached by this outside exploration. No edge with both endpoints in \(S\) has been queried, so after conditioning on the outside information and on the resulting set \(S\), the internal edges of \(S\) are still independent with their original parameters.

section_title: Russo formulae and the supercritical bound
text:
An edge $e\in\partial_E S$ is closed pivotal for $\{o\leftrightarrow\Lambda^c\}$ precisely when
\[
  o\in S
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  o\stackrel S\leftrightarrow e^-.
\]
Indeed, \(e^+\) is already connected to \(\Lambda^c\) by the outside exploration. Opening \(e\) connects \(o\) to the exterior exactly when \(o\) is connected to \(e^-\) inside \(S\); without that internal connection, opening \(e\) cannot change the event.
Russo's formula gives
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\Pb(o\leftrightarrow\Lambda^c)
  =
  \Eb\left[
  \1_{\{o\in S\}}
  \sum_{e\in\partial_E S}J(e)\1_{\{o\stackrel S\leftrightarrow e^-\}}
  \right].
\]
Conditioning on the random set $S$, the edges inside $S$ still have their product law, so
\[
  \Eb\!\left[
    \1_{\{o\stackrel S\leftrightarrow e^-\}}\mid S
  \right]
  =
  \Pb(o\stackrel S\leftrightarrow e^-).
\]
Since
\[
  J(e)\geq \frac{1-e^{-\beta J(e)}}{\beta},
\]
and since $\varphi_\beta(S)\geq 1$ for every finite $S\ni o$ when $\beta>\widetilde\beta_c$, we obtain
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\Pb(o\leftrightarrow\Lambda^c)
  \geq
  \frac1\beta\Pb(o\not\leftrightarrow\Lambda^c).
\]
Writing $f_\Lambda(\beta)=\Pb(o\leftrightarrow\Lambda^c)$, this is
\[
  f_\Lambda'(\beta)\geq \frac1\beta(1-f_\Lambda(\beta)).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
  (\beta f_\Lambda(\beta))'\geq 1.
\]
Integrating from $\widetilde\beta_c$ to $\beta$ gives
\[
  f_\Lambda(\beta)\geq \frac{\beta-\widetilde\beta_c}{\beta}.
\]
Letting $\Lambda$ exhaust the graph yields
\[
  \Pb(o\leftrightarrow\infty)
  \geq
  \frac{\beta-\widetilde\beta_c}{\beta}.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Harris-FKG inequality]
If $A$ and $B$ are increasing events depending on independent Bernoulli variables, then
\[
  \P(A\cap B)\geq \P(A)\P(B).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The functional form says that if $F$ and $G$ are nonnegative increasing functions, then
\[
  \E[FG]\geq \E[F]\E[G].
\]
For one Bernoulli coordinate this follows from the identity
\[
  \E[FG]-\E[F]\E[G]
  =
  \frac12\E\otimes\E
  \bigl[(F(\omega)-F(\omega'))(G(\omega)-G(\omega'))\bigr],
\]
whose integrand is nonnegative when $F$ and $G$ are increasing. The
finite-dimensional theorem follows by induction, conditioning on one
coordinate at a time. Suppose the result is known for \(n-1\) coordinates and
write
\[
  F_1(t)=\E[F\mid \omega(e_1)=t],
  \qquad
  G_1(t)=\E[G\mid \omega(e_1)=t],
\]
and
\[
  H_1(t)=\E[FG\mid \omega(e_1)=t].
\]
The conditional expectations \(F_1\) and \(G_1\) are increasing functions of
the remaining value \(t\): conditioning an increasing function on one
coordinate preserves monotonicity. By the induction hypothesis applied to the
remaining \(n-1\) coordinates,
\[
  H_1(t)\geq F_1(t)G_1(t).
\]
Taking expectations in \(t\) and applying the one-coordinate case to
\(F_1\) and \(G_1\) gives
\[
  \E[FG]\geq \E[F_1G_1]\geq \E F_1\,\E G_1=\E F\,\E G.
\]
For infinitely many coordinates, first truncate \(F\) and \(G\) to make them
bounded, enumerate the edges, and set
\[
  F_n=\E[F\mid \omega(e_1),\ldots,\omega(e_n)],
  \qquad
  G_n=\E[G\mid \omega(e_1),\ldots,\omega(e_n)].
\]
These conditional expectations are increasing cylinder functions. The
finite theorem gives
\[
  \E[F_nG_n]\geq\E F_n\,\E G_n,
\]
and martingale convergence lets \(n\to\infty\).
\end{proof}
The second inequality controls disjoint occurrence. If $A$ and $B$ are increasing events, write $A\circ B$ for the event that $A$ and $B$ occur using disjoint sets of open edges as witnesses.

\begin{theorem}[BK/Reimer inequality; quoted standard input]
For increasing events $A$ and $B$ depending on finitely many Bernoulli variables,
\[
  \P(A\circ B)\leq \P(A)\P(B).
\]
\end{theorem}

For infinite edge sets there are measurability subtleties in the definition of $A\circ B$: the event involves an existential quantifier over possible witness sets. For increasing events it can be realized as an analytic set and is universally measurable; alternatively one can work with finite-witness versions and pass to limits. Reimer's theorem proves a stronger finite statement without the increasing assumption, but the increasing BK inequality is the form most often used here.

The proof of BK is substantially subtler than Harris. The following paragraph
is only a proof sketch of the finite interpolation idea, included to explain
why independent copies enter the inequality. One proof interpolates between two
independent configurations. Let \(\widehat\P=\P\otimes\P\), sample
\((\omega,\omega')\), and define
\[
  \omega_j(e_i)=
  \begin{cases}
    \omega'(e_i), & i\leq j,\\
    \omega(e_i), & i>j.
  \end{cases}
\]
Let
\[
  \widehat A_j=\{(\omega,\omega'):\omega_j\in A\},
  \qquad
  \widehat B=\{(\omega,\omega'):\omega\in B\}.
\]
Then
\[
  \widehat\P(\widehat A_0\circ \widehat B)=\P(A\circ B).
\]
The two claims are
\[
  \widehat\P(\widehat A_j\circ\widehat B)
  \leq
  \widehat\P(\widehat A_{j+1}\circ\widehat B)
\]
for every \(j\), and
\[
  \limsup_{j\to\infty}
  \widehat\P(\widehat A_j\circ\widehat B)
  \leq
  \P(A)\P(B).
\]
The limit claim follows because \(\omega_j\) depends on \(\omega'\) on all
coordinates relevant to \(A\) once \(j\) is large, while \(\widehat B\) still
depends on \(\omega\); cylinder events are then handled exactly and general
events by approximation. For the monotonicity claim, condition on all bits
except the \(j\)th pair. There are three cases: disjoint occurrence is
impossible whatever those two bits are; it is forced whatever those bits are;
or the \(j\)th edge is genuinely used by one of the two witnesses. In the
last case, if the edge is used for the \(A\)-witness, moving it from
\(\omega\) to \(\omega'\) preserves the \(A\)-witness with the same marginal
probability; if it is used for the \(B\)-witness, the symmetric statement
holds with \(\omega\). Since \(\omega(e_j)\) and \(\omega'(e_j)\) have the
same Bernoulli law, the conditional probability cannot decrease. Iterating this
monotonicity is the heart of the finite proof and leads to
\[
  \P(A\circ B)\leq \P(A)\P(B).
\]
In applications, the takeaway is that an event requiring disjoint open structures can be bounded by the product of the probabilities of those structures.

For $k\geq2$, define the $k$-point function
\[
  \tau_\beta(x_1,\ldots,x_k)
  =
  \Pb(x_1,\ldots,x_k\text{ all lie in the same open cluster}).
\]
Tree-graph inequalities bound multi-point connection probabilities by sums over products of two-point functions.

\begin{prop}[Tree-graph and moment inequalities; proved here from BK]
For every \(k\geq2\),
\[
  \tau_\beta(x_1,\ldots,x_k)
  \leq
  \sum_{T\in\mathcal T_k}
  \sum_{x_{k+1},\ldots,x_{2k-2}}
  \prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(T)}\tau_\beta(x_i,x_j),
\]
where \(\mathcal T_k\) is a set of leaf-labelled binary trees with leaves
\(1,\ldots,k\) and \(k-2\) unlabeled internal vertices. Consequently
\[
  \Eb |K|^m
  \leq
  (2m-3)!!\,\chi(\beta)^{2m-1},
  \qquad m\geq 1.
\]
\end{prop}

\begin{proof}
Let us prove the proposition in the first few cases, since these are the
ones that recur in the later diagrammatic estimates. For three points,
\[
  \tau_\beta(x,y,z)
  \leq
  \sum_w
  \tau_\beta(x,w)\tau_\beta(y,w)\tau_\beta(z,w).
\]
Indeed, if $x,y,z$ are connected, take an open path from $x$ to $y$ and an open path from $x$ to $z$, and let $w$ be the last intersection point of these two paths before the second path goes to $z$. Then there are disjoint open connections from $w$ to $x$, $y$, and $z$. Taking a union over $w$ and applying BK gives the inequality.

Summing the three-point inequality over $x$ and $y$ yields
\[
  \Eb |K|^2
  =
  \sum_{x,y}\tau_\beta(o,x,y)
  \leq
  \sum_{w,x,y}
  \tau_\beta(o,w)\tau_\beta(w,x)\tau_\beta(w,y)
  =
  \chi(\beta)^3.
\]
For four points there are three possible binary tree topologies, and summing gives
\[
  \Eb |K|^3\leq 3\chi(\beta)^5.
\]

These moment bounds imply exponential tails whenever $\chi(\beta)<\infty$. Indeed, summing the moment estimates gives, for $r<1/(2\chi(\beta)^2)$,
\[
  \Eb[|K|e^{r|K|}]
  \leq
  \chi(\beta)\bigl(1-2r\chi(\beta)^2\bigr)^{-1/2}.
\]
Choosing $r$ of order $\chi(\beta)^{-2}$ and applying Markov's inequality gives
\[
  \Pb(|K|\geq n)\leq e^{-c_\beta n}
\]
for $\beta<\beta_c$. This completes the exponential-tail part of sharpness.
\end{proof}

Tree-graph inequalities also give a universal lower bound on the critical
volume tail in integrated form.

\begin{prop}[Aizenman--Barsky integrated lower tail; proved here from sharpness and tree-graph bounds]
For every transitive weighted graph with \(\chi(\beta)<\infty\) for
\(\beta<\beta_c\),
\[
  \E_{\beta_c}[|K|\wedge N]
  =
  \sum_{n=1}^N \P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)
  \geq
  cN^{1/2}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(N\), with \(c>0\) depending on the graph.
\end{prop}

\begin{proof}
Let
\[
  \zeta(\beta)=\frac{\Eb |K|^2}{\Eb |K|}.
\]
The tree-graph bound gives $\zeta(\beta)\leq \chi(\beta)^2$. If $X$ is a nonnegative random variable, then under the size-biased law,
\[
  \widehat\E F(X)=\frac{\E[XF(X)]}{\E X},
\]
Markov's inequality gives
\[
  \E\left[X\1_{\{X\leq 2\E X^2/\E X\}}\right]\geq \frac12\E X.
\]
Applying this to $X=|K|$ under $\Pb$ gives
\[
  \Eb[|K|\wedge 2\zeta(\beta)]\geq \frac12\chi(\beta).
\]
By monotonicity,
\[
  \E_{\beta_c}[|K|\wedge 2\zeta(\beta)]
  \geq
  \frac12\chi(\beta)
  \geq
  \frac12\sqrt{\zeta(\beta)}.
\]
As $\beta\uparrow\beta_c$, sharpness gives $\chi(\beta)\uparrow\infty$, and hence $\zeta(\beta)\to\infty$ along the same limit. Moreover, below criticality all cluster-size moments vary continuously, indeed real analytically, in \(\beta\): exponential tails give a uniformly summable expansion over finite clusters on compact subintervals of \([0,\beta_c)\). Thus \(\zeta(\beta)\) is continuous and unbounded below criticality. For each large \(N\), choose \(\beta<\beta_c\) with \(2\zeta(\beta)=N\). Substituting this choice gives
\[
  \E_{\beta_c}[|K|\wedge N]
  =
  \sum_{n=1}^N \P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)
  \geq
  cN^{1/2}.
\]
This proves the proposition. The bound says that the critical tail cannot be
substantially smaller than the mean-field \(n^{-1/2}\) tail on average.
Pointwise lower bounds require additional input.
\end{proof}

Let $G$ be a transitive weighted graph and write
\[
  T_\beta(x,y)=\tau_\beta(x,y)=\Pb(x\leftrightarrow y).
\]
It is useful to think of $T_\beta$ as a matrix indexed by $V\times V$. The \emph{triangle diagram} is
\[
  \nabla_\beta
  =
  \sum_{x,y\in V}T_\beta(o,x)T_\beta(x,y)T_\beta(y,o)
  =
  T_\beta^3(o,o).
\]
We say that $G$ satisfies the \emph{triangle condition} if $\nabla_{\beta_c}<\infty$.

The triangle condition is the fundamental sufficient condition for mean-field critical behaviour. It is known to hold for nearest-neighbour percolation in sufficiently high dimensions and for spread-out models above six dimensions by the lace expansion.

\begin{theorem}[Triangle-condition mean-field theorem; quoted classical theorem]
If a connected transitive weighted graph satisfies the triangle condition, with the standard integrability and unimodularity hypotheses used below, then percolation on the graph has mean-field critical behaviour in the sense that
\[
  \chi(\beta)\as (\beta_c-\beta)^{-1},\qquad
  \P_{\beta_c}(|K_0|\geq n)\as n^{-1/2},
\]
and
\[
  \theta(\beta)\as \beta-\beta_c
\]
in the appropriate near-critical regimes.
\end{theorem}

More precisely, Aizenman and Newman proved the susceptibility estimate, while Barsky and Aizenman proved the corresponding volume-tail and density estimates. Hara and Slade verified the triangle condition in high-dimensional Euclidean settings by the lace expansion. The point of this chapter is to explain the proof flow: the triangle condition supplies a reverse differential inequality for the susceptibility, and entropy comparison turns susceptibility control into the other mean-field exponents.

The status of the arguments in this chapter is as follows. The classical open-triangle proof is presented with the cluster-coupling and path-cutting estimates written out, while the localization and surgery estimates are treated as standard quoted inputs. The quantitative susceptibility inequality is proved through the boundary-susceptibility lemma, the three- and four-point diagram reductions, and the Ando--Hadamard comparison. The final passage from susceptibility to volume tails and density is carried out in the entropy chapter.

It is often useful to work with an open version of the triangle diagram. In graph-distance notation, one can define
\[
  \nabla_{\beta_c}(r)
  =
  \sup_{d(o,x)\geq r}T_{\beta_c}^3(o,x).
\]
In the classical proof one uses the technical fact that the finite triangle condition forces a corresponding open-triangle quantity to become small after sending the separation scale to infinity. We will treat this open-triangle decay as part of the standard triangle-condition theorem rather than reproving the localization argument here. A more pointwise notation is
\[
  T_\beta^3(x,y)
  =
  \sum_{u,v}\tau_\beta(x,u)\tau_\beta(u,v)\tau_\beta(v,y).
\]
The diagonal value $T_\beta^3(o,o)$ is the triangle diagram. The off-diagonal values measure the probability cost of connecting two separated macroscopic structures through three two-point links.

\begin{lemma}[Open-triangle localization from the triangle condition; quoted input]
If the triangle diagram is finite at \(\beta_c\), then the off-diagonal
three-link quantity \(T_{\beta_c}^3(u,v)\) tends to zero as the separation
between \(u\) and \(v\) tends to infinity, in the localized form needed by
the classical triangle-condition proof.
\end{lemma}

The classical proof first obtains a reverse susceptibility differential
inequality under the stronger assumption that a suitable open triangle is
strictly less than one. Then it applies the quoted localization lemma to show
that finite triangle implies such a small open triangle after passing to a
sufficiently large separation scale. The constants obtained this way can be
very poor, especially when the triangle diagram is finite but large. This
quantitative weakness is important in marginal settings, where the triangle
may diverge slowly.

A clean special case is obtained by assuming
\[
  \Delta_\beta^*=\sup_{x\neq y}T_\beta^3(x,y)
\]
is small enough that \(C\Delta_\beta^*<|J|\), where \(C\) is the constant appearing in the coupling error below. Since \(\tau_\beta\) is increasing in \(\beta\), any uniform control at \(\beta_c\) implies the corresponding subcritical control for all \(\beta<\beta_c\). The finite-triangle theorem replaces this global smallness assumption by a localization statement: after forcing the relevant endpoints to be separated by a large distance, the off-diagonal triangle becomes small.

The universal upper differential inequality is easy and does not use the triangle condition:
\[
  \chi_\beta'\leq |J|\chi_\beta^2.
\]
Indeed, by Russo's formula,
\[
  \chi_\beta'
  =
  \sum_x\sum_eJ(e)\Pb(e\text{ is closed pivotal for }o\leftrightarrow x).
\]
If $e=\{u,v\}$ is closed pivotal for $o\leftrightarrow x$, then either $o$ is connected to $u$ and $v$ is connected to $x$, or the same statement holds with $u$ and $v$ exchanged; these connections occur disjointly. BK gives
\[
  \Pb(e\text{ pivotal})
  \leq
  \tau_\beta(o,u)\tau_\beta(v,x)
  +
  \tau_\beta(o,v)\tau_\beta(u,x).
\]
Summing over $x$ and over oriented edges gives the stated bound. Integrating
\[
\left(\frac1{\chi_\beta}\right)'
=-\frac{\chi_\beta'}{\chi_\beta^2}
\]
up to $\beta_c$, where $\chi_{\beta_c}=\infty$, gives the universal mean-field lower bound
\[
  \chi_\beta\geq \frac{1}{|J|(\beta_c-\beta)}.
\]

To obtain the matching upper bound on $\chi_\beta$, one needs a lower differential inequality of the same order:
\[
  \chi_\beta'\geq c\chi_\beta^2.
\]
The triangle condition is the hypothesis that lets one prove this.
\section{Mass transport and independent clusters}

Assume now that the transitive weighted graph is unimodular. The mass-transport principle says that every diagonally invariant function $F:V\times V\to[0,\infty]$ satisfies
\[
  \sum_x F(o,x)=\sum_x F(x,o).
\]
For Cayley graphs this is just the change of variables $x\mapsto x^{-1}$ in group notation. In percolation diagrams, mass transport allows one to move the vertex pinned at the origin from one part of a diagram to another.

Using mass transport, Russo's formula for $\chi_\beta'$ can be rewritten in a form that exposes two clusters:
\[
  \chi_\beta'
  =
  \sum_{z,y,w}J(o,y)\,
  \Pb(o\leftrightarrow z,\;y\leftrightarrow w,\;o\not\leftrightarrow y).
\]
If the two clusters of $o$ and $y$ were independent and the condition $o\not\leftrightarrow y$ removed no mass, this sum would be exactly $|J|\chi_\beta^2$. The difficulty is to quantify the error made by pretending that the two clusters are independent.

The coupling argument is as follows. Sample the cluster of $o$ first. Then sample an independent candidate cluster from $y$, but give the first cluster priority: whenever the candidate exploration tries to use information already fixed by the first cluster, the coupling may fail to realize two disjoint clusters in the final percolation configuration. If there is no such failure, the events $\{o\leftrightarrow z\}$ and $\{y\leftrightarrow w\}$ occur in distinct clusters.

It is worth spelling out the coupling a little more, since this is the part of the proof that is easiest to remember incorrectly. Let \(\omega\) be the actual percolation configuration. First reveal \(K_o(\omega)\). Independently sample a second cluster \(\widetilde K_y\) with the law of \(K_y\). We now try to embed \(\widetilde K_y\) into the unrevealed part of \(\omega\). Edges whose status was not examined while discovering \(K_o\) can be coupled by using the same uniforms that define \(\omega\). If the exploration of \(\widetilde K_y\) asks for an edge whose status was already determined by the first exploration, then either the attempted cluster has hit \(K_o\) or it has asked for a closed boundary edge of \(K_o\). In both cases the attempt to realize two independent clusters inside one configuration has failed for a geometric reason that can be recorded by a first contact point. The event \(o\not\leftrightarrow y\) is therefore not discarded abstractly; it is produced by deleting precisely the cases in which this embedding attempt collides with the first cluster.

When failure occurs, some path in the second exploration hits the first cluster.
Here is the exact cutting picture. Work first with four marked vertices
\(x,y,z,w\). The independent coupling gives
\[
  \mathbb P_\beta(z\in K_x,\ w\in \widetilde K_y)
  =
  \tau_\beta(x,z)\tau_\beta(y,w).
\]
If \(y\notin K_x\) and \(w\in\widetilde K_y\) but \(w\notin K_y\) in the
real configuration, then every open path from \(y\) to \(w\) inside
\(\widetilde K_y\) has been cut by the previously explored cluster \(K_x\).
Choose such a path and let \(b\) be the first vertex of the path, starting
from \(y\), at which it meets the revealed information from \(K_x\). Now
choose a simple open path in \(K_x\) from \(x\) to \(z\). The point \(b\) is
connected inside \(K_x\) to this path; let \(a\) be the last point of the
\(x\)-to-\(z\) path visited by a chosen connection from \(b\) to that path.
Then the bad event is contained in the union over \(a,b\) of the disjoint
occurrence
\[
  \{x\leftrightarrow a\}
  \circ
  \{a\leftrightarrow z\}
  \circ
  \{a\leftrightarrow b\}
  \circ
  \{y\leftrightarrow b\}
  \circ
  \{b\leftrightarrow w\}.
\]
This is the path-cutting argument from the lecture: the failure is not caused
by the two clusters merely being close; it is caused by \(K_x\) intersecting
a path between two typical points of the second cluster.

BK then bounds the failure probability by a diagram consisting of five
two-point factors. Schematically,
\[
  \Pb(o\leftrightarrow z,\;y\leftrightarrow w,\;o\not\leftrightarrow y)
  \geq
  \tau_\beta(o,z)\tau_\beta(y,w)
  -
  \mathrm{Err}_\beta(o,y,z,w),
\]
where the error is controlled by an open-triangle diagram.
One representative form of the error is bounded by a sum of products such as
\[
  \mathrm{Err}_\beta(o,y,z,w)
  \pre
  \sum_{a,b}
  \tau_\beta(o,a)\tau_\beta(a,z)
  \tau_\beta(a,b)
  \tau_\beta(y,b)\tau_\beta(b,w),
\]
with variants depending on which path is hit first and where the split point is recorded. After summing over $z,y,w$ with the edge weight $J(o,y)$, the factors containing $z$ and $w$ produce susceptibilities while the remaining convolution is an open-triangle term. Thus the total error is bounded by
\[
  C\,\nabla_{\mathrm{open}}\,\chi_\beta^2
\]
in the small-open-triangle regime, which is the estimate used below.

A representative term in this error has the form
\[
  H_\beta(o,y,z,w)
  =
  \sum_{a,b}
  \tau_\beta(o,a)\tau_\beta(a,z)
  \tau_\beta(a,b)
  \tau_\beta(b,y)\tau_\beta(b,w).
\]
The interpretation is as follows. The vertex $a$ is the branch point in the first cluster separating the connection to $z$ from the part of the first cluster hit by the attempted second exploration. The vertex $b$ is the first hit point of the second exploration on the first cluster. The five two-point functions describe the two branches from $a$, the bridge from $a$ to $b$, and the two branches from $b$ to $y$ and $w$. The actual proof sums a finite number of such diagrams, with the roles of the endpoints and orientations interchanged, but this displayed term is the essential geometry.

The finite number of variants comes from two mundane choices rather than from new ideas. First, the edge \(\{o,y\}\) in Russo's formula is unoriented, so the cluster attached to \(o\) and the cluster attached to \(y\) may exchange roles. Second, the first contact between the attempted second exploration and the revealed information may occur at a vertex of \(K_o\), or at an edge leaving \(K_o\) whose closed status was learned during the first exploration. The latter case is handled by recording the endpoint of that boundary edge and paying one additional edge weight, which is harmless after summing because of the weighted degree bound. This is why the lecture proof can be described as a coupling with two independent clusters while the written proof becomes a small family of five-line diagrams.

After summing against $J(o,y)$ over $y,z,w$, the main term gives $|J|\chi_\beta^2$. The diagram $H_\beta$ can be estimated by first summing the two terminal branches and then recognizing an off-diagonal triangle:
\[
  \sum_{y,z,w}J(o,y)H_\beta(o,y,z,w)
  \leq
  \chi_\beta^2
  \sum_{a,b}
  \tau_\beta(o,a)\tau_\beta(a,b)
  \sum_y J(o,y)\tau_\beta(b,y),
\]
with the displayed expression standing for the representative orientation. The remaining weighted convolution is not yet an off-diagonal triangle, because in Russo's formula the endpoints \(o\) and \(y\) are adjacent in the weighted sense. The surgery step inserts a forced finite connection that moves these endpoints into well-separated boxes, after which the last display is bounded by
\[
  \sum_{y,z,w}J(o,y)H_\beta(o,y,z,w)
  \pre
  \chi_\beta^2\,
  \sup_{u\text{ far from }v}T_\beta^3(u,v)
\]
once the endpoints have been separated at the appropriate scale. This is the analytic reason the open triangle, rather than only the diagonal triangle $T_\beta^3(o,o)$, appears in the proof.

Under a small-open-triangle hypothesis, summing this estimate gives
\[
  \chi_\beta'\geq (|J|-C\nabla_{\mathrm{open}})\chi_\beta^2.
\]
If the open-triangle term is strictly smaller than the main coefficient, then
\[
  \chi_\beta'\geq c\chi_\beta^2.
\]
Integrating from $\beta$ to $\beta_c$ yields
\[
  \chi_\beta\leq \frac{C}{\beta_c-\beta}.
\]

The full finite-triangle proof adds a separation step. Define the open
triangle at scale \(r\) by
\[
  \nabla_\beta^{\mathrm{open}}(r)
  =
  \sup_{d(u,v)\geq r}T_\beta^3(u,v).
\]
The finite triangle condition implies
\[
  \nabla_{\beta_c}^{\mathrm{open}}(r)\longrightarrow0
  \qquad\text{as }r\to\infty,
\]
and hence the same is true uniformly for \(\beta<\beta_c\). Choose \(r\)
large enough that this quantity is much smaller than the main coefficient in
the lower differential inequality. A surgery argument then transfers the
estimate to the neighbouring configurations needed in Russo's formula. One
forces the two independent clusters to begin in well-separated boxes, applies
the small-open-triangle estimate at that separation, and then pays a bounded
connection cost to attach these boxes back to the original adjacent endpoints.
The finite triangle condition supplies summability of the error over all
possible surgery vertices. The price is that the constants depend on the
separation scale chosen to make the open triangle small.

This dependence is very ineffective. The localization argument says only that the off-diagonal triangle tends to zero; it does not give a usable scale at which it is small. Once that scale has been chosen, the surgery has to force a connection across a finite pattern whose probability may be exponentially small in the chosen separation. This is why the classical proof gives the right power laws but poor constants, and why the later quantitative triangle inequality is valuable.

One way to see why the open triangle becomes small is through Fourier analysis on \(\Z^d\). If \(\tau\) is translation invariant and summable enough that the triangle diagram is finite, then
\[
  \sum_{x,y}\tau(0,x)\tau(x,y)\tau(y,z)
\]
is the convolution cube \(\tau*\tau*\tau(z)\). Finiteness of the diagonal triangle says that this convolution cube is finite at the origin, or equivalently that \(\widehat\tau^3\) is integrable in the Fourier representation. The Riemann--Lebesgue lemma then implies that the off-diagonal convolution tends to zero as \(\norm{z}\to\infty\). On general transitive graphs one should not literally use this Fourier proof, but it explains the analytic meaning of the localization lemma: the finite triangle condition makes the three-link connection cost between far-separated structures vanish.
\section{A quantitative triangle inequality}
A more quantitative theorem gives a direct differential inequality in terms of the triangle diagram itself. Normalize the weights by $|J|=1$.

The theorem should be read as a quantitative replacement for the small-open-triangle argument. If $\nabla_\beta$ is bounded and $\chi_\beta$ is large, the right-hand side is of order $\chi_\beta^2$, exactly as required for mean-field susceptibility. If $\nabla_\beta$ grows slowly, the inequality still records that growth explicitly rather than hiding it in a large separation scale.

The proof has three inputs, each of which is useful in its own right. The first is a boundary-susceptibility lemma that does not require transitivity. For a finite set $S$, define
\[
  \Phi_\beta(S)
  =
  \sum_{e\in\partial_E^\rightarrow S}
  \sum_{v\notin S}
  J_e\,\Pb(e^+\leftrightarrow v\text{ off }S).
\]
Here $\partial_E^\rightarrow S$ is the set of oriented boundary edges with $e^-\in S$ and $e^+\notin S$, and ``off \(S\)'' means that the connecting path is not allowed to visit \(S\). Thus $\Phi_\beta(S)$ measures how much susceptibility is available outside \(S\) after crossing one boundary edge. It is the right object because Russo's formula for the derivative of \(\chi_\beta\) naturally explores a cluster and then asks how much new mass can be reached by opening an edge leaving it.

\begin{lemma}[Boundary susceptibility lower bound]
Let \(G=(V,E,J)\) be a countable weighted graph normalized so that
\[
  \sup_{v\in V}\sum_{e\in E_v^\rightarrow}J_e\leq 1.
\]
Let
\[
  \chi_\beta^{\min}=\inf_{v\in V}\E_\beta|K_v|,
  \qquad
  \chi_\beta^{\max}=\sup_{v\in V}\E_\beta|K_v|.
\]
Then for every finite set \(S\subseteq V\) and every \(\beta>0\),
\[
  \Phi_\beta(S)
  \geq
  \frac{
    \left(\chi_\beta^{\min}|S|-\sum_{u,v\in S}T_\beta(u,v)\right)^2
  }{
    \beta^2\chi_\beta^{\max}
    \sum_{u,v,w\in S}T_\beta(u,v)T_\beta(u,w)
  }.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let us spell out why this lemma has the shape it does. The amount of susceptibility leaving \(S\) is bounded below by
\[
  \sum_{u\in S}\sum_{w\notin S}T_\beta(u,w)
  \geq
  \chi_\beta^{\min}|S|
  -
  \sum_{u,v\in S}T_\beta(u,v),
\]
since the full susceptibility from each \(u\in S\) is at least
\(\chi_\beta^{\min}\), and the only contribution not leaving \(S\) is the
sum over \(v\in S\). We now give an upper bound on the same quantity. If
\(u\in S\) and \(w\notin S\) are connected, then the last edge by which a
simple open path from \(u\) to \(w\) leaves \(S\) gives a disjoint occurrence
\[
  \{u\leftrightarrow e^-\}
  \circ
  \{e\text{ open}\}
  \circ
  \{e^+\leftrightarrow w\text{ off }S\}.
\]
The BK inequality and \(1-e^{-\beta J_e}\leq \beta J_e\) therefore give
\[
  \sum_{u\in S}\sum_{w\notin S}T_\beta(u,w)
  \leq
  \beta
  \sum_{u,v\in S}T_\beta(u,v) f(v),
\]
where
\[
  f(v)=
  \1_{\{v\in S\}}
  \sum_{w\notin S}
  \sum_{e\in E_v^\rightarrow}
  \1_{\{e^+\notin S\}}J_e
  \Pb(e^+\leftrightarrow w\text{ off }S).
\]
Thus the left-hand side is at most
\[
  \beta\langle \1_S T_\beta\1_S,f\rangle
  \leq
  \beta\|\1_S T_\beta\1_S\|_2\|f\|_2.
\]
