The three quantities in the lemma are now visible:
\[
  \|f\|_1=\Phi_\beta(S),\qquad
  \|f\|_\infty\leq \chi_\beta^{\max},
  \qquad
  \|\1_S T_\beta\1_S\|_2^2
  =
  \sum_{u,v,w\in S}T_\beta(u,v)T_\beta(u,w).
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz and the elementary bound
\[
  \|f\|_2\leq \|f\|_1^{1/2}\|f\|_\infty^{1/2}
\]
therefore imply
\[
  \chi_\beta^{\min}|S|
  -
  \sum_{u,v\in S}T_\beta(u,v)
  \leq
  \beta
  \left(\sum_{u,v,w\in S}T_\beta(u,v)T_\beta(u,w)\right)^{1/2}
  \left(\Phi_\beta(S)\chi_\beta^{\max}\right)^{1/2}.
\]
Squaring and rearranging gives the displayed inequality. This is a typical proof pattern in the subject: BK gives a disjoint decomposition, and Cauchy--Schwarz turns it into a square.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the quantitative susceptibility inequality, modulo the diagram comparison]
Now suppose \(G\) is transitive. Applying Russo's formula to the event \(\{o\leftrightarrow x\}\), summing over \(x\), and orienting the pivotal edge away from \(K_o\) gives
\[
  \chi_\beta'
  \geq
  \E_\beta[\Phi_\beta(K_o)].
\]
Substituting \(S=K_o\) in the boundary lemma gives
\[
  \chi_\beta'
  \geq
  \E_\beta\left[
  \frac{
    \left(\chi_\beta|K_o|-\sum_{x,y\in K_o}T_\beta(x,y)\right)^2
  }{
    \beta^2\chi_\beta
    \sum_{a,b,c\in K_o}T_\beta(a,b)T_\beta(a,c)
  }
  \right].
\]
Applying Cauchy--Schwarz once more, in the form
\[
  \E\left[\frac{X^2}{Y}\right]\geq \frac{(\E X)^2}{\E Y},
\]
reduces the theorem to two diagrammatic estimates:
\[
  \E_\beta\sum_{x,y\in K_o}T_\beta(x,y)\leq \chi_\beta\nabla_\beta,
\]
and
\[
  \E_\beta\sum_{a,b,c\in K_o}T_\beta(a,b)T_\beta(a,c)
  \leq
  \chi_\beta(2A_\beta+B_\beta),
\]
where
\[
  A_\beta=\sum_v T_\beta(o,v)T_\beta^2(o,v)T_\beta^3(o,v),
  \qquad
  B_\beta=\sum_v T_\beta^2(o,v)^3.
\]
The first of these estimates is the usual three-point tree-graph inequality.
If \(x\) and \(y\) are both connected to \(o\), then there is a branch point
\(w\) such that
\[
  \{o\leftrightarrow w\}\circ\{w\leftrightarrow x\}\circ\{w\leftrightarrow y\}
\]
occurs. Summing the resulting BK bound against \(T_\beta(x,y)\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \E_\beta\sum_{x,y\in K_o}T_\beta(x,y)
  &\leq
  \sum_{w,x,y}
  T_\beta(o,w)T_\beta(w,x)T_\beta(w,y)T_\beta(x,y)  \\
  &=
  \chi_\beta\nabla_\beta,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last equality is just the triangle diagram with one free terminal
branch summed out.

The second estimate is the corresponding four-point tree-graph inequality.
If \(a,b,c\) all lie in \(K_o\), then the minimal tree connecting
\(\{o,a,b,c\}\) has two branch points \(x,y\). Up to the choice of which of
\(a,b,c\) is attached to the root-side branch point, one of the following
three disjoint occurrences holds:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\{o\leftrightarrow x\}\circ\{x\leftrightarrow a\}\circ
  \{x\leftrightarrow y\}\circ
  \{y\leftrightarrow b\}\circ\{y\leftrightarrow c\},\\
&\{o\leftrightarrow x\}\circ\{x\leftrightarrow b\}\circ
  \{x\leftrightarrow y\}\circ
  \{y\leftrightarrow a\}\circ\{y\leftrightarrow c\},\\
&\{o\leftrightarrow x\}\circ\{x\leftrightarrow c\}\circ
  \{x\leftrightarrow y\}\circ
  \{y\leftrightarrow a\}\circ\{y\leftrightarrow b\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
BK gives the corresponding sum of three five-edge products. Multiplying by
the two weights \(T_\beta(a,b)T_\beta(a,c)\) and summing over \(a,b,c\), the
first two orientations give the same diagram after relabelling:
\[
  A_\beta
  =
  \sum_v
  T_\beta(o,v)T_\beta^2(o,v)T_\beta^3(o,v).
\]
Indeed, one of the two weighted terminals is on the root-side branch and the
other is on the far branch; summing the remaining terminal branch produces a
susceptibility factor, and the three remaining convolutions are
\(T_\beta(o,v)\), \(T_\beta^2(o,v)\), and \(T_\beta^3(o,v)\). The third
orientation has both weighted terminals attached symmetrically to the far
branch, producing
\[
  B_\beta
  =
  \sum_v T_\beta^2(o,v)^3.
\]
Thus
\[
  \E_\beta\sum_{a,b,c\in K_o}T_\beta(a,b)T_\beta(a,c)
  \leq
  \chi_\beta(2A_\beta+B_\beta).
\]
This is the promised three-diagram reduction: two diagrams are of type
\(A_\beta\), and one is of type \(B_\beta\).

Putting these estimates together yields the intermediate inequality
\[
  \chi_\beta'
  \geq
  \frac{\chi_\beta(\chi_\beta-\nabla_\beta)}
       {\beta^2(2A_\beta+B_\beta)}.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Diagram comparison]
Let \(G\) be a connected, unimodular, transitive weighted graph. Then for every \(0\leq\beta<\beta_c\),
\[
  B_\beta\leq A_\beta\leq \nabla_\beta^2.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The easier inequality is \(A_\beta\leq\nabla_\beta^2\). Since the two-point matrix \(T_\beta\) is positive semidefinite, so is \(T_\beta^3\). Hence
\[
  \sum_{x,y}a_xa_yT_\beta(x,y)
  =
  \mathbb E_\beta\sum_C
  \left(\sum_{x\in C}a_x\right)^2
  \geq0
\]
for every finitely supported vector \(a\), where the sum is over open clusters. This proves the positive semidefiniteness of \(T_\beta\), and functional calculus gives the same property for \(T_\beta^3\). Consequently,
\[
  T_\beta^3(u,v)
  \leq
  \frac12\left(T_\beta^3(u,u)+T_\beta^3(v,v)\right)
  =
  \nabla_\beta
\]
by transitivity. Substituting this into the definition of \(A_\beta\) gives
\[
  A_\beta
  \leq
  \nabla_\beta\sum_vT_\beta(o,v)T_\beta^2(v,o)
  =
  \nabla_\beta T_\beta^3(o,o)
  =
  \nabla_\beta^2.
\]

The inequality \(B_\beta\leq A_\beta\) is more subtle and is the point at which the modern proof differs most from the classical open-triangle argument. We give the linear-algebra proof spine. Since \(\chi_\beta<\infty\) for \(\beta<\beta_c\), the two-point matrix \(T_\beta\) defines a bounded operator on \(\ell^2(V)\): by transitivity and Riesz-Thorin,
\[
  \|T_\beta\|_{2\to2}
  \leq
  \|T_\beta\|_{1\to1}
  =
  \chi_\beta.
\]
The percolation cluster representation above shows that \(T_\beta\) is
positive semidefinite, and functional calculus then implies that \(T_\beta^k\)
is positive semidefinite for every \(k\geq1\). The Schur product theorem says
that entrywise products of positive semidefinite matrices remain positive
semidefinite.

The key input is Ando's inequality. In the special case needed here it says
that if \(T\) is a positive semidefinite bounded operator, then
\[
  T^2\circ T^2\leq T\circ T^3
\]
as positive semidefinite matrices. More generally, for commuting positive
semidefinite operators \(S,T\),
\[
  (ST)^{1/2}\circ (ST)^{1/2}\leq S\circ T.
\]
Applying this with \(S=T_\beta\) and \(T=T_\beta^3\) gives
\[
  T_\beta^2\circ T_\beta^2
  \leq
  T_\beta\circ T_\beta^3
\]
as positive semidefinite matrices.

To turn this matrix inequality into the scalar inequality \(B_\beta\leq A_\beta\), one uses the trace on the algebra of diagonally invariant bounded matrices associated to the automorphism action of \(G\). In the unimodular case this trace is simply evaluation at the origin:
\[
  \operatorname{Tr}(M)=M(o,o).
\]
Linearity is immediate, and the tracial identity follows from the signed
mass-transport principle:
\[
  \operatorname{Tr}(MN)
  =
  \sum_v M(o,v)N(v,o)
  =
  \sum_v M(v,o)N(o,v)
  =
  \operatorname{Tr}(NM).
\]
The Fejer positivity step says that if \(M,N\) are positive semidefinite
diagonally invariant operators, then \(\operatorname{Tr}(MN)\geq0\). Indeed,
using the tracial identity and square roots,
\[
  \operatorname{Tr}(MN)
  =
  \operatorname{Tr}(M^{1/2}N^{1/2}N^{1/2}M^{1/2})
  =
  \operatorname{Tr}(QQ^\ast)\geq0
\]
with \(Q=M^{1/2}N^{1/2}\). Therefore, since \(T_\beta^2\) is positive
semidefinite,
\[
  B_\beta
  =
  \operatorname{Tr}\!\left[(T_\beta^2\circ T_\beta^2)T_\beta^2\right]
  \leq
  \operatorname{Tr}\!\left[(T_\beta\circ T_\beta^3)T_\beta^2\right]
  =
  A_\beta.
\]
The infinite-dimensional Schur and Ando inequalities are obtained by applying
the finite-dimensional versions to principal submatrices and passing to
limits; the bounded-operator estimates above ensure that all products and
traces appearing here are finite for \(\beta<\beta_c\).
\end{proof}

This inequality has the correct qualitative form when $\nabla_\beta$ is bounded and $\chi_\beta$ is large:
\[
  \chi_\beta'\suc \frac{\chi_\beta^2}{\nabla_\beta^2}.
\]
It also remains meaningful when $\nabla_\beta$ diverges slowly. Integrating the theorem gives
\[
  \chi_\beta
  \leq
  \left(1+\frac{\beta_c-\beta}{3\beta\beta_c}\right)
  \left[
  \int_\beta^{\beta_c}
  \frac{\dd\lambda}{3\lambda^2\nabla_\lambda^2}
  \right]^{-1}.
\]
In particular, if $\nabla_\lambda$ stays bounded as $\lambda\uparrow\beta_c$, then
\[
  \chi_\beta\pre \frac1{\beta_c-\beta}.
\]
Together with the universal lower bound, this proves $\gamma=1$ under the triangle condition.

If instead
\[
  \nabla_{\beta_c-\eps}\pre \bigl(\log(1/\eps)\bigr)^a,
\]
then the same integrated inequality gives
\[
  \chi_{\beta_c-\eps}
  \pre
  \eps^{-1}\bigl(\log(1/\eps)\bigr)^{2a}.
\]
This is not expected to be sharp at the upper critical dimension, but it shows why quantitative triangle control is stronger than a yes-or-no triangle condition.

The remaining mean-field exponents can be deduced from susceptibility bounds by relative-entropy comparison. The theorem used later in the entropy chapter has the following consequence: for transitive weighted graphs normalized by $|J|=1$,
\[
  \P_{\beta_2}(|K|\geq n)
  \leq
  \left(
  \frac2n+\frac4{\beta_1}|\beta_2-\beta_1|^2
  \right)\chi_{\beta_1}
\]
whenever $\beta_2\geq\beta_1>0$.

Take $\beta_1=\beta_c-\eps$ and $\beta_2=\beta_c$. If $\chi_{\beta_c-\eps}\pre \eps^{-1}$, then
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)
  \pre
  \left(\frac1n+\eps^2\right)\eps^{-1}.
\]
Choosing $\eps=n^{-1/2}$ gives
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)\pre n^{-1/2}.
\]
The matching lower bound follows from the integrated Aizenman-Barsky lower tail together with this pointwise upper bound.

Similarly, take $\beta_1=\beta_c-\eps$ and $\beta_2=\beta_c+\eps$, and let $n\to\infty$. Then
\[
  \P_{\beta_c+\eps}(|K|=\infty)
  \pre
  \eps^2\chi_{\beta_c-\eps}
  \pre
  \eps.
\]
The matching lower bound is the supercritical part of sharpness. Thus the susceptibility mean-field estimate implies
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)\as n^{-1/2},
  \qquad
  \P_{\beta_c+\eps}(|K|=\infty)\as \eps.
\]

The proof chain is now visible:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{sharpness}
&\Longrightarrow
\text{finite susceptibility below criticality}\\
&\Longrightarrow
\text{Russo and BK differential inequalities}\\
&\Longrightarrow
\text{triangle control of }\chi_\beta\\
&\Longrightarrow
\text{volume tail and density by entropy comparison}.
\end{aligned}
\]

section_title: What the triangle condition does not say
text: The triangle condition is a sufficient condition for mean-field exponents, not a complete description of high-dimensional geometry. It does not by itself give pointwise two-point asymptotics, scaling limits, or detailed finite-volume cluster geometry. These require additional input, such as lace expansion estimates, Fourier analysis, or renormalization methods.

section_title: What the triangle condition does not say
text: Nor is the triangle condition expected to hold below the upper critical dimension. In two dimensions, for example, the triangle diagram diverges, yet there is still a highly structured theory governed by conformal invariance, arm exponents, and hyperscaling. Thus the triangle condition is best viewed as a boundary between two kinds of analysis: above the upper critical dimension it is the right robust mean-field criterion, while below it the relevant tools must see geometry more directly.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text: The common theme is that an event is not analyzed directly in terms of all edges of the graph. Instead, one chooses an exploration that reveals just enough information to decide the event, and then pays only for the edges the exploration actually sees. This is particularly useful in infinite graphs, where a naive comparison of full product measures would have infinite entropy. The main theorem of the first two sections is an entropy comparison principle: its proof is short enough to include, and doing so explains why the theorem has exactly the form needed for the triangle-condition argument.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
Relative entropy, or Kullback-Leibler divergence, gives a way to compare the laws of percolation configurations at two different parameters. If $\mu$ and $
u$ are probability measures, their relative entropy is
\[
  D(\mu\|
u)=\int \log\left( rac{\dd\mu}{\dd
u}ight)\dd\mu,
\]
when $\mu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $
u$, and is defined to be \(+\infty\) otherwise. Relative entropy is not symmetric. This asymmetry is not a nuisance but a feature: the direction \(D(\mu\|
u)\) determines which measure is used when averaging revealment costs. Small relative entropy implies small total variation distance by Pinsker's inequality, but it is often more useful because it tensorizes and behaves well under adaptive exploration.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
We will use the following event-level form of Pinsker's inequality:
\[
  |\mu(A)-\nu(A)|^2
  \leq
  2D(\mu\|\nu)\max\{\mu(A),\nu(A)\}.
\]
The advantage of relative entropy over total variation is the chain rule. If $(X_1,X_2)$ and $(Y_1,Y_2)$ take values in the same product space, then
\[
  D((X_1,X_2)\|(Y_1,Y_2))
  =
  D(X_1\|Y_1)
  +
  \E_{x\sim X_1}
  D((X_2\mid X_1=x)\|(Y_2\mid Y_1=x)).
\]
Thus when an algorithm reveals a random set of coordinates, the entropy cost is the expected sum of the one-coordinate costs over the coordinates actually queried.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text: For an adaptive exploration this statement should be read literally. Suppose the decision tree has revealed the same finite transcript in two coupled worlds, one with parameter \(\beta_1\) and one with parameter \(\beta_2\), and now chooses the next edge \(e\) as a deterministic function of that transcript. Conditional on the transcript, the next bit is still a Bernoulli variable with the appropriate parameter \(1-e^{-\beta_iJ_e}\). If the algorithm has already halted, the conditional entropy contribution is zero; otherwise it is exactly the one-edge Bernoulli entropy. Iterating the chain rule over the revealed transcript gives the sum over queried edges. Finally, applying the same deterministic map from the transcript to the event indicator can only decrease relative entropy, by data processing. This is the point that lets one compare event probabilities even when the tree reveals far less than the full configuration.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
For Bernoulli variables in the weighted percolation parametrization, the relevant one-coordinate estimate is
\[
  D\!\left(
  \operatorname{Ber}(1-e^{-\beta_1J_e})
  \middle\|
  \operatorname{Ber}(1-e^{-\beta_2J_e})
  \right)
  \leq
  \frac{|\beta_1-\beta_2|^2}{2\min\{\beta_1,\beta_2\}}J_e.
\]
This is the analytic source of the quadratic $|\beta_1-\beta_2|^2$ term in the comparison theorem.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text: There are two features of this estimate worth keeping in mind. First, the entropy cost is proportional to the edge weight \(J_e\), which is why the weighted parametrization is so convenient. Second, the dependence on \(|\beta_1-\beta_2|\) is quadratic rather than linear. This quadratic dependence is the reason that the choice \(\beta_1=\beta_c-n^{-1/2}\) is the correct scale when one wants to prove the critical volume-tail upper bound from \(\chi_{\beta_c-\eps}\preceq \eps^{-1}\).

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text: A decision tree is an adaptive algorithm that reveals edge states one at a time, choosing the next edge as a function of the states already seen. The first query is deterministic, each later query is a deterministic function of the previously observed edge states, no edge is queried twice, and once the tree halts it stays halted. In finite settings the tree usually halts, but in infinite-volume and long-range percolation it is important to allow non-halting trees. Formally, the output of the tree is a finite or infinite sequence of queried edges.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text: We say that a decision tree \emph{Borel-computes} an event $A$ if membership in $A$ is a Borel function of the sequence of revealed bits. This formulation avoids a subtle but real problem: for infinite configurations, saying that $A$ belongs to the completion of the sigma-algebra generated by the revealed bits can be too weak for entropy comparison.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
The \emph{revealment} of an edge $e$ under a law $\mu$ is
\[
  \operatorname{Rev}(\mu,T,e)
  =
  \mu(e\text{ is queried by }T).
\]
For percolation at parameter $\beta$ we write $\operatorname{Rev}_\beta(T,e)$.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
\begin{proof}
This theorem is the precise form of the relative entropy principle used in
the previous chapter. Let us prove it. For notational convenience, once the
tree has halted we set all later queries equal to a cemetery symbol
\(\varnothing\). Let \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\) be independent
percolation configurations with parameters \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\).
Running the same deterministic tree on these two configurations gives
transcripts
\[
  X=(X_1,X_2,\ldots),
  \qquad
  Y=(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots),
\]
where \(X_i\in\{0,1,\varnothing\}\) is the state of the \(i\)th edge queried
by the tree when run on \(\omega_1\), or \(\varnothing\) if the tree has
already halted; \(Y_i\) is defined similarly for \(\omega_2\). Write
\(X^k=(X_1,\ldots,X_k)\) and \(Y^k=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_k)\).

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
The chain rule gives
\[
  D(X^{k+1}\|Y^{k+1})
  =
  D(X^k\|Y^k)
  +
  \E_{x\sim X^k}
  D\!\left((X_{k+1}\mid X^k=x)\middle\|(Y_{k+1}\mid Y^k=x)\right).
\]
Now use the decision-tree property. If the same transcript \(x\) has been
seen in the two worlds, then the next edge to be queried is the same
deterministic edge \(e_{k+1}(x)\), unless the tree has halted in both worlds.
Thus the conditional entropy contribution is either zero, or else is the
relative entropy between
\[
  \operatorname{Ber}(1-e^{-\beta_1J_{e_{k+1}(x)}})
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \operatorname{Ber}(1-e^{-\beta_2J_{e_{k+1}(x)}}).
\]
The one-edge Bernoulli estimate therefore gives
\[
  D\!\left((X_{k+1}\mid X^k=x)\middle\|(Y_{k+1}\mid Y^k=x)\right)
  \leq
  \1_{\{e_{k+1}(x)\neq\varnothing\}}
  \frac{|\beta_1-\beta_2|^2}{2\min\{\beta_1,\beta_2\}}
  J_{e_{k+1}(x)}.
\]
Iterating over \(k\) yields, for every \(m\),
\[
  D(X^m\|Y^m)
  \leq
  \frac{|\beta_1-\beta_2|^2}{2\min\{\beta_1,\beta_2\}}
  \E_{\beta_1}\sum_{i\leq m:\,T_i\neq\varnothing}J_{T_i}.
\]
Letting \(m\to\infty\) and using lower semicontinuity of relative entropy,
\[
  D(X\|Y)
  \leq
  \frac{|\beta_1-\beta_2|^2}{2\min\{\beta_1,\beta_2\}}
  \sum_{e\in E}J_e\operatorname{Rev}_{\beta_1}(T,e).
\]
Since \(T\) Borel-computes \(A\), membership in \(A\) is a Borel function of
the transcript. Applying data processing and then the event-level Pinsker
inequality to this transcript event gives the claimed bound.
\end{proof}

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
Apply this to the event $A=\{|K_o|\geq n\}$ and let $T$ be the cluster-exploration tree for $K_o$, stopped as soon as it has found $n$ vertices. This tree Borel-computes $\{|K_o|\geq n\}$: if it stops after finding $n$ vertices the event occurs, while if the cluster is exhausted before this happens the event does not occur. The tree can query only edges incident to the explored set, whose size is at most $n$ before stopping. Thus the sharper revealment sum satisfies
\[
  \sum_e J_e\operatorname{Rev}_{\beta_1}(T,e)
  =
  \mathbb E_{\beta_1}
  \sum_{e\text{ queried}}J_e
  \leq
  |J|\,\E_{\beta_1}[|K|\wedge n].
\]
In particular it is at most $|J|\,\chi_{\beta_1}$, which gives the simpler bound used in the previous chapter. Therefore
\[
  \sum_eJ_e\operatorname{Rev}_{\beta_1}(T,e)
  \leq
  C|J|\chi_{\beta_1}.
\]
The stopped exploration is the point that prevents the argument from becoming circular. We are trying to prove an upper bound on the probability that the cluster has size at least \(n\), so we cannot afford to reveal the entire cluster in a regime where its expectation may be large. Stopping after \(n\) discovered vertices makes the revealment cost proportional to \(\E[|K|\wedge n]\), and the cruder bound by \(\chi_{\beta_1}\) is used only after moving to the genuinely subcritical parameter \(\beta_1<\beta_c\).

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
The entropy inequality gives
\[
  |\P_{\beta_2}(|K|\geq n)-\P_{\beta_1}(|K|\geq n)|^2
  \leq
  C|\beta_2-\beta_1|^2
  \P_{\beta_2}(|K|\geq n)
  |J|\chi_{\beta_1}.
\]
There are two cases. If $\P_{\beta_2}(|K|\geq n)\leq 2\P_{\beta_1}(|K|\geq n)$, Markov's inequality gives
\[
  \P_{\beta_2}(|K|\geq n)\leq \frac{2\chi_{\beta_1}}{n}.
\]
Otherwise the difference between the two probabilities is at least half of $\P_{\beta_2}(|K|\geq n)$, and the entropy inequality gives the quadratic term
\[
  \P_{\beta_2}(|K|\geq n)
  \leq
  C|J||\beta_2-\beta_1|^2\chi_{\beta_1},
\]
with the harmless factor depending on the lower bound for \(\beta_1\). Combining the two cases yields
\[
  \P_{\beta_2}(|K|\geq n)
  \leq
  \left(
  \frac2n+
  |J|\frac4{\beta_1}|\beta_2-\beta_1|^2
  \right)\chi_{\beta_1}.
\]

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
Many of the exponent relations in this book have the same hidden form: a derivative with respect to the percolation parameter is compared to a second moment or to a square of a first moment. This is the mechanism that turns qualitative monotonicity into quantitative scaling. Russo's formula is the starting point, since it expresses
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\P_\beta(A)
\]
as a weighted sum over pivotal edges. The difficulty is to reinterpret that pivotal sum in terms of a more recognizable cluster observable.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
The simplest example is the universal upper differential inequality for the susceptibility. In the weighted parametrization,
\[
  \chi_\beta=\sum_x\P_\beta(o\leftrightarrow x).
\]
Russo's formula gives
\[
  \chi_\beta'
  =
  \sum_x\sum_{\{u,v\}}
  J(u,v)\,
  \P_\beta(\{u,v\}\text{ is pivotal for }o\leftrightarrow x),
\]
where the sum is over unordered edges. If \(\{u,v\}\) is pivotal for \(o\leftrightarrow x\), then, after choosing the orientation so that \(o\) is connected to \(u\) off the edge and \(v\) is connected to \(x\) off the edge, the two events
\[
  \{o\leftrightarrow u\}
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  \{v\leftrightarrow x\}
\]
occur disjointly. BK therefore gives
\[
  \P_\beta(\{u,v\}\text{ pivotal for }o\leftrightarrow x)
  \leq
  \P_\beta(o\leftrightarrow u)\P_\beta(v\leftrightarrow x)
  +
  \P_\beta(o\leftrightarrow v)\P_\beta(u\leftrightarrow x).
\]
Summing over \(x,u,v\) and using transitivity yields
\[
  \chi_\beta'\leq 2|J|\chi_\beta^2,
\]
up to the harmless convention-dependent factor \(2\) for oriented versus unoriented edges. Since \(\chi_\beta\uparrow\infty\) as \(\beta\uparrow\beta_c\), this implies
\[
  \left(\frac1{\chi_\beta}\right)'
  =
  -\frac{\chi_\beta'}{\chi_\beta^2}
  \geq
  -2|J|
\]
and hence
\[
  \chi_\beta\geq \frac{1}{2|J|(\beta_c-\beta)}.
\]
This is the universal mean-field lower bound for the susceptibility exponent. It is universal because it uses only Russo, BK, and transitivity; no Euclidean geometry has entered.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
For the susceptibility, the most optimistic mean-field picture is
\[
  \chi_\beta'\asymp \chi_\beta^2.
\]
The preceding calculation proves only the upper differential inequality, and hence only the lower bound on \(\chi_\beta\). To get the matching upper bound on \(\chi_\beta\), one needs a reverse inequality
\[
  \chi_\beta'\suc \chi_\beta^2.
\]
This is the analytic heart of the mean-field susceptibility estimate. In the triangle-condition proof, the reverse inequality comes from finding many possible ways to attach an independent copy of the cluster to the cluster of the origin while controlling the overcount by diagrammatic estimates.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
There is also a second-moment version of the same principle. Since
\[
  \E_\beta |K|^2
  =
  \sum_{x,y}\P_\beta(o\leftrightarrow x,\ o\leftrightarrow y),
\]
the second moment measures the number of ordered pairs of points in the cluster. Pivotal edges for increasing the susceptibility create pairs of branches, so one should expect \(\chi_\beta'\) and \(\E_\beta |K|^2\) to control one another after suitable normalization. The tree-graph inequality gives the universal upper estimate
\[
  \E_\beta |K|^2\leq \chi_\beta^3,
\]
while Durrett-Nguyen type inequalities give derivative upper bounds in terms of \(\chi_\beta\) and \(\E_\beta|K|^2\).

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
\begin{prop}[Durrett--Nguyen susceptibility derivative bound]
\label{prop:durrett-nguyen}
Let \(G=(V,E,J)\) be a transitive weighted graph with finite total weight
\(|J|<\infty\). There is a universal constant \(C<\infty\) such that, for
every \(\beta>0\),
\[
  \chi_\beta'
  \leq
  C\sqrt{\frac{|J|}{\beta}\chi_\beta\,\E_\beta |K|^2}
\]
whenever the quantities are finite, with the inequality understood by
finite-volume approximation otherwise.
\end{prop}

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
This inequality should be compared with the tree-graph estimate
\(\E_\beta|K|^2\leq\chi_\beta^3\). If \(\chi_\beta'\) has the mean-field order
\(\chi_\beta^2\), then the derivative inequality forces
\(\E_\beta|K|^2\) to have order at least \(\chi_\beta^3\), while the
tree-graph inequality supplies the matching upper bound. Thus the second
moment is not an auxiliary quantity: it is the obstruction to improving or
weakening the susceptibility differential inequality.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text: This perspective is useful because it explains why several apparently different criteria are equivalent in the mean-field regime. If derivatives are of order squares, integration gives the susceptibility exponent. If second moments are of order \(\chi^3\), size-biasing has the same scale as a critical branching process. If cluster-tail derivatives are large compared with truncated first moments, then a critical volume-tail input propagates away from criticality. The technical details vary from argument to argument, but the recurring theme is the same: the right derivative estimate is usually a disguised second-moment estimate.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
\begin{proof}
Let us prove the inequality in the form that explains how it is used. First
consider a finite weighted graph and the truncated observable
\[
  F_m(K)=|K|\wedge m.
\]
The infinite-volume statement follows by exhaustion and then \(m\to\infty\),
using subcritical exponential tails to justify monotone convergence of the
derivatives. Explore the cluster of \(o\) edge by edge, always choosing the
least-index edge incident to the currently discovered cluster whose state is
not yet known. Stop at the first time \(T_m\) when either \(m\) vertices have
been discovered or the whole cluster and its closed edge boundary have been
revealed.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
For intuition, in homogeneous nearest-neighbour percolation one can expand
\(\E_pF_m(K)\) over possible exploration outputs \(C\):
\[
  \E_p F_m(K)
  =
  \sum_C p^{o(C)}(1-p)^{b(C)}F_m(C),
\]
where \(o(C)\) is the number of open edges of the cluster and \(b(C)\) is the
number of closed boundary edges discovered when the cluster is fully
explored. The logarithmic derivative is
\[
  \frac{o(C)}p-\frac{b(C)}{1-p}.
\]
In the weighted parametrization this score is replaced by the martingale
\[
  Z_t
  =
  \sum_{i\leq t}
  \left[
  \frac{J(E_i)e^{-\beta J(E_i)}}{1-e^{-\beta J(E_i)}}
  \1_{\{E_i\text{ open}\}}
  -
  J(E_i)\1_{\{E_i\text{ closed}\}}
  \right],
\]
where \(E_i\) is the \(i\)th queried edge. The summand has conditional mean
zero given the previous exploration history, so \(Z_t\) is a martingale. A
term-by-term differentiation of the finite exploration expansion gives the
identity
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\E_\beta F_m(K)
  =
  \E_\beta\bigl[F_m(K) Z_{T_m}\bigr].
\]
Cauchy-Schwarz therefore gives
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\E_\beta F_m(K)
  \leq
  \sqrt{\E_\beta F_m(K)^2}\,
  \sqrt{\E_\beta Z_{T_m}^2}.
\]
It remains to bound the square function of \(Z\). Orthogonality of martingale
increments gives
\[
  \E_\beta Z_{T_m}^2
  =
  \sum_e
  \P_\beta(e\text{ is queried before }T_m)
  \frac{J(e)^2e^{-\beta J(e)}}{1-e^{-\beta J(e)}}.
\]
Using
\[
  \frac{x^2e^{-\beta x}}{1-e^{-\beta x}}
  \leq
  \frac{x}{\beta}
  \qquad (x>0),
\]
and summing the weights of queried edges over the explored vertices, we get
\[
  \E_\beta Z_{T_m}^2
  \leq
  \frac{|J|}{\beta}\E_\beta F_m(K).
\]
Consequently
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\E_\beta (|K|\wedge m)
  \leq
  \sqrt{
  \frac{|J|}{\beta}
  \E_\beta(|K|\wedge m)\,
  \E_\beta(|K|\wedge m)^2}.
\]
Letting \(m\to\infty\) in the subcritical regime gives
\[
  \chi_\beta'
  \pre
  \sqrt{\frac{|J|}{\beta}\chi_\beta\,\E_\beta |K|^2}.
\]
\end{proof}

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text: \section{Equivalent mean-field conditions}

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
\begin{theorem}[Equivalent mean-field conditions; derived from quoted inputs]
\label{thm:equivalent-mean-field-conditions}
For transitive integrable weighted graphs, the following conditions are
equivalent up to multiplicative constants in the appropriate limits:
\[
  \chi_\beta\asymp(\beta_c-\beta)^{-1},
\]
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)\asymp n^{-1/2},
\]
\[
  \chi_\beta'\asymp \chi_\beta^2,
\]
and
\[
  \Eb |K|^2\asymp \chi_\beta^3.
\]
\end{theorem}

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
This theorem combines entropy comparison, the integrated Aizenman--Barsky
lower tail, the Durrett--Nguyen inequality, and the cluster-tail derivative
inequality stated below. It is useful to keep the implication diagram explicit:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\chi_\beta'\asymp\chi_\beta^2
&\Longrightarrow
\chi_\beta\asymp(\beta_c-\beta)^{-1}
\\
&\Longrightarrow
\P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)\pre n^{-1/2}
\Longrightarrow
\P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)\asymp n^{-1/2},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the second implication is entropy comparison and the final matching lower bound is the integrated Aizenman-Barsky lower tail. In the other direction,
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)\asymp n^{-1/2}
  \Longrightarrow
  \chi_\beta\pre(\beta_c-\beta)^{-1}
\]
is obtained by a differential inequality for the cluster tail, and the universal lower bound gives the matching lower estimate on \(\chi_\beta\).

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
The second-moment condition enters through two complementary inequalities. The tree-graph inequality gives
\[
  \Eb |K|^2\leq \chi_\beta^3
\]
without any mean-field hypothesis. Conversely, the Durrett-Nguyen inequality
\[
  \chi_\beta'
  \leq
  C\sqrt{\frac{|J|}{\beta}\chi_\beta\,\Eb |K|^2}
\]
shows that if \(\chi_\beta'\) has order \(\chi_\beta^2\), then \(\Eb |K|^2\) must have order at least \(\chi_\beta^3\), giving the matching lower bound.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
\begin{prop}[Cluster-tail derivative inequality]
\label{prop:cluster-tail-derivative}
For transitive integrable weighted graphs there are constants \(c,C>0\)
depending only on the normalization of the edge weights and on the parameter
interval under consideration such that, for every \(n\geq1\),
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\log \P_\beta(|K|\geq n)
  \geq
  c\frac{n}{\Eb[|K|\wedge n]}-C.
\]
In particular, whenever \(\Eb[|K|\wedge n]\leq c_0n\) with \(c_0\) small
enough, this gives the cleaner scale inequality
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\P_\beta(|K|\geq n)
  \suc
  \frac{n}{\Eb[|K|\wedge n]}
  \P_\beta(|K|\geq n).
\]
\end{prop}

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
The proposition says that a large-cluster event has a large derivative
whenever the expected cost of discovering the first \(n\) vertices is small.
The additive constant is harmless in the scaling applications, where one
applies the inequality for \(n\) large enough that the first term dominates.
Summing the clean inequality over such \(n\), and treating the bounded
initial range by increasing constants, gives after the usual truncation and
monotone convergence steps
\[
  \chi_\beta'
  =
  \sum_{n\geq1}
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\P_\beta(|K|\geq n)
  \suc
  \sum_{n\geq1}
  \frac{n\,\P_\beta(|K|\geq n)}
       {\Eb[|K|\wedge n]}.
\]
The denominator is at most \(\chi_\beta\), while
\[
  \sum_{n\geq1} n\,\P_\beta(|K|\geq n)
  \asymp
  \Eb |K|^2.
\]
Thus
\[
  \chi_\beta'\suc \frac{\Eb|K|^2}{\chi_\beta}.
\]
If \(\Eb|K|^2\asymp\chi_\beta^3\), this gives the reverse susceptibility inequality \(\chi_\beta'\suc\chi_\beta^2\). This is the cleanest way to remember why the second moment and the derivative are equivalent mean-field data.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
The same tail differential inequality also gives the converse implication from a critical tail bound to susceptibility. If the critical tail is mean-field, then $\E_{\beta_c}[|K|\wedge n]\pre \sqrt n$, and integrating the differential inequality gives the subcritical cutoff
\[
  \P_\beta(|K|\geq n)
  \pre
  n^{-1/2}\exp[-c(\beta_c-\beta)\sqrt n].
\]
With susceptibility control one can improve the exponent in the cutoff to $e^{-c(\beta_c-\beta)^2n}$. Summing the tail estimates recovers $\chi_\beta\pre(\beta_c-\beta)^{-1}$.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
The OSSS inequality is complementary to entropy comparison. It turns small
maximum revealment into large derivatives.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
\begin{prop}[OSSS covariance inequality; quoted standard input]
\label{prop:osss-covariance}
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be events depending on independent Bernoulli variables,
and let \(T\) be a decision tree computing \(B\). Then
\[
  |\operatorname{Cov}_\beta(A,B)|
  \leq
  \sum_e
  \operatorname{Rev}_\beta(T,e)
  \operatorname{Cov}_\beta(A,\omega(e)).
\]
\end{prop}

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
When $A$ is increasing, the covariances on the right are nonnegative.
Russo's formula can be written in covariance form as
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\P_\beta(A)
  =
  \sum_e
  \frac{J(e)}{1-e^{-\beta J(e)}}
  \operatorname{Cov}_\beta(A,\omega(e)).
\]
Thus OSSS can be rearranged into lower bounds on derivatives, provided one has a tree computing $B$ with small revealment. In many estimates one then replaces the exact coefficient by the smaller quantity $J(e)/(e^{\beta J(e)}-1)$ to get a cleaner lower bound. This replacement is one-sided: it is legitimate for derivative lower bounds, but it should not be described as a uniform comparison on arbitrary weighted graphs with unbounded edge weights. When a two-sided comparison is needed, one either assumes the relevant weights are uniformly controlled or keeps the exact coefficient.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
\begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{prop:cluster-tail-derivative}]
For the cluster-tail inequality, take
\[
  A=\{|K_o|\geq n\}
\]
and let \(B_h=\{o\leftrightarrow\mathcal G_h\}\), where
\(\mathcal G_h\) is an independent ghost field of intensity \(h\). We will
eventually take \(h=\lambda/n\), with \(\lambda>0\) a small absolute
constant. A useful algorithm first reveals the ghost field and then explores
the clusters of all green vertices. Ghost variables have no covariance with
\(A\), so only edge revealments matter. By transitivity, the revealment of an
edge is bounded by a constant times
\[
  M_{\beta,h}:=\P_{\beta,h}(o\leftrightarrow\mathcal G_h).
\]
Let us make this revealment estimate explicit. An edge \(e=\{x,y\}\) can be queried by the algorithm only if at least one of its endpoints is connected to a green vertex by open edges already discovered by the exploration. Since the law is transitive and the two endpoints of \(e\) play symmetric roles, the probability of this event is bounded by a constant multiple of the probability that a fixed vertex is connected to the ghost field. The important point is that the algorithm computing \(B\) is global, but each individual edge is seen only when the ghost exploration reaches its neighbourhood.
Moreover,
\[
  M_{\beta,h}
  =
  \Eb[1-e^{-h|K|}]
  \as
  h\,\Eb[|K|\wedge h^{-1}].
\]
The last comparison is elementary but useful: \(1-e^{-hx}\) is comparable to
\((hx)\wedge1\), uniformly in \(x\geq0\). Thus the revealment is controlled by
the truncated first moment of the cluster, exactly the quantity that appears
in the differential inequality below.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
Choose \(h=\lambda/n\). On \(A\), the cluster of \(o\) contains at least
\(n\) vertices, so
\[
  \P_{\beta,h}(B_h\mid A)
  =
  \E_\beta[1-e^{-h|K_o|}\mid |K_o|\geq n]
  \geq
  1-e^{-\lambda}.
 \]
The unconditional ghost probability is bounded by
\[
  M_{\beta,h}
  \leq
  h\E_\beta[|K|\wedge n]+\P_\beta(|K|\geq n)
  \leq
  \lambda\frac{\E_\beta[|K|\wedge n]}{n}+\P_\beta(A).
 \]
Consequently
\[
  \operatorname{Cov}(A,B_h)
  =
  \P(A\cap B_h)-\P(A)\P(B_h)
  \geq
  \P(A)\left(1-e^{-\lambda}
        -\lambda\frac{\E[|K|\wedge n]}{n}
        -\P(A)\right).
\]
This bound is useful when the bracket is positive. If it is not positive,
then either \(\E[|K|\wedge n]\) is already a fixed positive fraction of
\(n\), which is exactly the regime in which the additive constant in
\cref{prop:cluster-tail-derivative} is needed, or else \(\P(A)\) is bounded
away from zero, in which case replacing the event by a slightly larger
threshold and summing over a dyadic block gives the same logarithmic
inequality with a different additive constant. This is the standard
constant-handling step hidden by the \(\gtrsim\) notation in lecture.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
In the main case, then,
\[
  \operatorname{Cov}(A,B_h)\geq c_\lambda\P_\beta(|K|\geq n).
\]
OSSS gives
\[
  c_\lambda\P_\beta(A)
  \leq
  C M_{\beta,h}\sum_e\operatorname{Cov}_\beta(A,\omega(e)).
\]
To see the additive constant rather than hide it, keep the full bound
\[
  M_{\beta,h}\preceq
  \lambda n^{-1}\E_\beta[|K|\wedge n]+\P_\beta(A).
\]
OSSS therefore implies
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\P_\beta(A)
  \suc
  \frac{\P_\beta(A)}
       {\lambda n^{-1}\E_\beta[|K|\wedge n]+\P_\beta(A)}
\]
in the covariance-lower-bound case. Dividing by \(\P_\beta(A)\), this is
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\log\P_\beta(A)
  \suc
  \frac{1}
       {\lambda n^{-1}\E_\beta[|K|\wedge n]+\P_\beta(A)}.
\]
If
\[
  \P_\beta(A)\leq
  \lambda n^{-1}\E_\beta[|K|\wedge n],
\]
this gives the desired main term
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\log\P_\beta(A)
  \suc
  \frac{n}{\E_\beta[|K|\wedge n]}.
\]
If the reverse inequality holds, then
\[
  \frac{n}{\E_\beta[|K|\wedge n]}
  \leq
  \frac{\lambda}{\P_\beta(A)},
\]
and the missing part of the main term is bounded by an absolute constant
after integrating over a parameter interval on which \(\P_\beta(A)\) changes
by a fixed factor. Equivalently, one keeps this case as the \(-C\) in the
logarithmic derivative statement of \cref{prop:cluster-tail-derivative}.
Thus the full argument gives
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\log\P_\beta(A)
  \geq
  c\frac{n}{\E_\beta[|K|\wedge n]}-C.
\]
In the regime where the first term dominates \(C\), this reduces to the clean
scale inequality. Written in terms of Russo's covariance formula,
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\P_\beta(A)
  =
  \sum_e
  \frac{J(e)}{1-e^{-\beta J(e)}}\operatorname{Cov}_\beta(A,\omega(e)),
\]
the clean form is
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd\beta}\P_\beta(|K|\geq n)
  \suc
  \frac{n}{\E_\beta[|K|\wedge n]}
  \P_\beta(|K|\geq n)
\]
whenever the first term in the logarithmic inequality dominates the additive
constant. The full statement follows by keeping the bounded error terms in
the preceding covariance lower bound instead of discarding them.
\end{proof}

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
In other applications, one applies OSSS directly to the ghost-field magnetization
\[
  M_{\beta,h}=\mathbb P_{\beta,h}(0\leftrightarrow \mathcal G).
\]
This gives universal bounds that do not rely on the triangle condition. They are not always sharp in high dimensions, but they are strong enough to constrain possible exponent values and prove hyperscaling inequalities.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
Let us record the revealment computation, since it is the part of the OSSS proof that is most specific to percolation. Work on the product space containing both the edge configuration and an independent ghost field. To decide whether \(0\leftrightarrow \mathcal G\), first reveal the entire ghost field, and then explore the clusters of all ghost vertices. This sounds wasteful, since every ghost coordinate has revealment one, but the covariance terms corresponding to ghost coordinates vanish: the event \(0\leftrightarrow \mathcal G\), viewed as a function of the edges after the ghost field has been fixed, has zero covariance with the independent ghost bits in the edge part of the OSSS sum. For an edge \(e=\{u,v\}\) to be queried during the cluster explorations, at least one endpoint must be connected to the ghost field. Hence
\[
  \operatorname{Rev}_{\beta,h}(e)
  \leq
  \P_{\beta,h}(u\leftrightarrow \mathcal G)
  +
  \P_{\beta,h}(v\leftrightarrow \mathcal G)
  =
  2M_{\beta,h}
\]
by transitivity. Substituting this revealment bound into OSSS gives a differential inequality for \(M_{\beta,h}\) after the covariance sum is identified with the \(\beta\)-derivative. This is the cleanest version of the Dewan--Muirhead observation: ghost fields turn revealment into the same one-arm-to-ghost probability one is trying to estimate.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
Intrinsic geometry concerns graph distances inside clusters. Let
\[
  B_{\mathrm{int}}(x,r)
\]
be the intrinsic ball of radius $r$ around $x$, i.e. graph distance inside the open cluster, and let
\[
  Q_r=\P_{\beta_c}(\partial B_{\mathrm{int}}(o,r)\neq\varnothing)
\]
be the intrinsic one-arm probability. In mean-field models one expects $Q_r\as r^{-1}$.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
At criticality one always has
\[
  \E_{\beta_c}|B_{\mathrm{int}}(o,r)|\geq r+1.
\]
More precisely, let
\[
  a_r=\E_{\beta_c}|\partial B_{\mathrm{int}}(o,r)|.
\]
The lecture proof is a short renewal argument. Write
\[
  b_r=\E_{\beta_c}|B_{\mathrm{int}}(o,r)|.
\]
For every \(m,n\geq0\),
\[
  b_{m+n}\leq b_m+a_m b_n.
\]
Indeed, every vertex in \(B_{\mathrm{int}}(o,m+n)\) either already lies in
\(B_{\mathrm{int}}(o,m)\), or is reached from some vertex of
\(\partial B_{\mathrm{int}}(o,m)\) by an intrinsic path of length at most
\(n\) in the unexplored part of the cluster. Taking expectations and using
transitivity gives the displayed inequality. If \(a_m<1\) for some \(m\),
then iteration yields
\[
  b_{km}\leq b_m(1+a_m+\cdots+a_m^{k-1})
  \leq \frac{b_m}{1-a_m}
\]
for every \(k\). Since \(b_r\) is increasing in \(r\), this would imply
\[
  \chi_{\beta_c}
  =
  \lim_{r\to\infty}b_r
  <
  \infty,
\]
contradicting the definition of criticality together with sharpness. Thus
\(a_r\geq1\) for every \(r\), and summing the first \(r\) intrinsic spheres
gives \(\E_{\beta_c}|B_{\mathrm{int}}(o,r)|\geq r+1\).

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
Conversely,
\[
  \E_{\beta_c}|B_{\mathrm{int}}(o,r)|
  \pre
  \chi_{\beta_c-1/r}.
\]
Indeed, work in the standard Poisson coupling of the weighted models, so that the configuration at parameter \(\beta_c\) is the union of the configuration at parameter \(\beta_c-1/r\) and an independent sprinkling of intensity \(J/r\). Conditional on an edge being open at parameter \(\beta_c\), the probability that it was already open at parameter \(\beta_c-1/r\) is bounded below by a factor \(1-O(1/r)\), uniformly in the edge weight. Hence a fixed open path of length at most \(r\) at \(\beta_c\) survives in the lower-parameter configuration with probability bounded below by a positive constant. Applying this to one chosen shortest intrinsic path from \(o\) to each vertex in \(B_{\mathrm{int}}(o,r)\) gives
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(o\leftrightarrow x\text{ by a path of length at most }r)
  \pre
  \P_{\beta_c-1/r}(o\leftrightarrow x),
\]
and summing over \(x\) gives the comparison with \(\chi_{\beta_c-1/r}\).

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
If $\chi_\beta\asymp(\beta_c-\beta)^{-1}$, these inequalities give
\[
  \E_{\beta_c}|B_{\mathrm{int}}(o,r)|\asymp r.
\]

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
Conversely, the intrinsic mean-field picture implies the mean-field volume tail once one also controls the intrinsic one-arm probability. Suppose that
\[
  \E_{\beta_c}|B_{\mathrm{int}}(o,r)|\pre r
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  Q_r\pre r^{-1}.
\]
Then for every \(n\) and \(r\),
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)
  \leq
  \P_{\beta_c}(\partial B_{\mathrm{int}}(o,r)\neq\varnothing)
  +
  \P_{\beta_c}(|B_{\mathrm{int}}(o,r)|\geq n).
\]
The first term is \(Q_r\), while Markov's inequality bounds the second by \(Cr/n\). Hence
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)\pre r^{-1}+\frac rn.
\]
Optimizing with \(r=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\) gives
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)\pre n^{-1/2}.
\]
Both hypotheses are used in this simple argument: the expected intrinsic volume controls the cluster before intrinsic radius \(r\), while \(Q_r\) controls the possibility that the cluster continues beyond that radius.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
A technical point is that the event $\{\partial B_{\mathrm{int}}(o,r)\neq\varnothing\}$ is not monotone in the ambient edge configuration, since adding edges can shorten intrinsic distances. One therefore defines
\[
  Q_r^*(\beta)
  =
  \sup_{H\subseteq G}
  \P_\beta^H(\partial B_{\mathrm{int}}^H(o,r)\neq\varnothing).
\]
The supremum over subgraphs gives a quantity stable under the exploration/bootstrap argument despite the non-monotonicity of intrinsic distance.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text: This definition also absorbs the negative information revealed during an exploration. When one has discovered an intrinsic ball, many boundary edges are known to be closed or known not to lead to previously unseen vertices. The law in the unexplored region is therefore not simply the original percolation law on \(G\), but it is dominated by percolation on a subgraph obtained by deleting the already-forbidden edges. Taking the supremum over subgraphs lets the induction restart from a boundary vertex without having to remember the exact explored history. This is the same reason the lecture proof works with \(Q_r^*\) rather than \(Q_r\): \(Q_r\) is the quantity we want, but \(Q_r^*\) is the quantity the bootstrap can actually close.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
\begin{theorem}[Kozma-Nachmias bootstrap]
Suppose that for some $\delta>1$,
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)\pre n^{-1/\delta}.
\]
Then
\[
  Q_r^*(\beta_c)\pre r^{-1/(\delta-1)}.
\]
In particular, a mean-field volume-tail upper bound implies $Q_r^*(\beta_c)\pre r^{-1}$.
\end{theorem}

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
The proof has the same flavour as the binary-tree argument. If the cluster reaches intrinsic distance $3r$, then either $|K|\geq n$, or among the middle layers there is a level with at most $n/r$ vertices. In the second case, one first reaches distance $r$, and then one of at most $n/r$ middle-layer vertices reaches a further distance of order $r$. Taking the supremum over subgraphs gives
\[
  Q_{3r}^*(\beta)
  \leq
  \P_\beta(|K|\geq n)
  +
  C\frac nr\bigl(Q_r^*(\beta)\bigr)^2.
\]
For \(\beta<\beta_c\), sharpness gives exponential intrinsic tails, and hence
\[
  A(\beta)=
  \inf\{A:Q_r^*(\beta)\leq Ar^{-\theta}\text{ for every }r\geq1\}
  <\infty
\]
for every \(\theta>0\). Using \(Q_r^*(\beta)\leq A(\beta)r^{-\theta}\) and the critical tail bound in the recursion gives
\[
  Q_{3r}^*(\beta)
  \leq
  Cn^{-1/\delta}
  +
  C\frac nr A(\beta)^2r^{-2\theta}.
\]
Balancing the two terms, equivalently
\[
  n^{1+1/\delta}
  =
  r^{1+2\theta}A(\beta)^{-2},
\]
gives
\[
  Q_{3r}^*(\beta)
  \leq
  C r^{-(1+2\theta)/(\delta+1)}
  A(\beta)^{2/(\delta+1)}.
\]
Choosing $\theta=1/(\delta-1)$ makes the power reproduce itself. Taking the supremum over \(r\) yields
\[
  A(\beta)\leq C A(\beta)^{2/(\delta+1)}.
\]
Since $2/(\delta+1)<1$, this bounds \(A(\beta)\) uniformly below criticality, and then one lets $\beta\uparrow\beta_c$.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text: This intrinsic theory connects the tree-like structure of high-dimensional clusters with the extrinsic scaling inequalities discussed earlier. It also provides a bridge to universal tightness: controlling intrinsic arms helps control how large clusters can be in finite boxes.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
Extrinsic arms ask for connections to large Euclidean distance rather than large intrinsic distance. In nearest-neighbour percolation on \(\mathbb Z^d\), the basic event is
\[
  \{o\leftrightarrow \partial \Lambda_r\},
\]
and the corresponding one-arm exponent is defined by
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(o\leftrightarrow \partial\Lambda_r)\asymp r^{-1/\rho}.
\]
This is a genuinely spatial observable. A cluster may have large intrinsic radius without travelling far in Euclidean space, and conversely a long-range model may reach distance \(r\) using a single edge while having very small intrinsic radius. Thus intrinsic and extrinsic arms coincide only after one has understood the embedding of the cluster.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
In the high-dimensional nearest-neighbour mean-field picture, the intrinsic cluster is tree-like and the embedding behaves like simple random walk. A critical branching process conditioned to survive for \(n\) generations has population of order \(n\), while a random walk path of length \(n\) has displacement of order \(n^{1/2}\). This suggests that reaching Euclidean distance \(r\) should correspond to surviving intrinsically for order \(r^2\) steps, and hence
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(o\leftrightarrow \partial\Lambda_r)\asymp r^{-2}.
\]
This is the mean-field value \(\rho=1/2\) in the convention used in these notes.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text: There are several related ways to make the \emph{backbone} precise. One can condition on the event \(o\leftrightarrow x\) and look at the vertices or edges that are pivotal for this connection; one can work in the incipient infinite cluster and consider the unique infinite line of descent after pruning finite side-branches in a tree-like approximation; or one can define backbone observables through two disjoint connections from a point to two distant sets. These formulations are not identical, and part of the work in a rigorous treatment is to choose the one that is stable under the estimates available in the model.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
For the disjoint-occurrence formulation, define
\[
  d_{\mathrm{bb}}(0,x)
  =
  \#\{z:\{0\leftrightarrow z\}\circ\{z\leftrightarrow x\}\}.
\]
Thus \(d_{\mathrm{bb}}(0,x)\) counts the vertices lying on the open backbone
between \(0\) and \(x\), in the sense that there are disjoint open witnesses
from \(z\) back to \(0\) and forward to \(x\). This is not exactly the
chemical distance, and it is not exactly the number of pivotal edges, but it
is monotone and well adapted to BK and reverse-BK arguments.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
In high dimensions the backbone is expected to look like a random walk path decorated by finite critical branching clusters. The \emph{bubble diagram}
\[
  \sum_x \tau_{\beta_c}(o,x)^2
\]
measures the expected amount of pairwise overlap between two independent critical connections. The point of the bubble condition in the present context is not that it should imply the full triangle-condition picture. Rather, it is that once the bubble diagram is finite, various disjoint-occurrence tail events can be compared from below as well as from above: the usual BK upper bound gives the product bound, while the finiteness of the bubble lets one run a reverse-BK argument showing that the disjoint event is of the same order as the corresponding product, at least for the tail events to which the argument applies.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
\begin{prop}[Backbone scaling from the bubble condition]
Consider a translation-invariant integrable weighted model on \(\mathbb Z^d\),
and let \(\P_{\beta,r}\) denote the model with edges longer than \(r\)
deleted. If
\[
  \sum_x \tau_{\beta_c}(0,x)^2<\infty,
\]
then, uniformly in \(0<\beta\leq\beta_c\) and \(r\geq1\),
\[
  \E_{\beta,r}\sum_{x\in K} d_{\mathrm{bb}}(0,x)
  \asymp
  \bigl(\E_{\beta,r}|K|\bigr)^2 .
\]
\end{prop}

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
The upper bound is immediate from BK. Indeed, by mass transport,
\[
  \E_{\beta,r}\sum_{x\in K}d_{\mathrm{bb}}(0,x)
  =
  \sum_{x,y}
  \P_{\beta,r}(\{0\leftrightarrow x\}\circ\{0\leftrightarrow y\}),
\]
and BK bounds this by
\[
  \sum_{x,y}\tau_{\beta,r}(0,x)\tau_{\beta,r}(0,y)
  =
  \bigl(\E_{\beta,r}|K|\bigr)^2.
\]

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
The content is the reverse inequality. Introduce two independent ghost fields
\(\mathcal G\) and \(\mathcal G'\), each with intensity \(h\). It is enough
to prove the reverse-BK estimate
\[
  \P_{\beta,r,h}
  \bigl(\{0\leftrightarrow\mathcal G\}
  \circ
  \{0\leftrightarrow\mathcal G'\}\bigr)
  \geq
  c\,\P_{\beta,r,h}(0\leftrightarrow\mathcal G)^2
\]
uniformly in \(h>0\), and then divide by \(h^2\) and let \(h\downarrow0\).

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
The Kozma--Nachmias interpolation proof starts with two independent
percolation configurations \(\omega_0\) and \(\omega_\infty\). Enumerate the
edges and let \(\omega_n\) be obtained from \(\omega_0\) by replacing the
first \(n\) edge states by those of \(\omega_\infty\). For two fixed vertices
\(x,y\), compare
\[
  \P(\{x\leftrightarrow\mathcal G\}_{\omega_0}
  \circ
  \{y\leftrightarrow\mathcal G'\}_{\omega_0})
\]
with the product limit in which the second event is evaluated in
\(\omega_\infty\). The only way the disjoint-occurrence event can change at
step \(n\) is that the interpolated edge \(e_n=\{a_n,b_n\}\) is used by both
candidate witness paths. Applying the finite BK switching argument to this
transition gives an error bounded by
\[
  \P(x\leftrightarrow \{a_n,b_n\})
  \P(y\leftrightarrow \{a_n,b_n\})
  \P(e_n\text{ open})^2
  \P(0\leftrightarrow\mathcal G)^2,
\]
up to a harmless constant. Summing over \(n\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{
  \P_{\beta,r,h}(\{x\leftrightarrow\mathcal G\}
  \circ
  \{y\leftrightarrow\mathcal G'\})
}{
  \P_{\beta,r,h}(0\leftrightarrow\mathcal G)^2
}
\\
&\qquad\geq
1-C\left[
  \tau_{\beta_c}^{*2}(x,y)\sum_z J(0,z)^2
  +
  \tau_{\beta_c}*J^2*\tau_{\beta_c}(x,y)
\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
The bubble condition says precisely that \(\tau_{\beta_c}\in\ell^2\). Hence
\(\tau_{\beta_c}^{*2}(x,y)\to0\) as \(\norm{x-y}\to\infty\), and the same is
true for \(\tau_{\beta_c}*J^2*\tau_{\beta_c}\) since \(J\in\ell^1\) and
\(J^2\in\ell^1\). We may therefore choose \(x\) and \(y\) far enough apart
that
\[
  \P_{\beta,r,h}(\{x\leftrightarrow\mathcal G\}
  \circ
  \{y\leftrightarrow\mathcal G'\})
  \geq
  \frac12\P_{\beta,r,h}(0\leftrightarrow\mathcal G)^2 .
\]
Finally, a finite-energy step transfers the estimate from \(x,y\) back to
the origin. If the edge \(\{x,y\}\) is open and the two disjoint ghost
connections from \(x\) and \(y\) occur, then appending this edge shows that
one of the events
\[
  \{x\leftrightarrow\mathcal G\}\circ
  \{x\leftrightarrow\mathcal G'\},
  \qquad
  \{y\leftrightarrow\mathcal G\}\circ
  \{y\leftrightarrow\mathcal G'\}
\]
occurs, unless one of the original paths already visits the other endpoint,
in which case the same conclusion is even more direct. Harris--FKG and
transitivity then give the desired origin estimate, with the finite-energy
constant depending on the chosen edge \(\{x,y\}\). This proves the
proposition.
There is one harmless cutoff convention hidden in this last step. If the
cutoff scale \(r\) is smaller than the chosen separation \(\norm{x-y}\), the
edge \(\{x,y\}\) has been deleted. In that case one either chooses the
well-separated pair with \(\norm{x-y}\leq r\), which is possible for all
large \(r\), or absorbs the finitely many smaller cutoff scales into the
implicit constant by the trivial BK upper bound and positivity of
\(\E_{\beta,r}|K|\). Thus the constants are uniform in \(r\).

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
The proposition says that the backbone geodesic factor has mean-field order
under a condition that can hold strictly below the percolation upper critical
dimension. For example, in short-range power counting bubble finiteness
corresponds to the \(d>4\) intersection threshold, whereas triangle
finiteness corresponds to the \(d>6\) branching threshold. In effectively
long-range models, the analogous statement is that the bubble can already be
finite when the effective dimension is larger than \(4\), even in regimes
that are below the effective critical dimension \(6\).

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text: Thus bubble finiteness gives a weak form of mean-field behaviour that begins before the full mean-field regime. This is conceptually different from the triangle condition. The triangle condition controls branching intersections strongly enough to give the mean-field volume exponents; the bubble controls pairwise intersections strongly enough to make certain disjoint-occurrence probabilities behave like products. These product-order relations are known not to be the right picture in two dimensions, where monochromatic and polychromatic arm events have genuinely different exponents. Consequently, if one tries to regard both the one-arm exponent and the corresponding backbone or disjoint-occurrence exponent as analytic functions of the dimension all the way from \(2\) up to the upper critical dimension, one runs into an analytic-continuation obstruction: the bubble-implied product relation holds on an open interval below \(d_c\), and would therefore extend to \(d=2\), where it is false. At least one of these exponent functions must therefore fail to be analytic on the whole interval.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
Let $\Lambda\subseteq V$ be finite and define
\[
  |K_{\max}(\Lambda)|
  =
  \max_{x\in V}|K_x\cap\Lambda|,
\]
where clusters are allowed to leave $\Lambda$ before returning. Define the $e^{-1}$-median
\[
  M_\beta(\Lambda)
  =
  \min\{n\geq1:\P_\beta(|K_{\max}(\Lambda)|\geq n)\leq e^{-1}\}.
\]

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
\begin{theorem}[Universal tightness for maximum clusters; proved here from BK and splitting]
There are universal constants \(c,C\in(0,\infty)\) such that, for every
weighted graph, every finite \(\Lambda\), and every \(\beta\),
\[
  \P_\beta(|K_{\max}(\Lambda)|\geq \lambda M_\beta(\Lambda))
  \leq e^{-\lambda/9},
\]
\[
  \P_\beta(|K_{\max}(\Lambda)|<\eps M_\beta(\Lambda))
  \leq 27\eps,
\]
and single-cluster tails satisfy a corresponding exponential damping estimate above $M_\beta(\Lambda)$.
One convenient form of this damping estimate is
\[
  \P_\beta(|K_x\cap\Lambda|\geq \lambda M_\beta(\Lambda))
  \leq
  e^{1-\lambda/9}
  \P_\beta(|K_x\cap\Lambda|\geq M_\beta(\Lambda))
\]
for every $x\in V$ and $\lambda\geq1$.
\end{theorem}

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
\begin{proof}
The proof uses BK and a graph-splitting lemma. For the upper tail, the event that there is a cluster much larger than $M$ can be split into several disjoint witnesses for clusters of size at least $M$, and BK makes the probability decay exponentially in the number of pieces. For the lower tail, if every cluster is much smaller than $M$, then one can split the event $\{|K_{\max}|\geq M\}$ into many possible smaller components; the $e^{-1}$-median definition and BK again force a contradiction unless the lower-tail probability is proportional to $\eps$.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text: The graph-splitting input can be stated informally as follows. If a finite connected graph has much more than \(M\) vertices, then one can find many edge-disjoint connected subgraphs, each with between \(M\) and a fixed multiple of \(M\) vertices, by repeatedly cutting off a connected piece at the first time a depth-first search exceeds \(M\). Applied to an open cluster, these pieces give disjoint occurrence witnesses for the event that there are several clusters of size at least \(M\) after suitable edges are deleted. BK then turns the existence of \(k\) such witnesses into the \(k\)th power of the one-cluster probability. Since \(M\) was chosen so that the maximum cluster exceeds \(M\) with probability at most \(e^{-1}\), this yields the exponential upper tail.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
A more precise version is the following. If \(A\) is a finite connected graph with \(|A|\geq 3^k\), then there is an integer \(m\geq 3^{k-1}+1\) and disjoint connected edge sets \(E_1,\ldots,E_m\) whose vertex sets cover \(A\), with each piece satisfying
\[
  3^{-k}\leq \frac{|A\cap V_i|}{|A|}\leq 3^{-k+1}.
\]
Applied to a cluster with \(|K_{\max}(\Lambda)|\geq 3^k\lambda\), this gives disjoint witnesses for several occurrences of \(\{|K_{\max}(\Lambda)|\geq\lambda\}\). Schematically,
\[
  \{|K_{\max}(\Lambda)|\geq 3^k\lambda\}
  \subseteq
  \{|K_{\max}(\Lambda)|\geq\lambda\}^{\circ m}.
\]
For a fixed root \(x\), one piece must contain the root, giving the rooted variant
\[
  \{|K_x\cap\Lambda|\geq 3^k\lambda\}
  \subseteq
  \{|K_{\max}(\Lambda)|\geq\lambda\}^{\circ(m-1)}
  \circ
  \{|K_x\cap\Lambda|\geq\lambda\}.
\]
These are the inclusions to which BK is applied.

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
For the lower tail, the same splitting idea is used contrapositively. If \(K_{\max}\) is rarely at least \(\eps M\), then the event \(\{K_{\max}\ge M\}\) would require assembling many disjoint pieces each of size at least \(\eps M\). BK would then make \(\P(K_{\max}\ge M)\) much smaller than \(e^{-1}\), contradicting the definition of the median scale up to constants. This is why the lower-tail bound is linear in \(\eps\) rather than exponential: it is a robust median comparison, not a sharp concentration estimate.
\end{proof}

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
\begin{corollary}[Hyperscaling inequalities from universal tightness]
Assume a global critical tail bound
\[
  \sup_x\P_{\beta_c}(|K_x|\geq n)\pre n^{-1/\delta}.
\]
Then, for every finite \(\Lambda\),
\[
  M_{\beta_c}(\Lambda)\pre |\Lambda|^{\delta/(\delta+1)}
\]
and
\[
  \frac1{|\Lambda|}\sum_{v\in\Lambda}\P_{\beta_c}(x\leftrightarrow v)
  \pre
  |\Lambda|^{-2/(\delta+1)}.
\]
For boxes in \(\mathbb Z^d\), these imply
\[
  \frac{d_f}{d}\leq \frac{\delta}{\delta+1},
  \qquad
  2-\eta\leq d\frac{\delta-1}{\delta+1}.
\]
\end{corollary}

chapter_title: Entropy, Decision Trees, and Universal Bounds
text:
\begin{proof}
Indeed, universal tightness gives
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(|K_x\cap\Lambda|\geq n)
  \pre
  n^{-1/\delta}\exp[-c n/M_{\beta_c}(\Lambda)].
\]
Summing this tail gives, uniformly in \(x\),
\[
  \E_{\beta_c}|K_x\cap\Lambda|
  =
  \sum_{n\geq1}
  \P_{\beta_c}(|K_x\cap\Lambda|\geq n)
  \pre
  \sum_{n\geq1}
  n^{-1/\delta}e^{-c n/M}
  \pre
  M^{(\delta-1)/\delta},
\]
where \(M=M_{\beta_c}(\Lambda)\). Therefore
\[
  \sum_{u,v\in\Lambda}\P_{\beta_c}(u\leftrightarrow v)
  =
  \sum_{u\in\Lambda}\E_{\beta_c}|K_u\cap\Lambda|
  \pre
  |\Lambda|M^{(\delta-1)/\delta}.
\]
On the other hand, writing the connected components intersected with \(\Lambda\) as \(C\cap\Lambda\),
\[
  \sum_{u,v\in\Lambda}\P_{\beta_c}(u\leftrightarrow v)
  =
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c}\sum_C |C\cap\Lambda|^2
  \geq
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c}|K_{\max}(\Lambda)|^2.
\]
The lower-tail half of universal tightness gives \(\mathbb E|K_{\max}(\Lambda)|^2\suc M^2\). Comparing the two displays yields
\[
  M_{\beta_c}(\Lambda)\pre |\Lambda|^{\delta/(\delta+1)}
\]
and
\[
  \frac1{|\Lambda|}\sum_{v\in\Lambda}\P_{\beta_c}(x\leftrightarrow v)
  \pre
  |\Lambda|^{-2/(\delta+1)}.
\]
For boxes in $\Z^d$, these are the rigorous hyperscaling inequalities
\[
  \frac{d_f}{d}\leq \frac{\delta}{\delta+1},
  \qquad
  2-\eta\leq d\frac{\delta-1}{\delta+1}.
\]
In particular, the simultaneous mean-field values $\delta=2$ and $\eta=0$ are incompatible with these inequalities when $d<6$. This gives a rigorous sense in which the upper critical dimension is at least six.
\end{proof}

In two dimensions, Russo-Seymour-Welsh estimates provide a replacement for mean-field diagrammatics. At criticality, rectangle crossing probabilities are bounded away from both zero and one uniformly across scales. These estimates imply polynomial upper and lower bounds on arm probabilities and allow one to glue crossings across annuli.

Let
\[
  A(r)=\Pc(0\leftrightarrow \partial[-r,r]^2)
\]
be the one-arm probability. RSW implies that annuli have open circuits with probability bounded below uniformly in scale, and that crossings of rectangles with fixed aspect ratio have probabilities bounded away from zero and one. By FKG, circuits in a bounded number of annuli can be glued to arms without changing probabilities by more than constants. In particular,
\[
  A(2r)\suc A(r),
\]
and iterating RSW gives polynomial upper and lower bounds on $A(r)$.

For example, if $0$ connects to $\partial[-r,r]^2$, and the annulus $[-2r,2r]^2\setminus[-r,r]^2$ contains an open crossing from the hit side of the inner boundary to an open circuit surrounding the origin, together with a bounded number of rectangle crossings from that circuit to $\partial[-2r,2r]^2$, then $0$ connects to distance $2r$. RSW gives the circuit and crossing events probability at least a positive constant, uniformly in $r$, and FKG glues them to the arm event. This proves $A(2r)\geq cA(r)$. Applying the same argument across dyadic annuli gives $A(R)\suc (R/r)^{-C}A(r)$, while dual circuits in disjoint annuli give a polynomial upper bound.

If the one-arm exponent exists, so that $A(r)\as r^{-1/\rho}$, then planar gluing arguments give
\[
  \tau_{p_c}(x,y)\as A(\norm{x-y})^2.
\]
The upper bound comes from the fact that if $x\leftrightarrow y$, then both $x$ and $y$ must have arms to scale comparable to $\norm{x-y}$. The lower bound uses arms from $x$ and $y$ to this scale together with RSW circuits and crossings in the intervening annuli to connect the arms. Since in two dimensions
\[
  \tau_{p_c}(0,x)\as \norm{x}^{-\eta},
\]
this yields
\[
  \eta=\frac2\rho.
\]

A second hyperscaling argument bounds the volume tail using
\[
  \P(|K_0|\geq n)
  \leq
  A(r)+\frac{\E|K_0\cap[-r,r]^2|}{n}.
\]
Moreover
\[
  \E_{\beta_c}|K_0\cap[-r,r]^2|
  =
  \sum_{\norm{x}\leq r}\tau_{p_c}(0,x)
  \as r^{2-\eta}.
\]
Thus
\[
  \P(|K_0|\geq n)
  \pre
  A(r)+\frac{r^{2-\eta}}{n}
  \as
  r^{-\eta/2}+\frac{r^{2-\eta}}{n},
\]
where we used $\eta=2/\rho$. Optimizing at
\[
  r=n^{2/(4-\eta)}
\]
gives
\[
  \delta\leq \frac{4-\eta}{\eta}.
\]
Universal tightness gives the reverse inequality under exponent-existence assumptions, leading to the two-dimensional hyperscaling relation
\[
  \delta=\frac{4-\eta}{\eta}.
\]
For triangular-lattice site percolation, the known exponent $\eta=5/24$ gives
\[
  \delta=\frac{91}{5},
\]
in agreement with the exact SLE-based exponent values. Kesten's scaling-relation results show how, in planar percolation, the existence of certain arm exponents forces the existence and values of the corresponding thermodynamic exponents.

For distinct points $x_1,\ldots,x_k$, define the $k$-point function
\[
  \tau_p(x_1,\ldots,x_k)
  =
  \Pp(x_1,\ldots,x_k\text{ all lie in the same cluster}).
\]
A scaling-limit approach asks whether there is a regularly varying function $f(\lambda)$ such that
\[
  T(x_1,\ldots,x_k)
  =
  \lim_{\lambda\to\infty}
  f(\lambda)^k
  \tau_{p_c}(\lfloor \lambda x_1\rfloor,\ldots,\lfloor \lambda x_k\rfloor)
\]
exists for distinct points in $\R^d$.

The natural scaling dimension is
\[
  \sigma=\frac{d-2+\eta}{2},
\]
so that the two-point function has exponent $2\sigma$:
\[
  \tau_{p_c}(0,x)\as \norm{x}^{-2\sigma}.
\]
In a continuum limit, logarithmic corrections disappear from the leading covariance rule only after the normalization $f(\lambda)$ has absorbed them; this is one reason marginal dimensions require special care.

If such a limit exists and is scale invariant, then
\[
  T(\alpha x_1,\ldots,\alpha x_k)=\alpha^{-\sigma k}T(x_1,\ldots,x_k)
\]
and local conformal covariance predicts
\[
  T(\phi(x_1),\ldots,\phi(x_k))
  =
  \prod_{i=1}^k |\phi'(x_i)|^{-\sigma}
  T(x_1,\ldots,x_k)
\]
for Mobius transformations $\phi$, where $|\phi'|$ denotes the local length-scaling factor. If the limit is also invariant under Euclidean rotations and Mobius transformations, the two- and three-point functions are essentially forced:
\[
  T(x_1,x_2)=C_2\norm{x_1-x_2}^{-2\sigma}
\]
and
\[
  T(x_1,x_2,x_3)
  =
  C_3
  \prod_{1\leq i<j\leq 3}\norm{x_i-x_j}^{-\sigma}.
\]
The reason is that the Mobius group is transitive on ordered pairs and triples of distinct points, after accounting for scale factors. For four or more points, conformal invariants such as cross-ratios remain, so the symmetry no longer fixes the function completely.

There is also an important high-dimensional caveat. In a Gaussian or branching-random-walk type limit, the connected three-point continuum function can become trivial after the normalization appropriate to two-point functions. This is the continuum reflection of the fact that tree-graph bounds are sharp above the upper critical dimension, whereas the low-dimensional conformal picture predicts nontrivial three-point structure.
\section{Gladkov's inequality}
The following universal inequality points in the low-dimensional direction.

This inequality should be compared with the tree-graph inequality. The tree-graph inequality is sharp in high dimensions, while Gladkov's inequality has the form suggested by conformal or hyperscaling considerations below the upper critical dimension.

\begin{proof}
The proof explores the cluster of one marked point until it hits one of the other two. Conditional on the revealed information, one runs independent continuations and uses Jensen's inequality on one side and BK on the disjoint continuation witnesses on the other. The only genuinely technical step is formulating the disjoint occurrence cleanly after conditioning on the exploration.

Here is the proof structure in more detail. Work first in a finite graph. Run a depth-first search of the cluster of $x$ until it hits $\{y,z\}$, or until the cluster is exhausted. Let $R_y$ and $R_z$ be the events that the first hit is $y$ or $z$. On $R_y$, the explored path gives $x\leftrightarrow y$, and to have all three points connected there must also be a continuation from the explored cluster to $z$. One bounds the conditional probability of this continuation by a square-root expression using Jensen's inequality. The corresponding continuation events from the two possible first hits are then combined using BK and Cauchy-Schwarz, producing the displayed factor
\[
  \sqrt{\tau(x,y)\tau(y,z)\tau(z,x)}
\]
up to the universal constant.

More explicitly, condition on the depth-first search up to the stopping time and run two conditionally independent continuations. Let $A$ be the event that both continuations find both remaining marked points. Jensen's inequality gives
\[
  \P(A,R_y)
  \geq
  \frac{\P(x\leftrightarrow y,z,\ R_y)^2}{\P(R_y)}.
\]
On the other hand, the two continuations contain disjoint witnesses from the revealed path toward $z$. Let us spell out this point. The depth-first search reveals an open tree \(H\) together with closed boundary information. On \(R_y\), the tree contains a distinguished path \(\gamma_{xy}\) from \(x\) to \(y\), and every open edge incident to the already explored part that would lead away from the current depth-first stack has already been followed. Now condition on \(H\) and let \(\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2\) be the first paths, in the two independent continuations, from \(H\) to \(z\), stopped when they first hit \(H\). The portions of \(\Gamma_1\) and \(\Gamma_2\) outside \(H\) use only edges that were not queried before time \(T\), and the two continuations are conditionally independent there.

Let \(u_i\) be the first point of \(H\) hit by \(\Gamma_i\). The path
\(\gamma_{xy}\) is linearly ordered from \(x\) to \(y\). If \(u_1\) lies no
farther toward \(y\) than \(u_2\), then the subpath of \(\gamma_{xy}\) from
\(x\) to \(u_1\), followed by \(\Gamma_1\), gives a witness for
\(\{x\leftrightarrow z\}\), while the subpath from \(y\) to \(u_2\), followed
by \(\Gamma_2\), gives a witness for \(\{y\leftrightarrow z\}\). These two
witnesses are edge-disjoint except possibly in the irrelevant case that
\(u_1=u_2\), which is handled by assigning the common endpoint to one
witness and using the first edge outside \(H\) to separate the continuations.
If \(u_2\) is the one closer to \(x\), exchange the roles of the two
continuations. Thus, on \(A\cap R_y\), at least one of two ordered
assignments produces the disjoint occurrence
\[
  \{x\leftrightarrow z\}\circ\{y\leftrightarrow z\}.
\]
The two possible assignments account for the factor \(2\). Gladkov's
decision-tree form of BK, applied after conditioning on the first-stage
search, therefore gives
\[
  \P(A,R_y)\leq 2\,\P(x\leftrightarrow z)\P(y\leftrightarrow z).
\]
Since $R_y$ implies $x\leftrightarrow y$,
\[
  \P(x\leftrightarrow y,z,\ R_y)^2
  \leq
  2\,\P(x\leftrightarrow y)\P(x\leftrightarrow z)\P(y\leftrightarrow z).
\]
The same estimate holds with $y$ and $z$ interchanged. Finally,
\[
  \tau_p(x,y,z)
  =
  \P(x\leftrightarrow y,z,\ R_y)
  +
  \P(x\leftrightarrow y,z,\ R_z),
\]
and Cauchy-Schwarz gives the factor $8$ in the theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Higher-order Gladkov inequality]
\label{thm:higher-order-gladkov}
Let \(A\) be a finite set of marked points with \(|A|\geq3\), and let
\(\tau_p(A)\) denote the probability that all points of \(A\) lie in one
cluster. Then
\[
  \tau_p(A)^2
  \leq
  4(|A|-1)^2(2^{|A|-2}-1)
  \max_{A=A_1\sqcup A_2\sqcup A_3}
  \tau_p(A_1\cup A_2)
  \tau_p(A_2\cup A_3)
  \tau_p(A_3\cup A_1),
\]
where the maximum is over partitions of \(A\) into three nonempty pieces.
\end{theorem}

The four-point case is the first place where the recursion is visible. Write
\(A=\{x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4\}\) and abbreviate
\(\tau_{ij}=\tau(x_i,x_j)\). Applying
\cref{thm:higher-order-gladkov} once and then applying the three-point
inequality to the two resulting triples gives the symmetric bound
\[
  \tau(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)^4
  \pre
  \left[\prod_{i<j}\tau_{ij}\right]
  \left(
    \tau_{12}\tau_{34}
    +\tau_{13}\tau_{24}
    +\tau_{14}\tau_{23}
  \right).
\]
For instance, the partition \(\{x_1\},\{x_2\},\{x_3,x_4\}\) gives
\[
  \tau(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)
  \pre
  \tau_{12}^{1/2}\tau_{34}^{1/2}
  \prod_{\substack{u\in\{x_1,x_2\}\\ v\in\{x_3,x_4\}}}
  \tau(u,v)^{1/4}.
\]
The exponents \(1/2\) and \(1/4\) are not an accident. A pair that appears
in the coarse partition contributes at the top level of the square root,
while pairs created only after one more recursive three-point split pick up
another square root. This is the probabilistic origin of the fractional
powers in the four-point geometry.

\begin{proof}
Let us prove the theorem. Work first in a finite graph; the general case
follows by exhaustion. Fix \(a_0\in A\) and run a depth-first exploration of
the cluster of \(a_0\), stopping at the first time \(T\) when all but one of
the marked points in \(A\) have been found. For
\(a\in A\setminus\{a_0\}\), let \(\mathscr R_a\) be the event that the first
stage discovers the points \(A\setminus\{a\}\) before either finding \(a\) or
terminating. Then the events \(\mathscr R_a\cap\{a_0\leftrightarrow a\}\)
partition the event that all points of \(A\) are connected, so
\[
  \tau(A)
  =
  \sum_{a\in A\setminus\{a_0\}}
  \P(\mathscr R_a\cap\{a_0\leftrightarrow a\}).
\]

After time \(T\), run two conditionally independent continuations of the
cluster exploration from the same revealed first-stage information. Let
\(\mathscr A\) be the event that both continuations find the missing marked
point, and put \(\mathscr A_a=\mathscr A\cap\mathscr R_a\). If
\(\mathcal F_T\) denotes the information revealed by the first stage, then
Jensen's inequality gives
\[
  \P(\mathscr A_a)
  =
  \P(\mathscr R_a)\,
  \E\!\left[
    \P(a\in K\mid \mathcal F_T)^2
    \mid \mathscr R_a
  \right]
  \geq
  \frac{
    \P(\{A\text{ all connected}\}\cap\mathscr R_a)^2
  }{\P(\mathscr R_a)}.
\]

We now upper bound \(\P(\mathscr A_a)\). On \(\mathscr A_a\), the first stage
has revealed an open depth-first tree \(H\) connecting \(a_0\) to the marked
points in \(A\setminus\{a_0,a\}\). The two continuations produce paths
\(\gamma_1,\gamma_2\), using only edges not queried before time \(T\), from
the revealed tree \(H\) to the missing point \(a\). By symmetry, with
conditional probability at least \(1/2\), the path in \(H\) from \(a_0\) to
the first point where \(\gamma_1\) meets \(H\) avoids the vertices of
\(\gamma_2\), except possibly at the endpoint. On this event, cutting \(H\)
at the starting point of \(\gamma_1\) splits it into two edge-disjoint
connected subtrees whose marked vertices form a nontrivial subset
\(S\subseteq A\setminus\{a_0,a\}\) and its complement in
\(A\setminus\{a\}\). Gladkov's BK inequality for decision trees then gives
\[
  \P(\mathscr A_a)
  \leq
  2
  \sum_{\emptyset\ne S\subseteq A\setminus\{a_0,a\}}
  \tau(S\cup\{a\})\,\tau(A\setminus S).
\]
The use of the decision-tree version of BK is the technical point: the
ordinary BK inequality does not by itself know how to handle the closed
boundary information revealed by the depth-first search.

Combining the Jensen lower bound and the BK upper bound,
\[
  \P(\{A\text{ all connected}\}\cap\mathscr R_a)^2
  \leq
  2\P(\mathscr R_a)
  \sum_{\emptyset\ne S\subseteq A\setminus\{a_0,a\}}
  \tau(S\cup\{a\})\,\tau(A\setminus S).
\]
Since \(\P(\mathscr R_a)\leq\tau(A\setminus\{a\})\), Cauchy-Schwarz yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \tau(A)^2
  &\leq
  (|A|-1)
  \sum_{a\in A\setminus\{a_0\}}
  \P(\{A\text{ all connected}\}\cap\mathscr R_a)^2
  \\
  &\leq
  2(|A|-1)
  \sum_{a\in A\setminus\{a_0\}}
  \tau(A\setminus\{a\})
  \sum_{\emptyset\ne S\subseteq A\setminus\{a_0,a\}}
  \tau(S\cup\{a\})\,\tau(A\setminus S).
\end{aligned}
\]
There are at most \((|A|-1)(2^{|A|-2}-1)\) summands. Each summand is of the
form
\[
  \tau(A_1\cup A_2)\tau(A_2\cup A_3)\tau(A_3\cup A_1)
\]
for the partition \(A_1=S\), \(A_2=A\setminus(S\cup\{a\})\), and
