\(A_3=\{a\}\). Bounding the sum by its maximum gives the theorem, with the
slightly looser displayed constant \(4(|A|-1)^2(2^{|A|-2}-1)\).
\end{proof}

The higher-order inequalities become more transparent when packaged into a recursively defined geometric quantity. For a finite set $A\subseteq\R^d$, define $S(A)$ by
\[
  S(\{x,y\})=\norm{x-y}^2
\]
and, for $|A|\geq 3$,
\[
  S(A)=
  \min_{A_1,A_2,A_3}
  \sqrt{
    S(A_1\cup A_2)
    S(A_2\cup A_3)
    S(A_3\cup A_1)
  },
\]
where the minimum is over partitions of $A$ into three nonempty sets. The minimum appears because connection probabilities are negative powers of the relevant distances.

For three points this gives the concrete formula
\[
  S(\{x,y,z\})=\norm{x-y}\norm{y-z}\norm{z-x}.
\]
For four points, the recursion takes the minimum over the possible ways of separating the four points into three groups. The resulting expression includes terms with square-root powers, such as products in which one effective pairing contributes with exponent $1/2$ and another with exponent $1/4$. This is the discrete recursive counterpart of the fact that four-point conformal covariance leaves cross-ratio dependence unfixed.

If the two-point function satisfies
\[
  \tau_{p_c}(x,y)\pre \norm{x-y}^{-d+2-\eta},
\]
the higher-order Gladkov inequality gives a bound of the form
\[
  \tau_{p_c}(A)
  \pre_{|A|}
  S(A)^{-\sigma}.
\]
The power is exactly the scaling dimension $\sigma=(d-2+\eta)/2$. The same recursion that arises from repeated three-point inequalities produces an object with the correct covariance rule under Mobius transformations. If $\phi$ is Mobius and $\lambda_\phi(x)=|\phi'(x)|$ is its local length-scaling factor, then
\[
  S(\phi(A))
  =
  S(A)\prod_{x\in A}\lambda_\phi(x).
\]
This follows from the basic Mobius distance identity
\[
  \norm{\phi(x)-\phi(y)}
  =
  \lambda_\phi(x)^{1/2}\lambda_\phi(y)^{1/2}\norm{x-y}
\]
and induction through the recursion defining $S$.

There is also a more geometric version. Choose an arborescence on $A$, meaning a directed tree whose edges point toward a root. For each $x\in A$, let $A_x$ be the set containing $x$, the vertex pointed to by $x$, and all descendants of $x$. Define
\[
  \operatorname{Sweep}(A)
  =
  \min_{\text{arborescences on }A}
  \prod_{x\in A}\operatorname{diam}(A_x),
\]
where for the root we set \(A_{\mathrm{root}}=A\). The product includes this
root term. With this convention
\(\operatorname{Sweep}(\{x,y\})=\norm{x-y}^2\), matching
\(S(\{x,y\})\).
For fixed $|A|$, one has
\[
  S(A)\asymp_{|A|}\operatorname{Sweep}(A).
\]
Let us spell out the comparison, since it is the combinatorial heart of the
recursive geometry. First suppose that \(A=A_1\sqcup A_2\sqcup A_3\) is a
partition that nearly realizes the minimum in the definition of \(S(A)\).
By induction, choose arborescences for
\(A_1\cup A_2\), \(A_2\cup A_3\), and \(A_3\cup A_1\) whose sweep products
are comparable to the corresponding \(S\)-values. These three trees can be
glued by choosing one representative from each \(A_i\) and orienting the
three representative connections toward a common root. Every diameter that
appears in the glued tree is bounded, up to a constant depending only on
\(|A|\), by one of the diameters appearing in the three recursive pieces.
Multiplying the descendant-set diameters gives
\[
  \operatorname{Sweep}(A)
  \pre_{|A|}
  \sqrt{
    S(A_1\cup A_2)
    S(A_2\cup A_3)
    S(A_3\cup A_1)
  }
  \asymp S(A).
\]

Conversely, start with an arborescence \(T\) whose sweep product is nearly
minimal. Choose a vertex \(v\) so that the descendant subtree below \(v\) has
between a fixed positive fraction and its complement between a fixed positive
fraction of the leaves; such a centroid vertex exists in every finite tree.
Cutting at \(v\), and if necessary cutting once more among the remaining
branches at \(v\), gives a three-way partition
\[
  A=A_1\sqcup A_2\sqcup A_3
\]
in which every pairwise union \(A_i\cup A_j\) is controlled by descendant
sets already present in \(T\). Applying the induction hypothesis to these
three pairwise unions yields
\[
  S(A)
  \leq
  \sqrt{
    S(A_1\cup A_2)
    S(A_2\cup A_3)
    S(A_3\cup A_1)
  }
  \pre_{|A|}
  \operatorname{Sweep}(A).
\]
The constants are harmless because \(|A|\) is fixed: the centroid cut may
create a bounded number of leftover branches, but each is charged to one of
the descendant diameters in the original arborescence.

The elementary tree fact used here is the following: every finite rooted tree
admits either a vertex or a pair of adjacent vertices whose removal produces
at most three unions of descendant branches, each carrying a controlled
fraction of the leaves, with the descendant diameters charged to the original
sweep product up to a constant depending only on the number of leaves. This
is the same centroid principle that appeared in the universal-tightness
splitting lemma, but now the cost is multiplicative rather than probabilistic.

For four points \(A=\{a,b,c,d\}\), the arborescence that joins \(a\) and
\(b\) near the root and treats \(c,d\) as the opposite pair gives a sweep
term comparable to
\[
  \norm{a-b}\,\norm{c-d}
  \prod_{\substack{u\in\{a,b\}\\ v\in\{c,d\}}}
  \norm{u-v}^{1/2},
\]
after taking the square-root normalization implicit in the recursion. This
is the geometric counterpart of the four-point Gladkov estimate with
\(\tau(a,b)^{1/2}\tau(c,d)^{1/2}\) and cross terms with exponent \(1/4\):
when \(\tau(u,v)\approx \norm{u-v}^{-2\sigma}\), the two formulae match after
raising the sweep term to the power \(-\sigma\).

\begin{theorem}[Planar \(k\)-point lower bound from RSW gluing]
\label{thm:planar-k-point-gluing}
Consider nearest-neighbour bond percolation on \(\Z^2\) at
\(p_c=1/2\). Suppose that for some \(\eta>0\),
\[
  \P_{1/2}(x\leftrightarrow y)\asymp \norm{x-y}_2^{-\eta}
  \qquad (x\neq y).
\]
Then for every fixed \(k\geq2\) and every distinct
\(x_1,\ldots,x_k\in\Z^2\),
\[
  \tau_{1/2}(x_1,\ldots,x_k)
  \asymp_k
  S(x_1,\ldots,x_k)^{-\eta/2}
  \asymp_k
  \operatorname{Sweep}(x_1,\ldots,x_k)^{-\eta/2}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The upper bound is the recursive Gladkov bound combined with the assumed
two-point estimate and the comparison \(S(A)\asymp_k\operatorname{Sweep}(A)\).
Let us prove the lower bound. Write \(A=\{x_1,\ldots,x_k\}\), choose an
arborescence achieving \(\operatorname{Sweep}(A)\) up to a constant, and for
each marked point \(x\in A\) write
\[
  R_x=\operatorname{diam}(A_x),
\]
where \(A_x\) is the descendant set used in the definition of the sweep. By
Kesten's planar scaling relation,
\[
  \P_{1/2}(x\leftrightarrow y)
  \asymp
  \P_{1/2}\!\left(0\leftrightarrow\partial[-\norm{x-y}_2,\norm{x-y}_2]^2\right)^2,
\]
and hence the hypothesis implies the one-arm estimate
\[
  \P_{1/2}(0\leftrightarrow\partial[-r,r]^2)
  \asymp r^{-\eta/2}.
\]

Let \(\mathscr A\) be the event that, for every \(x\in A\), the vertex \(x\)
is connected to the boundary of the box
\[
  x+[-8R_x,8R_x]^2.
\]
Harris-FKG gives
\[
  \P_{1/2}(\mathscr A)
  \geq
  \prod_{x\in A}
  \P_{1/2}\!\left(0\leftrightarrow\partial[-8R_x,8R_x]^2\right)
  \asymp_k
  \operatorname{Sweep}(A)^{-\eta/2}.
\]
Let \(\mathscr B\) be the event that for every \(x\in A\) there is an open
circuit in the annulus
\[
  x+\bigl([-4R_x,4R_x]^2\setminus[-2R_x,2R_x]^2\bigr).
\]
RSW gives \(\P_{1/2}(\mathscr B)\geq c^k\), after adjusting constants when
some of the finitely many radii are of order one. A further application of
Harris-FKG gives
\[
  \P_{1/2}(\mathscr A\cap\mathscr B)
  \suc_k
  \operatorname{Sweep}(A)^{-\eta/2}.
\]

It remains to say why \(\mathscr A\cap\mathscr B\) forces all marked points
to lie in one cluster. Root the arborescence. If \(y\) points to \(x\), then
the definition of \(R_y\) ensures that the boxes and annuli around the
descendant set of \(y\) sit inside the larger scale associated with \(x\),
with a bounded amount of slack coming from the constants \(2,4,8\). The arm
from \(y\) reaches its outer boundary, the annular circuit around \(y\)
surrounds all smaller descendant arms, and the corresponding arm/circuit at
the parent scale must cross it. Planarity then forces the two open
structures to intersect. Iterating this topological observation up the
arborescence glues every descendant cluster to its parent, and therefore all
points of \(A\) are connected. This proves the lower bound and hence the
theorem.
\end{proof}

Thus in two dimensions, assuming the relevant power-law two-point estimate
together with RSW gluing, the recursive geometry is sharp. This is a weak but
robust form of conformal covariance for \(k\)-point functions: it does not
identify an exact continuum limit, but it shows that the correct
multiplicative geometry is already forced by arm gluing and the universal
Gladkov inequality. In particular,
\[
  \tau_{p_c}(\phi(A))
  \asymp_{|A|,\phi}
  \prod_{x\in A}\lambda_\phi(x)^{-\eta/2}
  \tau_{p_c}(A)
\]
in the two-dimensional power-law setting.

Long-range percolation replaces nearest-neighbour edges by a complete graph with distance-dependent edge probabilities. Let $J:\Z^d\times\Z^d\to[0,\infty)$ be symmetric and translation invariant, and suppose that
\[
  \sum_{x\in\Z^d} J(0,x)<\infty.
\]
For each $\beta\geq 0$, the edge $\{x,y\}$ is open independently with probability
\[
  1-e^{-\beta J(x,y)}.
\]
The most important case is
\[
  J(x,y)\as \norm{x-y}^{-d-\alpha}
\]
for some $\alpha>0$.

The basic qualitative transition is already slightly different from the nearest-neighbour case. If $\alpha>0$, then $0<\beta_c<\infty$ exactly when either $d\geq2$, or $d=1$ and $0<\alpha\leq1$. In one dimension with $\alpha>1$ there is no phase transition, while at the marginal point $d=\alpha=1$ the phase transition is discontinuous: an infinite cluster exists at criticality. By contrast, when $\alpha<d$ there is no infinite cluster at criticality.

The condition $\alpha=d$ has a simple geometric meaning. If two boxes of side length $r$ are separated by distance of order $r$, then the expected number of direct long edges between their bulk volumes is roughly
\[
  r^{2d}r^{-d-\alpha}=r^{d-\alpha}.
\]
Thus $\alpha=d$ is the threshold at which bulk-to-bulk connections between comparable boxes stop being numerous. This is not usually the universality threshold: the long-range/short-range crossover is governed by more delicate competition between bulk long edges and boundary-to-boundary short-range connections. But $\alpha=d$ is a robust geometric boundary that explains why many qualitative statements become easier below it.

The more refined comparison behind Sak's prediction is the following. Suppose that on the short-range model at criticality the two-point function has exponent
\[
  \tau_{\mathrm{SR}}(0,x)\as \norm{x}^{-d+2-\eta_{\mathrm{SR}}}.
\]
A direct long edge from $0$ to $x$ has probability of order $\norm{x}^{-d-\alpha}$, but this is not the right quantity to compare with the short-range connection probability: in a macroscopic connection, the long edge can attach to many possible points in the critical clusters near the two endpoints. If the short-range critical cluster has scaling dimension encoded by $\eta_{\mathrm{SR}}$, then the effective boundary-to-boundary cost of using the short-range medium competes with the long edge at the value
\[
  \alpha=2-\eta_{\mathrm{SR}}.
\]
For $\alpha<2-\eta_{\mathrm{SR}}$, the long edges are relevant and the model should have genuinely long-range critical behaviour. For $\alpha>2-\eta_{\mathrm{SR}}$, the long edges are irrelevant at large scales and the model should flow to the short-range universality class. The point $\alpha=d$ is therefore a geometric connectivity threshold, while Sak's value is a universality threshold.

This distinction is particularly important in two dimensions. There, $\eta_{\mathrm{SR}}=5/24$ for triangular-lattice site percolation, so Sak's prediction places the crossover at $\alpha=43/24$, not at $\alpha=2$ and not at $\alpha=d=2$. In high dimensions, where $\eta_{\mathrm{SR}}=0$, Sak's value becomes $\alpha=2$, agreeing with the random-walk intuition that finite-variance kernels behave short-range while infinite-variance kernels behave long-range.

For long-range percolation with power-law exponent $\alpha$, the analogue of the simple random walk Green function is governed by an $\alpha$-stable process rather than Brownian motion, at least when $\alpha<2$. The mean-field two-point prediction becomes
\[
  \tau_{\beta_c}(0,x)\as \norm{x}^{-d+\alpha}
\]
in effectively long-range high-dimensional regimes. The corresponding upper critical dimension is expected to be
\[
  d_c=3\alpha
\]
when the model is genuinely long-range.

It is often useful to phrase this in terms of an effective dimension
\[
  d_{\mathrm{eff}}=\max\left(d,\frac{2d}{\alpha}\right).
\]
This is motivated by the random walk with jump kernel proportional to $\norm{x-y}^{-d-\alpha}$: for $\alpha<2$ it rescales to an $\alpha$-stable Levy process, while for $\alpha>2$ it rescales to Brownian motion. The borderline $\alpha=2$ carries logarithmic corrections for the random walk. Percolation inherits this intuition, but with an important caveat: in low dimensions the crossover between effectively long-range and effectively short-range behaviour is expected to occur at Sak's value $\alpha=2-\eta_{\mathrm{SR}}$, not simply at $\alpha=2$.

For the volume exponent in the low-dimensional long-range regime, hyperscaling predicts
\[
  \delta=\frac{d+\alpha}{d-\alpha},
\]
while above the effective critical dimension one has the mean-field value $\delta=2$. A useful schematic phase diagram is therefore organized by the lines $\alpha=2$, $d=6$, and $d=3\alpha$, together with the Sak crossover in the genuinely low-dimensional part of the picture.

One should distinguish four high-dimensional-looking regimes that have different spatial scales:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{regime} & \text{condition, schematically} & \text{spatial picture}\\
\hline
\text{LR-HD} & d>3\alpha,\ \alpha<2 & \alpha\text{-stable branching}\\
\text{mSR-HD} & d>6,\ \alpha=2 & \text{short-range with logarithmic spatial correction}\\
\text{SR-HD} & d>6,\ \alpha>2 & \text{Brownian branching}\\
\text{LR-CD} & d=3\alpha<6 & \text{long-range critical dimension}
\end{array}
\]
The special point $(d,\alpha)=(6,2)$ behaves like the marginal short-range high-dimensional boundary rather than like the genuinely long-range critical line $d=3\alpha<6$.

\begin{theorem}[Hierarchical long-range critical exponents; benchmark theorem]
For hierarchical long-range percolation with
\(J(x,y)\asymp\langle x-y\rangle^{-d-\alpha}\) and \(0<\alpha<d\),
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(x\leftrightarrow y)
  \asymp
  \langle x-y\rangle^{-d+\alpha}
\]
and
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)\asymp
  \begin{cases}
    n^{-1/2}, & d>3\alpha,\\
    n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{1/4}, & d=3\alpha,\\
    n^{-(d-\alpha)/(d+\alpha)}, & d<3\alpha.
  \end{cases}
\]
\end{theorem}

The proof of the hierarchical two-point estimate is a useful warm-up for the
low-dimensional methods. Let \(\Lambda_n\) be the hierarchical block of side
length \(L^n\) containing the origin, and let
\[
  M_n(\beta)
  =
  \inf\left\{
  k\geq1:
  \mathbb P_\beta(|K_{\max}(\Lambda_n)|\geq k)\leq e^{-1}
  \right\},
\]
where clusters are restricted to use edges inside \(\Lambda_n\). The key
runaway-observable estimate is the following.

\begin{prop}[Hierarchical runaway observable]
If \(0<\alpha<d\), then for every \(\beta\leq\beta_c\),
\[
  M_n(\beta)\pre (L^n)^{(d+\alpha)/2}
\]
uniformly in \(n\).
\end{prop}

\begin{lemma}[Runaway amplification]
There is \(\ell_0<\infty\) such that for every \(\ell\geq\ell_0\) there is
\(A=A(\ell)<\infty\) with the following property. If
\[
  M_n(\beta)^2\geq \frac A\beta L^{(d+\alpha)n},
\]
then
\[
  M_{n+\ell}(\beta)^2
  \geq
  \frac A\beta L^{(d+\alpha)(n+\ell)} .
\]
\end{lemma}

Indeed, the block \(\Lambda_{n+\ell}\) contains \(L^{d\ell}\) disjoint
\(n\)-blocks. By the definition of the \(e^{-1}\)-median, each such subblock
has probability bounded below, uniformly in \(n\), to contain a cluster of
size at least a fixed multiple of \(M_n(\beta)\). A standard binomial
concentration estimate then says that with probability bounded away from
zero, a positive fraction of the \(L^{d\ell}\) subblocks are good.

On this event, condition on the internal configurations of the good
subblocks and look only at direct long edges between their large clusters.
If \(A\) and \(B\) are two such clusters in distinct \(n\)-blocks inside
\(\Lambda_{n+\ell}\), then every edge between them has hierarchical scale
at most \(L^{n+\ell}\), so
\[
  \mathbb P_\beta(A\leftrightarrow B\text{ by a direct edge}
  \mid A,B)
  \geq
  1-\exp\{-c\beta L^{-(d+\alpha)(n+\ell)}|A||B|\}.
\]
Under the hypothesis of the lemma, this connection probability is at least a
positive constant once \(A(\ell)\) is large enough. Thus the good clusters
stochastically dominate vertices of an Erdős--Rényi graph, or more precisely
a multiplicative coalescent, with edge probabilities bounded below on the
scale
\[
  \beta L^{-(d+\alpha)(n+\ell)}M_n^2.
\]
Since there are \(L^{d\ell}\) good vertices, the relevant merge intensity is
roughly
\[
  \beta L^{-(d+\alpha)n}M_n^2 L^{(d-\alpha)\ell}.
\]
For \(\ell\) large, \(L^{(d-\alpha)\ell}\) absorbs all constants. A giant
component of good subblock clusters then forms inside \(\Lambda_{n+\ell}\),
with volume at least a constant multiple of \(L^{d\ell}M_n(\beta)\). Squaring
this lower bound gives
\[
  M_{n+\ell}(\beta)^2
  \suc
  L^{2d\ell}M_n(\beta)^2
  \geq
  \frac A\beta L^{(d+\alpha)(n+\ell)}
  L^{(d-\alpha)\ell},
\]
and the final factor is again absorbed by the choice of \(\ell\). This proves
the amplification lemma.

Now suppose first that \(\beta<\beta_c\). Sharpness gives exponential tails
for the cluster in every finite block, uniformly in the block, and hence
\[
  M_n(\beta)=O_\beta(n)
\]
as \(n\to\infty\). If the runaway bound failed at some scale with the
constant \(A(\ell)\), the amplification lemma would propagate the failure to
scales \(n+k\ell\), forcing \(M_{n+k\ell}(\beta)\) to grow exponentially in
k. This contradicts the subcritical linear bound. Thus the proposition holds
for \(\beta<\beta_c\), and the endpoint \(\beta=\beta_c\) follows by
monotone convergence as \(\beta\uparrow\beta_c\).

The next step is an expected-size recursion. Let $K_n$ be the origin cluster inside $\Lambda_n$. A sibling-block argument gives
\[
  \E_{\beta_c}|K_{n+1}|
  \suc
  L^{-\alpha n}\bigl(\E_{\beta_c}|K_n|\bigr)^2.
\]
Here is the proof. Let \(\Lambda_n'\) be a sibling of \(\Lambda_n\) inside
their common parent \(\Lambda_{n+1}\), and condition on all edges internal
to the two sibling blocks. If \(C\) ranges over the open clusters inside
\(\Lambda_n'\), then
\[
  \E_{\beta_c}\!\left[|K_{n+1}|\mid \mathcal F\right]
  \geq
  \sum_{C\subseteq \Lambda_n'}
  |C|
  \left(1-\exp\{-cL^{-(d+\alpha)n}|K_n|\,|C|\}\right),
\]
where the constant uses that every edge between the two sibling blocks has
weight of order \(L^{-(d+\alpha)n}\). The runaway bound and universal
tightness let us discard only a fixed small part of the mean by restricting
to clusters with \(|K_n||C|\leq c^{-1}L^{(d+\alpha)n}\), so on the remaining
mass the exponential can be linearized. Independence of the two sibling
blocks then gives
\[
  \E_{\beta_c}|K_{n+1}|
  \suc
  L^{-(d+\alpha)n}
  \E_{\beta_c}|K_n|
  \E_{\beta_c}\sum_{C\subseteq\Lambda_n'}|C|^2 .
\]
Finally
\[
  \sum_{C\subseteq\Lambda_n'}|C|^2
  =
  \sum_{x\in\Lambda_n'}|K_x^{\Lambda_n'}|,
\]
and transitivity inside the sibling block turns its expectation into
\(L^{dn}\E_{\beta_c}|K_n|\). This proves the displayed recursion.

If $\E_{\beta_c}|K_n|$ were ever much larger than $L^{\alpha n}$, this recursion would force growth faster than the volume $L^{dn}$. More explicitly, the recursion has the same runaway form as \(a_{n+1}\suc L^{-\alpha n}a_n^2\); once \(a_n/(L^{\alpha n})\) is large enough, this ratio grows superexponentially until it exceeds the trivial bound \(a_m\leq L^{dm}\), a contradiction. Hence $\E_{\beta_c}|K_n|\pre L^{\alpha n}$. Distance-transitivity then converts this averaged block estimate into the restricted two-point bound. Removing the box restriction requires decomposing a connection according to the first scale at which it leaves the current block and summing the resulting BK bounds over scales. The lower bound comes from $\varphi_{\beta_c}(\Lambda_n)\geq1$, which hierarchical symmetry converts back into $\E_{\beta_c}|K_n|\suc L^{\alpha n}$.

Let us spell out the lower bound, since it is a useful instance of the sharpness technology reappearing in a new geometry. At criticality,
\[
  \varphi_{\beta_c}(\Lambda_n)
  =
  \sum_{\substack{e=(u,v)\\ u\in\Lambda_n,\ v\notin\Lambda_n}}
  \beta_c J(e)
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(0\leftrightarrow u\text{ in }\Lambda_n)
  \geq1.
\]
On the hierarchical lattice, the total boundary weight from any fixed \(u\in\Lambda_n\) to \(V\setminus\Lambda_n\) is of order \(L^{-\alpha n}\), uniformly in \(u\). Hence
\[
  1
  \pre
  \beta_c L^{-\alpha n}
  \sum_{u\in\Lambda_n}
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(0\leftrightarrow u\text{ in }\Lambda_n)
  =
  \beta_c L^{-\alpha n}\E_{\beta_c}|K_n|.
\]
This gives \(\E_{\beta_c}|K_n|\suc L^{\alpha n}\). Together with the upper
bound and distance-transitivity, it gives the restricted two-point estimate:
if \(x\in\Lambda_n\setminus\Lambda_{n-1}\), then
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(0\stackrel{\Lambda_n}{\longleftrightarrow}x)
  \asymp
  L^{-(d-\alpha)n}.
\]

It remains to remove the box restriction. Let \(\Lambda_n\) be the smallest
hierarchical block containing both \(0\) and \(x\). Decompose according to the
first scale at which a connection appears:
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(0\leftrightarrow x)
  =
  \P_{\beta_c}(0\stackrel{\Lambda_n}{\longleftrightarrow}x)
  +
  \sum_{k\geq1}
  \P_{\beta_c}\!\left(
  0\stackrel{\Lambda_{n+k}}{\longleftrightarrow}x
  \text{ but not inside }\Lambda_{n+k-1}
  \right).
\]
On the \(k\)th event, every open path from \(0\) to \(x\) must use at least
one edge crossing from a child block of \(\Lambda_{n+k}\) to another child
block at scale \(n+k\). Choose the first such edge \(e=(u,v)\) along the path,
with the side containing \(0\) ending at \(u\) and the side containing \(x\)
beginning at \(v\). The two pieces of the path on either side of \(e\) occur
disjointly from the edge event, so BK gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\P_{\beta_c}\!\left(
  0\stackrel{\Lambda_{n+k}}{\longleftrightarrow}x
  \text{ but not inside }\Lambda_{n+k-1}
  \right)
\\
&\qquad\pre
  \sum_{u,v\in\Lambda_{n+k}}
  \P_{\beta_c}(0\stackrel{\Lambda_{n+k}}{\longleftrightarrow}u)\,
  J(u,v)\,
  \P_{\beta_c}(v\stackrel{\Lambda_{n+k}}{\longleftrightarrow}x),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the sum is restricted to pairs in different scale-\((n+k-1)\) child
blocks and \(J(u,v)\asymp L^{-(d+\alpha)(n+k)}\) on this scale. Summing the
restricted connection from \(0\) to \(u\) gives
\(\E_{\beta_c}|K_{n+k}|\pre L^{\alpha(n+k)}\). For the \(x\)-side, only the
mass in the scale-\(n\) block containing \(x\) is needed after the first exit,
and the restricted estimate gives a contribution of order \(L^{\alpha n}\).
Thus the \(k\)th term is bounded by
\[
  L^{\alpha(n+k)}
  L^{-(d+\alpha)(n+k)}
  L^{\alpha n}
  =
  L^{-(d-\alpha)n}L^{-dk}.
\]
The sum over \(k\geq1\) is a geometric series, and hence
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(0\leftrightarrow x)
  \pre
  L^{-(d-\alpha)n}
  \asymp
  \langle x\rangle^{-d+\alpha}.
\]
The restricted lower bound gives the matching unrestricted lower bound. This
completes the proof of the hierarchical two-point estimate.

section_title: Critical two-point functions and known long-range results
text:
\begin{theorem}[Euclidean long-range two-point estimates; quoted status summary]
For Euclidean power-law kernels \(J(x,y)\asymp\norm{x-y}^{-d-\alpha}\),
the averaged upper bounds used in the cutoff theory are available
non-perturbatively in the long-range setting. Pointwise Sak-type estimates
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(x\leftrightarrow y)\asymp \norm{x-y}^{-d+\alpha}
\]
are quoted here only in the regimes where the relevant regularity and
localization inputs are known, in particular in the non-perturbative
\(\alpha<1\) range discussed below, and in perturbative high-dimensional
regimes where lace-expansion two-point estimates are supplied.
\end{theorem}
The table is intentionally conservative. In particular, statements about ``effectively long-range'' behaviour in low dimensions should be read as conditional on (CL) or (wCL), with unconditional corollaries only in ranges where those conditions have been verified, such as the \(\alpha<1\) regimes discussed below.

section_title: Critical two-point functions and known long-range results
text:
On $\Z^d$, one can also prove averaged and pointwise two-point results that support Sak's prediction. A representative averaged upper bound, in the power-law models considered in the reference papers, says that if
\[
  J(x,y)\suc \norm{x-y}^{-d-\alpha},
\]
then
\[
  \frac1{r^d}\sum_{x\in[-r,r]^d}
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(0\leftrightarrow x)
  \pre r^{-d+\alpha}.
\]
Conversely, under matching upper bounds on the kernel, averaged lower bounds of Baumler and Berger give the same power for $\alpha<1$, with logarithmic or short-range-like modifications at and above $\alpha=1$. In particular, for $\alpha<1$ one obtains the long-range two-point exponent in an averaged sense, and in recent work the corresponding pointwise estimate
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(x\leftrightarrow y)
  \asymp \norm{x-y}^{-d+\alpha}
\]
has been proved in the same range.

Once two-point information is available, the next question is whether critical clusters have the same intrinsic moment structure as critical branching processes. The newest high-dimensional results answer this affirmatively in the regimes covered by the high-dimensional hypotheses (HD):
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{(i)} & d>3\alpha,\\
\text{(ii)} & d>6\text{ and }\P_{\beta_c}(x\leftrightarrow y)\pre \norm{x-y}^{-d+2},\\
\text{(iii)} & d=6,\ \alpha=2\text{ and }
  \P_{\beta_c}(x\leftrightarrow y)\pre
  (\log\norm{x-y})^{-1}\norm{x-y}^{-d+2}.
\end{array}
\]
The first case is the non-perturbative long-range cutoff theorem; the second and third include spread-out short-range or marginally short-range models when the needed lace-expansion two-point estimates are available.

\begin{theorem}[High-dimensional cutoff moments and volume tail; quoted input]
\label{thm:hd-cutoff-moments-book}
Assume that one of the high-dimensional hypotheses \emph{(HD)} above holds.
With the normalization conventions for the power-law kernel used in the
reference papers, there is a positive constant \(A\) such that, for every
fixed integer \(m\geq1\),
\[
  \E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^m
  \sim
  (2m-3)!!\,A^{m-1}\frac{\alpha}{\beta_c}
  r^{(2m-1)\alpha}
\]
as \(r\to\infty\). Moreover,
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)
  \sim
  \frac{\alpha}{\beta_c}\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi A}}\,
  n^{-1/2}
\]
as \(n\to\infty\).
\end{theorem}

We quote this theorem as a proved input. The cutoff-renormalization chapter
below gives the main mechanism of the proof: the first-moment bootstrap, the
higher-moment ODE induction, and the ghost-field comparison that removes the
cutoff. Equivalently, if
\[
  \widehat m_r
  =
  \frac{\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2}{\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|},
\]
then the moment assertion can be written as
\[
  \E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^m
  \sim
  (2m-3)!!\,\widehat m_r^{\,m-1}\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|.
\]
After size-biasing by \(|K|\), the normalized cutoff cluster volume has
moments matching those of \(N^2\), where \(N\) is standard normal. This is the
intrinsic mean-field assertion: before asking where the cluster sits in
space, its genealogy has the same moment recursion as a critical branching
process.

The broader high-dimensional short-range regimes \(d>6\) with \(\alpha\geq d/3\), and the doubly marginal point \((d,\alpha)=(6,2)\), are covered by analogous cutoff volume and moment conclusions when the needed two-point estimates are supplied, for example by lace expansion in spread-out models. Their spatial scaling is Brownian or marginally Brownian rather than stable, but the intrinsic volume powers remain mean-field. In the long-range critical-dimensional case \(d=3\alpha<6\), the volume tail has the logarithmic correction
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)\asymp n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{1/4}.
\]
The later cutoff-renormalization chapter sketches why these powers and logarithms appear.

The high-dimensional scale table is useful enough to record explicitly:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{regime} & N(r) & V(r) & \eta(r)=N(r)V(r)/r^d\\
\hline
\text{LR-HD} & r^{d-3\alpha} & r^{2\alpha} & r^{-\alpha}\\
\text{mSR-HD} & r^{d-6}(\log r)^3 & r^4/(\log r)^2 & (\log r)/r^2\\
\text{SR-HD} & r^{d-6} & r^4 & r^{-2}\\
\text{LR-CD} & \log r & r^{2\alpha}/\sqrt{\log r} & r^{-\alpha}\sqrt{\log r}.
\end{array}
\]
Here $r$ is the physical spatial scale. This is not quite the same role played by $r$ in the cutoff ODE chapter, where $r$ is the cutoff length; in the genuinely long-range regimes these scales are comparable, while in the marginally short-range line $\alpha=2$ the physical spatial scale includes an additional $\sqrt{\log r}$ factor. The quantity $N(r)$ is the number of important large clusters at physical scale $r$, $V(r)$ is their typical volume, and $\eta(r)$ is the probability that the origin belongs to one of them. The distinction between many-cluster geometry and few-cluster geometry is encoded in $N(r)$.

The high-dimensional volume theory is not merely a statement about the one-dimensional random variable $|K|$. Once the two-point function and the spatial moments are under control, the critical cluster can be rescaled as a random measure. In the genuinely long-range high-dimensional regime this measure should converge to the canonical cluster measure of a superprocess whose underlying motion is the symmetric $\alpha$-stable process. In the effectively short-range high-dimensional regime the corresponding limit is super-Brownian motion. The exponents are the same in the two mean-field regimes, but the spatial processes are different.

Let us describe the normalization informally. In a ball of radius $r$ in the stable regime, the important critical clusters have volume of order
\[
  r^{2\alpha},
\]
and there are of order
\[
  r^{d-3\alpha}
\]
such clusters in a box of volume $r^d$. Thus a cluster conditioned to be large enough to be seen at scale $r$ should be normalized by the mass scale $r^{2\alpha}$ and the spatial scale $r$. The limiting object is not a deterministic density: it is a random compactly supported measure whose genealogy is tree-like and whose embedding is generated by stable jumps along that genealogy.

This picture explains why the same two ingredients keep reappearing. The tree-like part is encoded by the critical branching-process moment constants
\[
  (2m-3)!!,
\]
or, under size-biasing, by the moments of $N^2$. The spatial part is encoded by the second spatial moment and its higher analogues. When $\alpha<2$, a typical large displacement is produced by a long edge of comparable size to the macroscopic scale, so the stable process remains visible in the limit. When $\alpha>2$, the long edges have finite second moment and the displacement is instead built up from many shorter increments, leading to Brownian scaling. At $\alpha=2$, the Brownian limit survives but the normalization carries logarithmic corrections.

A more theorem-shaped normalization is the following. Let
\[
  \zeta(r)=\frac{\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2}{\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|}
\]
be the size-biased volume scale, and let \(\sigma(r)\) be the spatial scale determined by the radius of gyration. In the stable high-dimensional regime \(\sigma(r)\asymp r\) and \(\zeta(r)\asymp r^{2\alpha}\); in the Brownian high-dimensional regime \(\sigma(r)\asymp r^{\alpha/2}\); at \(\alpha=2\) there is a logarithmic correction. The cutoff random measure is
\[
  \mu_r=
  \frac1{\zeta(r)}
  \sum_{x\in K}\delta_{x/\sigma(r)}.
\]
The cutoff theorem identifies the limiting mixed moments of \(\mu_r\) under a size-biased or conditioned law. Removing the cutoff and conditioning the full critical cluster on \(|K|\geq n\) gives, schematically,
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}\left(
  \frac1n\sum_{x\in K}\delta_{x/\sigma(n)}
  \in\cdot\;\middle|\; |K|\geq n
  \right)
  \Longrightarrow
  \text{integrated superprocess}.
\]
Here \(\sigma(n)\asymp n^{1/(2\alpha)}\) when \(\alpha<2\), \(\sigma(n)\asymp n^{1/4}\) when \(\alpha>2\), and the marginal cases carry logarithmic corrections. The word ``integrated'' means that the limiting measure is the occupation measure accumulated over a continuum random tree, with spatial motion given by the stable or Brownian process decorating that tree. A fully precise statement requires specifying the topology on finite measures, the canonical superprocess measure, and the conditioning convention; here we record the mechanism and normalization, leaving those analytic details to the reference theorem.

One should not confuse convergence of cluster volumes with convergence of embedded clusters. The volume tail
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)\asymp n^{-1/2}
\]
is insensitive to whether the embedding is stable or Brownian. The scaling limit is sensitive to exactly this distinction. This is why the original course plan treated high-dimensional cluster moments and high-dimensional superprocess scaling as separate topics: the first proves the intrinsic mean-field genealogy, while the second identifies the extrinsic motion decorating that genealogy.

The cutoff-renormalization method is well adapted to this separation. The moment ODEs first prove the intrinsic size-biased limit. Spatial moment ODEs then decide which motion appears in the embedding. Finally, a ghost-field comparison removes the cutoff and transfers the result from the regularized model back to the original critical model. The later chapter follows this order, separating the differential-inequality proofs from the tighter convergence inputs that are quoted from the research papers.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
Let $J$ be a long-range kernel. For $r\geq 1$, define the cutoff kernel
\[
  J_r(x,y)=
  \mathbf 1_{\{\norm{x-y}\leq r\}}
  \int_{\norm{x-y}}^r s^{-d-\alpha-1}\,\dd s,
\]
in the pure power-law case, or use a smooth analogue. Let $\mathbb P_{\beta,r}$ denote percolation with edge probabilities derived from $\beta J_r$. Studying how cluster moments depend on the cutoff $r$ gives a renormalization perspective on the critical model.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
One should think of this as decomposing the model by edge length. The full kernel can be written, up to normalization, as
\[
  J(x,y)=\int_{\norm{x-y}}^\infty s^{-d-\alpha-1}\,\dd s,
\]
while $J_r$ keeps only the contribution from scales at most $r$. Differentiating in $r$ therefore adds a thin annulus of potential edges of length comparable to $r$, and Russo's formula converts this infinitesimal change of scale into pivotal-edge expressions. The normalization of the display suppresses harmless constants, such as factors of $d+\alpha$ or constants depending on the chosen norm. In the proofs these constants are fixed once and for all so that differentiating the cutoff has the clean form
\[
  \frac{\partial}{\partial r}J_r(x,y)
  =
  \mathbf 1_{\{\norm{x-y}\leq r\}}r^{-d-\alpha-1}
\]
up to the same deterministic normalization. None of the exponent statements depends on this choice.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text: For each fixed finite $r$, the cutoff kernel is pointwise dominated by a strict multiple of the full kernel. Thus $\mathbb P_{\beta_c,r}$ is dominated by a genuinely subcritical full-kernel model, and sharpness implies that all cluster moments appearing below are finite. This is what makes the cutoff derivative formulae legitimate despite working at the full model's critical point.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
The basic observables are
\[
  \E_{\beta_c,r}|K|,\qquad
  \E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2,\qquad
  \E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^3,\qquad
  \E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^4,
\]
and spatial moments such as
\[
  \sum_x \norm{x}^{2}\,\mathbb P_{\beta_c,r}(0\leftrightarrow x).
\]
Russo's formula gives differential or difference inequalities in the cutoff parameter. Tree-graph inequalities close the resulting moment hierarchy in the high-dimensional and critical-dimensional regimes.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
In the high-dimensional effectively long-range regime, the first moment under the cutoff measure grows like
\[
  \E_{\beta_c,r}|K|\as r^\alpha.
\]
The second and higher moments follow corresponding mean-field powers. At the critical dimension $d=3\alpha$, logarithmic corrections appear. The moment flow has the flavour of a renormalization group calculation, but is phrased in probabilistic inequalities rather than perturbative field theory.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text: The mechanism can be summarized as follows. Increasing the cutoff adds possible long edges in a thin annulus of lengths. The derivative of a cluster moment with respect to the cutoff is expressed in terms of pivotal long edges. The probability of pivotality is bounded using connection probabilities and tree-graph estimates. If the two-point function has the expected power law, the resulting integrals close and identify the moment growth.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
Before specializing to the first moment, the mean-field moment flow has the form
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd r}\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^p
  \sim
  \beta_c r^{-\alpha-1}
  \sum_{\ell=0}^{p-1}
  \binom p\ell
  \E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^{\ell+1}
  \E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^{p-\ell}.
\]
The summand with index \(\ell\) corresponds to the newly added long edge splitting the \(p\) marked vertices between the two sides of the edge. The binomial coefficient records the choice of marked vertices assigned to one side. The difficult part of the theorem is proving that the error made by treating the two sides as independent is negligible in high effective dimension, marginally controlled at the critical dimension, and incompatible with low-dimensional hyperscaling.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
Let us spell this out for the first moment in the high-dimensional long-range regime $d>3\alpha$. For convenience write
\[
  f_{\beta}(r)=\mathbb E_{\beta,r}|K|.
\]
Russo's formula in the cutoff parameter gives, schematically,
\[
  \frac{\partial}{\partial r}f_\beta(r)
  =
  \beta r^{-d-\alpha-1}
  \mathbb E_{\beta,r}\left[
    \sum_{y\in B_r}
    \mathbf 1_{\{0\not\leftrightarrow y\}}
    |K_0|\,|K_y|
  \right].
\]
If the two clusters in this expression behaved independently, the sum over $B_r$ would contribute a factor $r^d$, leaving the closed ODE
\[
  f_\beta'(r)\approx \beta r^{-\alpha-1}f_\beta(r)^2.
\]
More precisely, after dividing by the annular derivative \(\beta |J'(r)|\), the first two moment equations have the form
\[
  \frac{1}{\beta |J'(r)|}
  \frac{\dd}{\dd r}\E_{\beta,r}|K|
  =
  |B_r|\bigl(\E_{\beta,r}|K|\bigr)^2
  -
  \sum_{y\in B_r}\mathscr D_r^{(1)}(0,y),
\]
and
\[
  \frac{1}{\beta |J'(r)|}
  \frac{\dd}{\dd r}\E_{\beta,r}|K|^2
  =
  3|B_r|\E_{\beta,r}|K|\E_{\beta,r}|K|^2
  -
  3\sum_{y\in B_r}\mathscr D_r^{(2)}(0,y).
\]
Here
\[
  \mathscr D_r^{(1)}(x,y)
  =
  \bigl(\E_{\beta,r}|K|\bigr)^2
  -
  \E_{\beta,r}\!\left[
    |K_x|\,|K_y|\mathbf 1_{\{x\not\leftrightarrow y\}}
  \right],
\]
and \(\mathscr D_r^{(2)}\) is the analogous deficit for the second-moment splitting. These deficits measure the failure of the two endpoint clusters of the new long edge to behave as independent clusters. In high effective dimension their contribution is lower order; at the critical dimension their second-order asymptotics produce the logarithm.
At the level of this proof sketch, the corresponding error term has the form
\[
  f_\beta'(r)
  =
  (1-\varepsilon_{\beta,r})
  \beta r^{-\alpha-1}f_\beta(r)^2,
\]
where the error in this independence approximation is controlled by the overlap term
\[
  \varepsilon_{\beta,r}
  \pre
  \frac{
    \mathbb E_{\beta,r}\bigl[|K|^2\,|K\cap B_r|\bigr]
  }{
    |B_r|\,\bigl(\mathbb E_{\beta,r}|K|\bigr)^2
  }.
\]
Using $|K\cap B_r|\leq |K|$ and tree-graph moment estimates, this is at most of order
\[
  \frac{\mathbb E_{\beta,r}|K|^3}{r^d\,\bigl(\mathbb E_{\beta,r}|K|\bigr)^2}.
\]
If $f_\beta(r)$ has the expected size $r^\alpha$, the error is $O(r^{3\alpha-d})$, which tends to zero precisely in the regime $d>3\alpha$.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
At $\beta=\beta_c$, the full susceptibility is infinite, so the ODE is integrated with boundary condition $f_{\beta_c}(\infty)=\infty$. This predicts
\[
  f_{\beta_c}(r)\sim \frac{\alpha}{\beta_c}r^\alpha.
\]
The proof is a bootstrap. For $\beta<\beta_c$, define $r_0(\beta)$ to be the first scale after which
\[
  f_\beta(R)\leq 2\frac{\alpha}{\beta_c}R^\alpha
  \qquad\text{for every }R\geq r_0(\beta).
\]
This scale is finite by subcriticality. On scales above \(r_0(\beta)\), the
definition of \(r_0\) and the tree-graph bound give
\[
  \varepsilon_{\beta,r}\pre r^{3\alpha-d}.
\]
Thus, after choosing a deterministic scale \(r_{00}\), the error is at most
\(10^{-2}\) whenever \(r\geq r_0(\beta)\vee r_{00}\). On slightly smaller
scales, monotonicity of \(f_\beta\) gives
\[
  \varepsilon_{\beta,r}\pre r_0(\beta)^{3\alpha}r^{-d}.
\]
Since $d>3\alpha$, this is still small for
\[
  r\geq C r_0(\beta)^{1-\eps}
\]
for some $\eps>0$. Thus, for \(\beta_c/2\leq\beta<\beta_c\), once the constants have been chosen and \(r_0(\beta)\) is large enough, one may use
\[
  f_\beta'(r)\geq (1-\eta)\,\beta r^{-\alpha-1}f_\beta(r)^2
\]
with, say, \(\eta=10^{-2}\), on every \(r\geq C r_0(\beta)^{1-\eps}\).
Equivalently,
\[
  \left(\frac1{f_\beta(r)}\right)'
  \leq
  -(1-\eta)\beta r^{-\alpha-1}.
\]
Integrating from \(r\) to \(\infty\) and using
\(f_\beta(\infty)=\chi_\beta<\infty\) gives
\[
  \frac1{f_\beta(r)}
  \geq
  \frac1{\chi_\beta}
  +
  \frac{(1-\eta)\beta}{\alpha}r^{-\alpha}
  \geq
  \frac{(1-\eta)\beta}{\alpha}r^{-\alpha}.
\]
For \(\beta\) sufficiently close to \(\beta_c\), this improves the generous constant \(2\alpha/\beta_c\) to a smaller constant, say
\[
  f_\beta(r)\leq \frac{3\alpha}{2\beta_c}r^\alpha
  \qquad
  \text{for }r\geq C r_0(\beta)^{1-\eps}.
\]
The definition of $r_0(\beta)$ then forces
\[
  r_0(\beta)\leq C r_0(\beta)^{1-\eps},
\]
so $r_0(\beta)$ is uniformly bounded as $\beta\uparrow\beta_c$.
Letting \(\beta\uparrow\beta_c\) yields
\[
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|
  \leq
  2\frac{\alpha}{\beta_c}r^\alpha
\]
for all sufficiently large \(r\), which makes the error term vanish at
criticality. Returning to the differential equation and integrating once
more, now with \(\varepsilon_{\beta_c,r}=O(r^{-\eps})\), gives the sharper
asymptotic
\[
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|
  =
  \frac{\alpha}{\beta_c}r^\alpha
  \bigl(1+O(r^{-\eps})\bigr).
\]

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
For the second and higher moments it is useful to write the Russo calculation
once. At criticality with cutoff \(r\), differentiating in \(r\) adds
potential edges of length of order \(r\). Suppressing harmless constants from
the smooth cutoff normalization, Russo's formula gives
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd r}\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^p
  =
  \beta_c r^{-d-\alpha-1}
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}\!\left[
    \sum_{x\in K}
    \sum_{y\in B_r(x)}
    \1_{\{x\not\leftrightarrow y\}}
    \bigl((|K|+|K_y|)^p-|K|^p\bigr)
  \right].
\]
Moving the root from \(x\) back to \(0\) by transitivity and expanding the
binomial gives
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd r}\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^p
  =
  \beta_c r^{-d-\alpha-1}
  \sum_{k=1}^p \binom pk
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}\!\left[
    \sum_{y\in B_r}
    |K|^{p-k+1}|K_y|^k
    \1_{\{0\not\leftrightarrow y\}}
  \right].
\]
The high-dimensional input is that, after summing over \(y\in B_r\), the two
clusters \(K\) and \(K_y\) are asymptotically independent:
\[
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}\!\left[
    \sum_{y\in B_r}
    |K|^{p-k+1}|K_y|^k
    \1_{\{0\not\leftrightarrow y\}}
  \right]
  =
  |B_r|\,\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^{p-k+1}
        \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^k
  -
  \text{overlap error}.
\]
The factor \(|B_r|\asymp r^d\) cancels the \(r^{-d}\) in the edge-addition
rate, producing the moment flow displayed above.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
For \(p=2\), the two binomial terms are the same after swapping the two
endpoint clusters, and their coefficients add to \(3\). Thus
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd r}\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2
  =
  3\beta_c r^{-\alpha-1}
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|\,
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2
  -
  O\!\left(
    r^{-d-\alpha-1}\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^4
  \right).
\]
The needed error estimate is slightly stronger than the crude tree-graph
bound:
\[
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^4
  \pre
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2
  \bigl(\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|\bigr)^4.
\]
Diagrammatically, one applies the tree-graph inequality but, instead of
pulling off only first moments at each branch, chooses an independent pair of
marked leaves to carry the second moment and pulls first moments off the
remaining branches. The finitely many four-point tree topologies are handled
in the same way. With
\(\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|\asymp r^\alpha\), the error is smaller than the
main term by a factor \(r^{3\alpha-d}\), hence by a power of \(r\) when
\(d>3\alpha\). Therefore
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd r}\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2
  =
  \bigl(1+O(r^{-\eps})\bigr)
  3\beta_c r^{-\alpha-1}
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|\,
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2 .
\]
Substituting the first-moment asymptotic yields
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd r}\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2
  =
  \bigl(1+O(r^{-\eps})\bigr)
  \frac{3\alpha}{r}
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2,
\]
and hence the logarithmic derivative of
\(r^{-3\alpha}\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2\) is integrable at infinity. It
follows that there is a non-universal constant \(A\in(0,\infty)\) such that
\[
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2\sim A r^{3\alpha}.
\]
In particular
\[
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2\as r^{3\alpha}.
\]
More generally, for each fixed integer $m\geq1$ one obtains
\[
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^m
  \as_m
  \bigl(\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|\bigr)^{2m-1}.
\]
The induction for higher moments is driven by linear ODEs with regularly varying forcing terms.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
A useful elementary lemma, in the forcing-dominated case needed for the higher-moment induction, is the following. Suppose
\[
  f'(r)\sim \frac a r f(r)+\frac{h(r)}r,
\]
where $h$ is regularly varying of index $b>a$. Then
\[
  f(r)\sim \frac{h(r)}{b-a}.
\]
This is just the integrating-factor solution of a first-order linear ODE together with Karamata's theorem. If $b=a$, logarithmic factors can appear; if $b<a$, the homogeneous solution may dominate depending on boundary data. In the moment induction, the displayed lemma is applied only when the lower-moment forcing dominates the homogeneous exponent. The double-factorial constants arise because the forcing recursion is the same as the moment recursion for a size-biased critical branching process.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
More precisely, if
\[
  \widehat m_r=
  \frac{\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2}
       {\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|},
\]
then the higher moments satisfy
\[
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^m
  \sim
  (2m-3)!!
  \widehat m_r^{\,m-1}
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|.
\]
The constants $(2m-3)!!$ are the binary-tree constants familiar from the tree-graph expansion.
Let us spell out the coefficient calculation. Write \(M_p(r)=\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^p\) and assume inductively that
\[
  M_j(r)\sim A_j\widehat m_r^{\,j-1}M_1(r),
  \qquad 1\leq j<p,
\]
with \(A_1=A_2=1\). In the \(p\)th moment ODE, the endpoint terms \(k=1\)
and \(k=p\) contain \(M_p\) itself and give
\[
  \beta_c r^{-\alpha-1}(p+1)M_1(r)M_p(r)
  \sim
  \frac{(p+1)\alpha}{r}M_p(r),
\]
using \(M_1(r)\sim(\alpha/\beta_c)r^\alpha\). The remaining terms give the
forcing
\[
  \frac{\alpha}{r}
  \left(
    \sum_{k=2}^{p-1}
    \binom pk A_kA_{p-k+1}
  \right)
  \widehat m_r^{\,p-1}M_1(r).
\]
This forcing is regularly varying with exponent \((2p-1)\alpha\), while the
homogeneous coefficient has exponent \((p+1)\alpha\). The excess exponent is
\[
  (2p-1)\alpha-(p+1)\alpha=\alpha(p-2).
\]
Applying the elementary ODE lemma therefore divides the forcing coefficient
by \(\alpha(p-2)\). Equivalently, writing \(A_m\) for the limiting normalized
\(m\)th moment, the ODE induction gives the recursion
\[
  A_p
  =
  \frac1{p-2}
  \sum_{k=2}^{p-1}
  \binom pk A_kA_{p-k+1},
  \qquad p\geq3,
\]
whose solution is \(A_p=(2p-3)!!\). This recurrence is the algebraic shadow of binary branching: the new long edge splits the marked points into two nonempty groups, and the normalization divides by the excess growth exponent \(p-2\).

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
At the long-range critical dimension $d=3\alpha<6$, the first-moment argument remains stable, but the second moment no longer follows from the high-dimensional error estimate. The heuristic error
\[
  r^{3\alpha-d}
\]
is now of order one rather than tending to zero. This does not destroy the method; instead it means that the leading power is still visible but the logarithmic correction is determined by a second-order term.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
\begin{theorem}[Long-range critical-dimensional logarithms; quoted theorem]
At the long-range critical dimension \(d=3\alpha<6\), under the
critical-dimensional hypotheses of the reference theorem,
\[
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2
  \asymp
  \frac{r^{3\alpha}}{\sqrt{\log r}},
  \qquad
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)
  \asymp
  n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{1/4}.
\]
The corresponding higher cutoff moments have the same double-factorial
size-biased recursion with size scale \(r^{2\alpha}/\sqrt{\log r}\).
\end{theorem}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
The proof has the same first appearance as the high-dimensional argument but
a different second act. Write
\[
  \mathbb E_r=\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r},\qquad
  m_r=\mathbb E_r|K|,\qquad
  f_r=\mathbb E_r|K|^2,\qquad
  V_r=\frac{f_r}{m_r^3}.
\]
The first moment is still
\[
  m_r\sim \frac{\alpha}{\beta_c}r^\alpha.
\]
If the high-dimensional second-moment equation remained true without any
correction, it would give \(f_r\asymp r^{3\alpha}\). At \(d=3\alpha\), however,
the error term is marginal. The relevant correction is the first term that
measures the failure of two cutoff clusters to behave independently.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
\begin{prop}[Second-order cutoff equation at \(d=3\alpha\); quoted input]
Let \(B_r\) be the range-\(r\) cutoff ball, normalized so that
\[
  |J'(r)|\,|B_r|=r^{-\alpha-1}(1+o(1))
\]
up to an error whose integral against \(\dd r/r\) is finite. Define the two
deficits
\[
  \mathscr D_r^{(1)}(x,y)
  =
  m_r^2
  -
  \mathbb E_r\!\left[
    |K_x|\,|K_y|\,
    \1_{\{x\not\leftrightarrow y\}}
  \right]
\]
and
\[
  \mathscr D_r^{(2)}(x,y)
  =
  m_r f_r
  -
  \mathbb E_r\!\left[
    |K_x|\,|K_y|^2\,
    \1_{\{x\not\leftrightarrow y\}}
  \right].
\]
Set
\[
  \mathcal E_{1,r}
  =
  \frac{\sum_{y\in B_r}\mathscr D_r^{(1)}(0,y)}
       {|B_r|m_r^2},
  \qquad
  \mathcal E_{2,r}
  =
  \frac{\sum_{y\in B_r}\mathscr D_r^{(2)}(0,y)}
       {|B_r|m_r f_r}.
\]
Then the exact cutoff Russo formulae have the form
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd r}m_r
  =
  \beta_c |J'(r)|\,|B_r|\,m_r^2(1-\mathcal E_{1,r})
\]
and
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd r}f_r
  =
  3\beta_c |J'(r)|\,|B_r|\,m_r f_r(1-\mathcal E_{2,r}).
\]
Moreover, if \(\kappa\) denotes the continuum stopped stable kernel appearing
in the critical-dimensional spatial moment theorem and
\[
  I_j=\int_B\kappa^{*j}(y)\,\dd y,
\]
then
\[
  \sum_{y\in B_r}\mathscr D_r^{(1)}(0,y)
  \sim
  I_3\frac{f_r^2}{m_r}
\]
and
\[
  \sum_{y\in B_r}\mathscr D_r^{(2)}(0,y)
  \sim
  (I_3+2I_4)\frac{f_r^3}{m_r^2}.
\]
\end{prop}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
Let us unpack the proposition, since this is the point at which the
logarithm enters. The quantities \(\mathscr D_r^{(1)}\) and
\(\mathscr D_r^{(2)}\) are deficit terms: they compare the product of two
unconditioned cluster moments with the corresponding moment in which the two
marked clusters are required not to have merged. In dimensions above the
critical dimension these deficits are lower order. At \(d=3\alpha\) their
integral over the cutoff ball is just large enough to affect the leading
slowly varying term.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
Here is the proof spine behind that statement. Couple \(K_x\) and \(K_y\) by
first sampling \(K_x\) and an independent cluster \(\widetilde K_y\), then
using the edge statuses already revealed by \(K_x\) whenever the exploration
of \(\widetilde K_y\) tries to reuse them. In this coupling, vertices of
\(\widetilde K_y\) may be cut off from \(y\) by intersections with \(K_x\).
The deficit \(\mathscr D_r^{(1)}(x,y)\) is the expected amount of this lost
mass, weighted by the size of \(K_x\). The deficit
\(\mathscr D_r^{(2)}(x,y)\) is the analogous lost mass with one additional
marked copy of the \(y\)-cluster.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
The ordinary \(k\)-point scaling theorem gives a vertex factor
\[
  V_r=\frac{f_r}{m_r^3}
\]
at each branching point of a large cutoff cluster. The new cut-off-by-another
cluster operation has, a priori, a different vertex factor, call it
\(\widetilde V_r\), because it measures not just a branching event but the
ratio between an actual intersection with a connecting path and the
tree-graph upper bound for such an intersection. Diagrammatically the first
deficit has one ordinary branch and one cut-off interaction:
\[
  \mathscr D_r^{(1)}(x,y)
  \approx
  r^{-d}m_r^5 V_r\widetilde V_r\,
  \kappa^{*3}\!\left(\frac{x-y}{r}\right).
\]
The second deficit has two ordinary branchings and one cut-off interaction:
\[
  \mathscr D_r^{(2)}(x,y)
  \approx
  r^{-d}m_r^7 V_r^2\widetilde V_r\,
  \left(\kappa^{*3}+2\kappa^{*4}\right)
  \!\left(\frac{x-y}{r}\right).
\]
The \(\kappa^{*3}\) term corresponds to the diagram in which the two root
clusters are joined by a three-line chain; the two \(\kappa^{*4}\) terms are
the two diagrams in which the additional marked copy of \(K_y\) attaches on
one side or the other of the interaction.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
The reference theorem proves these diagrammatic estimates in the sense of
polynomial moments. Its crucial additional conclusion is
\[
  \widetilde V_r\sim V_r.
\]
Its proof differentiates the correction moments in the cutoff parameter. The
derivative contains merging terms, whose asymptotics are supplied by the
already-proved mixed-moment theorem, and triple-interaction terms, where
three distinct clusters interact. A separate triple-interaction lemma reduces
these to sums of pair-interaction terms plus negligible errors. The resulting
ODEs give recurrence relations for the polynomial moments of the deficits.
Those recurrences are exactly the continuum identities satisfied by
\(\kappa^{*3}\) and by \(\kappa^{*3}+2\kappa^{*4}\), so the limiting constants
are identified and the equality \(\widetilde V_r\sim V_r\) is forced.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
With this input, summing the two displayed diagram estimates over \(B_r\) and
using \(V_r=f_r/m_r^3\) gives the integrated deficit estimates
\[
  \mathcal E_{1,r}
  \sim
  I_3 R_r,
  \qquad
  \mathcal E_{2,r}
  \sim
  (I_3+2I_4)R_r,
  \qquad
  R_r=\frac{f_r^2}{|B_r|m_r^3}.
\]

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
There is then a cancellation that is easy to miss if one writes only the
schematic equation. Define \(\mathcal H_r\) by
\[
  m_r=(1+\mathcal H_r)\frac{\alpha}{\beta_c}r^\alpha.
\]
Solving the first-moment differential equation to second order gives
\[
  \mathcal H_r\sim \mathcal E_{1,r}
\]
up to an error whose integral against \(\dd r/r\) is finite. Substituting the
first-moment expansion into the second-moment equation therefore gives
\[
  (1+\mathcal H_r)(1-\mathcal E_{2,r})
  =
  1-\bigl[(I_3+2I_4)-I_3+o(1)\bigr]R_r.
\]
The \(I_3\) term produced by the first deficit cancels the \(I_3\) part of
the second deficit. The surviving correction is precisely
\[
  2I_4=2\int_B\kappa^{*4}(y)\,\dd y.
\]
Thus the rigorous second-order equation is
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd r}f_r
  =
  \frac{3\alpha}{r}
  \left(
    1-
    \bigl[2I_4+o(1)\bigr]
    \frac{f_r^2}{|B_r|m_r^3}
    +\delta_r
  \right)f_r,
\]
where \(\delta_r\) is logarithmically integrable.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
\begin{lemma}[Marginal ODE]
Let \(a,\gamma,C>0\). Suppose \(g\) is positive and satisfies
\[
  g'(r)
  =
  \frac{a}{r}
  \left(
    1-(C+o(1))(r^{-a}g(r))^\gamma+\delta_r
  \right)g(r),
\]
where \(\int^\infty |\delta_r|\,\dd r/r<\infty\). Then
\[
  g(r)\sim (a\gamma C\log r)^{-1/\gamma}r^a.
\]
\end{lemma}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
\begin{proof}
Set \(t=\log r\) and \(u(t)=e^{-at}g(e^t)\). Then
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd t}\log u(t)
  =
  -a(C+o(1))u(t)^\gamma+a\delta_{e^t}.
\]
Writing \(w(t)=u(t)^{-\gamma}\), this becomes the linear equation
\[
  w'(t)+a\gamma\delta_{e^t}w(t)=a\gamma(C+o(1)).
\]
Since \(\int^\infty|\delta_{e^t}|\,\dd t<\infty\), the integrating factor has
a finite positive limit. Integrating the last display therefore gives
\[
  w(t)\sim a\gamma C\,t.
\]
Returning to \(r=e^t\) proves \(r^{-a}g(r)\sim(a\gamma C\log r)^{-1/\gamma}\).
\end{proof}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
Applying the lemma with \(a=3\alpha\) and \(\gamma=2\), and using
\[
  |B_r|m_r^3
  \sim
  \left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta_c}\right)^3 r^{6\alpha},
\]
gives the sharper asymptotic
\[
  f_r
  \sim
  \frac{\alpha}{\beta_c}
  \frac{1}{\sqrt{12\beta_c I_4}}\,
  \frac{r^{3\alpha}}{\sqrt{\log r}}.
\]
In particular,
\[
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2
  \asymp
  \frac{r^{3\alpha}}{\sqrt{\log r}}.
\]
The higher moments then follow the same double-factorial recursion, but with
this logarithm propagated through the size-biased scale
\[
  \widehat m_r
  =
  \frac{f_r}{m_r}
  \asymp
  \frac{r^{2\alpha}}{\sqrt{\log r}}.
\]

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
This still does not by itself identify the cluster tail. The cutoff-to-full comparison must be redone with the logarithmic scale. In place of the high-dimensional choice $r\asymp h^{-1/(2\alpha)}$, one chooses $r$ so that
\[
  \widehat m_r\asymp h^{-1},
  \qquad\text{that is}\qquad
  \frac{r^{2\alpha}}{\sqrt{\log r}}\asymp h^{-1}.
\]
With this modified cutoff choice, the resulting ghost-field singularity is
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(0\leftrightarrow\mathcal G_h)
  \asymp
  h^{1/2}(\log(1/h))^{1/4},
\]
and Karamata's theorem converts this into
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)
  \asymp
  n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{1/4}.
\]
The important point is conceptual: at the critical dimension the superprocess-type moment recursion is established first, with an unknown slowly varying factor, and the slowly varying factor is then identified by the marginal second-order correction. This is why the critical-dimensional proof is not a formal substitution of $d=3\alpha$ into the high-dimensional argument.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
section_title: Size biasing and the volume tail
text:
Define the size-biased cutoff law by
\[
  \widehat{\mathbb E}_r[F(K)]
  =
  \frac{\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}[|K|F(K)]}
       {\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|}.
\]
\begin{corollary}[Size-biased cutoff volume limit; derived from cutoff moments]
Under the hypotheses of the high-dimensional cutoff moment theorem,
\[
  \frac{|K|}{\widehat m_r}\Longrightarrow N^2,
\]
where $N$ is a standard normal random variable. Indeed,
\[
  \widehat{\mathbb E}_r
  \left[
    \left(\frac{|K|}{\widehat m_r}\right)^p
  \right]
  \longrightarrow
  (2p-1)!!,
\]
which are the moments of $N^2$.
\end{corollary}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
section_title: Size biasing and the volume tail
text:
\begin{prop}[Volume tail from size-biased cutoff asymptotics]
Suppose
\[
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|\sim A_1r^\alpha,
  \qquad
  \widehat m_r
  =
  \frac{\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2}{\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|}
  \sim A_2 f(r),
\]
where \(f\) is regularly varying of index \(a\alpha\) for some \(a>0\). Let
\(Q_r\) be the law of \(|K|/\widehat m_r\) under the size-biased cutoff law,
and suppose that \(Q_r\Rightarrow Q_\infty\), where \(Q_\infty\) has no atom
at zero. Then
\[
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c}\bigl[1-e^{-h|K|}\bigr]
  \sim
  A_3 f^{-1}(1/h)^\alpha h
\]
as \(h\downarrow0\), and
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)
  \sim
  A_4\frac{f^{-1}(n)^\alpha}{n}
\]
as \(n\to\infty\). The constants are
\[
  A_3=
  \frac{A_1}{A_2^{1/a}}
  \lim_{\lambda\to\infty}
  \lambda^{-(a-1)/a}
  \int_0^\infty\frac{1-e^{-\lambda x}}{x}\,\dd Q_\infty(x),
  \qquad
  A_4=\frac{A_3}{\Gamma(1/a)}.
\]
\end{prop}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
section_title: Size biasing and the volume tail
text:
\begin{proof}
Let \(\mathcal G_h\) be an independent ghost field in which each vertex is
green with probability \(1-e^{-h}\). Then
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(0\leftrightarrow \mathcal G_h)
  =
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c}\left[1-e^{-h|K|}\right].
\]
Monotonicity gives the lower comparison with the cutoff model. For the upper
comparison, couple the full and cutoff configurations monotonically. If the
full cluster reaches the ghost but the cutoff cluster does not, then the
cutoff cluster of the origin contains no green vertex and the full connection
must first use an omitted edge of length larger than \(r\). Revealing the
cutoff cluster and using BK for this first omitted edge and the subsequent
ghost connection gives
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(0\leftrightarrow \mathcal G_h)
  \leq
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c,r}(0\leftrightarrow \mathcal G_h)
  +
  C r^{-\alpha}
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}[|K|e^{-h|K|}]
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(0\leftrightarrow \mathcal G_h).
\]
Here \(r^{-\alpha}\) is the tail of the omitted kernel and the factor
\(e^{-h|K|}\) is the conditional probability that the cutoff cluster contains
no ghost vertex.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
section_title: Size biasing and the volume tail
text:
Choose
\[
  r=f^{-1}(\lambda/(A_2h)),
\]
first keeping \(\lambda\) fixed while \(h\downarrow0\). Since
\(h\widehat m_r\to\lambda\), size biasing gives
\[
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}[|K|e^{-h|K|}]
  =
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|\,
  \widehat{\mathbb E}_r[e^{-h|K|}]
  \sim
  A_1r^\alpha
  \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda x}\,\dd Q_\infty(x).
\]
The prefactor \(r^{-\alpha}\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|\) stays bounded, and the
last integral tends to zero as \(\lambda\to\infty\) because \(Q_\infty\) has
no atom at zero. Thus the cutoff-to-full comparison error can be made
arbitrarily small by taking \(\lambda\) large.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
section_title: Size biasing and the volume tail
text:
It remains to evaluate the cutoff ghost probability:
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c,r}(0\leftrightarrow\mathcal G_h)
  =
  \frac{\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|}{\widehat m_r}
  \int_0^\infty
  \frac{1-e^{-h\widehat m_r x}}{x}\,\dd Q_r(x).
\]
With the above choice of \(r\), weak convergence of \(Q_r\) gives
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c,r}(0\leftrightarrow\mathcal G_h)
  \sim
  \frac{A_1 f^{-1}(\lambda/(A_2h))^\alpha h}{\lambda}
  \int_0^\infty
  \frac{1-e^{-\lambda x}}{x}\,\dd Q_\infty(x).
\]
Regular variation of \(f^{-1}\) rewrites this as the displayed
\(A_3 f^{-1}(1/h)^\alpha h\) asymptotic after taking
\(\lambda\to\infty\). Karamata's theorem, in the form stated near the
beginning of the book, then converts the Laplace singularity into the stated
tail asymptotic.
\end{proof}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
section_title: Size biasing and the volume tail
text:
In the regimes considered here, the size-biased cutoff limit is \(N^2\), the
square of a standard normal random variable. This follows from the moment
recursion:
\[
  \int_0^\infty x^p\,\dd Q_r(x)
  =
  \frac{\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^{p+1}}
       {\widehat m_r^p\,\mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}|K|}
  \longrightarrow (2p-1)!!,
\]
and Carleman's criterion identifies the limiting moment sequence. For
\(Q_\infty=N^2\),
\[
  \int_0^\infty\frac{1-e^{-\lambda x}}{x}\,\dd Q_\infty(x)
  =
  \sqrt{2\lambda+1}-1.
\]
Thus in the high-dimensional case \(\widehat m_r\sim Ar^{2\alpha}\) one
recovers
\[
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c}[1-e^{-h|K|}]\sim
  \frac{\alpha}{\beta_c}\sqrt{2}\,A^{-1/2}h^{1/2},
  \qquad
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)\sim
  \frac{\alpha}{\beta_c}\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\,A^{-1/2}n^{-1/2}.
\]
At the long-range critical dimension,
\[
  \widehat m_r
  \sim
  \frac{1}{\sqrt{12\beta_c I_4}}\,
  \frac{r^{2\alpha}}{\sqrt{\log r}},
\]
so \(f^{-1}(n)^\alpha/n\asymp n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{1/4}\), giving the
logarithmic tail stated above. Keeping the constants yields
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)
  \sim
  \frac{\alpha}{\beta_c}\sqrt{\frac2\pi}
  \left(
    \frac{6\beta_c}{\alpha}
    \int_B\kappa^{*4}(y)\,\dd y
  \right)^{1/4}
  n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{1/4}.
\]

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
To identify the scaling limit one also needs spatial information. Fix
\(u\in\mathbb R^d\). Odd projected moments vanish by symmetry, so the first
useful quantity is
\[
  S_2(r;u)=
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}\left[
    \sum_{x\in K}\langle x,u\rangle^2
  \right].
\]
Russo differentiation gives a pivotal-edge expression. After applying the
mass-transport principle to recenter at the first endpoint of the pivotal
edge, one obtains
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd r}S_2(r;u)
  =
  \beta_c |J'(r)|
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}\!\left[
    \sum_{x\in K}
    \sum_{y\in B_r}
    \1_{\{y\notin K\}}
    \sum_{z\in K_y}
    \langle z-x,u\rangle^2
  \right],
\]
where \(K_y\) is the cutoff cluster of \(y\) after the cluster of the origin
has been revealed. Write
\[
  z-x=(z-y)+y-x.
\]
Equivalently, before the mass-transport simplification one may write
\(z-x=(z-y)+y-0+(0-x)\). Expanding the square gives a main displacement term,
two homogeneous spatial-moment terms, and three cross terms. The rigorous
estimate is the following.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
\begin{lemma}[Second spatial moment derivative]
Under the high-dimensional hypotheses used for the cutoff moment theorem,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac{1}{\beta_c |J'(r)|}\frac{\dd}{\dd r}S_2(r;u)
 &=
 2|B_r|\,m_r\,S_2(r;u)
 +m_r^2\sum_{y\in B_r}\langle y,u\rangle^2  \\
 &\qquad
 \pm O\!\left(
   \|u\|^2 r^2
   \mathbb E_r[|K|^2|K\cap B_r|]
 \right) \\
 &\qquad
 \pm O\!\left(
   \mathbb E_r\!\left[
     |K|\,|K\cap B_r|
     \sum_{x\in K}\langle x,u\rangle^2
   \right]
 \right).
\end{aligned}
\]
The two error terms are \(o(|B_r|m_rS_2(r;u)+m_r^2r^{d+2})\) in the
effectively high-dimensional regimes; in the genuinely long-range case
\(d>3\alpha\) they are logarithmically integrable after normalization.
\end{lemma}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
\begin{proof}
Expand \(z-x=(z-y)+y-x\), or equivalently
\((z-y)+y-0+(0-x)\), in the derivative formula. The terms containing
\(\langle z-y,u\rangle^2\) and \(\langle x,u\rangle^2\) are equal after
mass transport, producing
\[
  2|B_r|\,m_r\,S_2(r;u)
\]
when the two clusters are factored. The term containing
\(\langle y,u\rangle^2\) produces
\[
  m_r^2\sum_{y\in B_r}\langle y,u\rangle^2.
\]
The factorization errors for these two positive terms are controlled by the
same disjoint-cluster covariance estimate used in the volume-moment proof:
\[
  0\leq
  m_r^2-
  \mathbb E_r\!\left[
    |K|\,|K_y|\,
    \1_{\{y\notin K\}}
  \right]
  \leq
  \mathbb E_r[|K|^2\1_{\{y\in K\}}].
\]
After summing over \(y\in B_r\), this gives the first displayed error term.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
For the cross terms, subtract the product of the two independent expectations,
which is zero by symmetry. For example,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E_r\!\left[
  \1_{\{y\notin K\}}
  \sum_{x\in K}\langle x,u\rangle
  \sum_{z\in K_y}\langle z-y,u\rangle
\right]  \\
&\quad =
\sum_{x,z}
\bigl[
  \mathbb P_r(0\leftrightarrow x,\ y\leftrightarrow z,\ 0\not\leftrightarrow y)
  -
  \mathbb P_r(0\leftrightarrow x)\mathbb P_r(y\leftrightarrow z)
\bigr]
\langle x,u\rangle\langle z-y,u\rangle .
\end{aligned}
\]
The bracket is bounded by the probability that the two clusters interact;
BK and the disjoint-connection estimate dominate it by a four-point
tree-graph event. Using
\[
  |\langle x,u\rangle|\,|\langle z-y,u\rangle|
  \leq
  \frac12\bigl(\langle x,u\rangle^2+\langle z-y,u\rangle^2\bigr)
\]
and applying mass transport again gives the second displayed error. The
remaining cross term with \(\langle y,u\rangle\) is identical except that one
also uses \(|\langle y,u\rangle|\leq \|u\|r\) for \(y\in B_r\).

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
It remains to see that the errors are lower order. In the regime \(d>3\alpha\),
the spatially weighted tree-graph inequality gives
\[
  \mathbb E_r\!\left[
    |K|\,|K\cap B_r|
    \sum_{x\in K}\langle x,u\rangle^2
  \right]
  \preceq
  m_r^4 S_2(r;u),
\]
so after division by \(r^d m_r S_2(r;u)\) the error is
\[
  O(m_r^3/r^d)=O(r^{3\alpha-d}),
\]
which is logarithmically integrable. The term
\(r^2\mathbb E_r[|K|^2|K\cap B_r|]\) is handled by the same tree-graph
estimate used for the first-moment cutoff error. In the critical-dimensional
and two-point-function cases one replaces this last bound by the corresponding
Gladkov or two-point estimates from the reference theorem; the algebra is the
same, but the input needed to make the error negligible is stronger.
\end{proof}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
Multiplying the main terms by \(\beta_c|J'(r)|\) and using
\[
  |J'(r)|\,|B_r|\sim r^{-\alpha-1},
  \qquad
  m_r\sim\frac{\alpha}{\beta_c}r^\alpha,
\]
the two homogeneous spatial terms give
\[
  2\beta_c r^{-\alpha-1}
  S_2(r;u)m_r
  \sim
  \frac{2\alpha}{r}S_2(r;u).
\]
The new-displacement term gives
\[
  \beta_c |J'(r)|m_r^2
  \sum_{y\in B_r}\langle y,u\rangle^2
  \sim
  \frac{\alpha^2}{\beta_c}
  r^{\alpha+1}
  \int_{B_1}\langle y,u\rangle^2\,\dd y.
\]
Thus the second spatial moment satisfies the ODE
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd r}
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}\left[
    \sum_{x\in K}\langle x,u\rangle^2
  \right]
  \sim
  \frac{2\alpha}{r}
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c,r}\left[
    \sum_{x\in K}\langle x,u\rangle^2
  \right]
  +
  \frac{\alpha^2}{\beta_c}r^{\alpha+1}
  \int_{B_1}\langle y,u\rangle^2\,\dd y.
\]
The comparison between the homogeneous exponent $2\alpha$ and the forcing exponent $\alpha+2$ is exactly where the long-range/short-range distinction enters the high-dimensional scaling limit.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
\begin{theorem}[Cutoff spatial mixed moments and superprocess convergence; quoted conditional input]
For polynomials \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\) and with the correct spatial scale
\(\sigma(r)\), the high-dimensional spatial theory proves asymptotics of the
form
\[
  \begin{aligned}
  &\E_{\beta_c,r}\!\left[
    \sum_{x_1,\ldots,x_n\in K}
    \prod_{i=1}^n P_i(x_i/\sigma(r))
  \right]
  \\
  &\qquad =
  \left(
    \sum_{T\in\mathbb T_n}
    \idotsint
    \prod_{i\sim j}\kappa(x_i-x_j)
    \prod_{i=1}^n P_i(x_i)\,
    \dd x_1\cdots \dd x_{2n-1}
    +o(1)
  \right)
  \widehat m_r^{\,n-1}\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|.
  \end{aligned}
\]
Here \(\mathbb T_n\) is the set of binary trees with leaves labelled
\(0,1,\ldots,n\), root leaf \(0\) fixed at \(x_0=0\), and all non-leaf
vertices unlabelled of degree three. The product \(i\sim j\) ranges over the
edges of the tree. The kernel \(\kappa\) is the continuum potential kernel of
the limiting spatial motion: stable in the genuinely long-range case and
Brownian in the effectively short-range case. This is the moment formula for
the integrated superprocess.
\end{theorem}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
Let us spell out why this theorem has the same binary-tree form as the
volume moment theorem. Differentiating a mixed moment with \(n\) marked
points again inserts one pivotal cutoff edge. Removing that edge splits the
marked points into two nonempty subfamilies, and the BK/tree-graph
decomposition records the branch point at which the split occurs. Thus the
ODE for the \(n\)-point polynomial moment is driven by products of lower
moments, one for each binary partition of the marked leaves. The intrinsic
part of the calculation is the same recursion that produced
\((2n-3)!!\) for the volume moments.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
The spatial part records the displacement accumulated along the edges of the
limiting genealogy. In the moment formula each edge of a tree carries a copy
of the continuum kernel \(\kappa\). The internal vertices are integrated over,
corresponding to summing over possible branch locations in the discrete
tree-graph expansion. The vertex factor
\[
  V_r=\frac{\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2}{(\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|)^3}
\]
is the normalization attached to each branching point; after the volume
moment asymptotics are inserted, the \(n-1\) vertex factors and the \(2n-1\)
two-point lines combine exactly into
\(\widehat m_r^{\,n-1}\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|\). When all \(P_i\equiv1\), each
diagram integral is one and the theorem reduces to the cutoff volume moment
asymptotic
\[
  \E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^n
  \sim
  (2n-3)!!\,\widehat m_r^{\,n-1}\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|.
\]

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
The reason these diagram moments identify the integrated superprocess is a
standard property of the continuum random tree. Under the size-biased law in
which the total mass is biased by \(\mu^{n-1}\), the reduced tree spanned by
the root and \(n\) independent mass-sampled leaves has a uniform shape in
\(\mathbb T_n\), and its \(2n-1\) edge lengths are independent
\(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) random variables. Equivalently, if the original
size-biased total mass has the \(N^2\) law, the additional \(\mu^{n-1}\) bias
turns it into a chi-squared law with \(2n-1\) degrees of freedom; mixing the
unit-mass CRT distances over this mass law changes the total reduced-tree
length into a gamma variable, hence into a sum of independent exponentials.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
Once spatial motion is run independently along the edges of this reduced
tree, integrating over the exponential edge lengths gives exactly the kernel
\(\kappa\) on each edge. Thus the continuum random measure has the same
polynomial mixed moments as the limits displayed above. The polynomial
moments are determinate, by the same Carleman-type bounds that control the
volume moments together with the spatial moment estimates, and tightness of
the rescaled cutoff measures turns moment convergence into weak convergence.
This is why the scaling limit can be computed before the precise slowly
varying normalization is known: the normalization enters through
\(\widehat m_r\) and \(\sigma(r)\), while the limiting genealogy and diagram
constants are already fixed by the ODE recursion.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
\begin{defn}[Correlation-length condition (CL)]
For each \(p>0\), define
\[
  \xi_p(\beta_c,r)^p
  =
  \frac{
    \E_{\beta_c,r}\bigl[\sum_{x\in K_o}\norm{x}^p\bigr]
  }{
    \E_{\beta_c,r}|K_o|
  },
\]
with the evident modification when \(p=\infty\). Thus \(\xi_p(\beta_c,r)\) is the \(p\)th radius of gyration of the cutoff cluster, biased by the cluster mass in the same way that the two-point function biases spatial averages. The model satisfies (CL) if for each \(p>0\) there exists \(C_p<\infty\) such that
\[
  \xi_p(\beta_c,r)\leq C_p r
\]
for every $r\geq 1$.
\end{defn}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
Another useful way to remember the condition is through the cutoff two-point function. In an effectively long-range regime one expects, very roughly,
\[
  \P_{\beta_c,r}(x\leftrightarrow y)
  \asymp
  \norm{x-y}^{-d+\alpha}h(\norm{x-y}/r),
\]
where \(h\) decays rapidly at infinity. This is not the definition we shall use, since making the quantifiers and regularity assumptions precise takes work, but it captures the intended meaning: after the cutoff at scale \(r\), connections much longer than \(r\) should be strongly suppressed, while connections below scale \(r\) should still have the long-range critical power law.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
\begin{defn}[Weak cutoff localization (wCL)]
The model satisfies (wCL) if for each \(\eps>0\), there exists
\(C<\infty\) such that
\[
  \E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^q
  \leq
  (1+\eps)\E_{\beta_c,r}|K\cap B_{Cr}|^q
\]
for \(q=1,2,3,4\) and every \(r\). This four-moment localization condition is not the definition of effective long-range behaviour, but it is one of the practical inputs extracted from it. The reason the first four moments appear is not arbitrary: the moment ODE for the \(p\)th moment produces error terms involving the \((p+2)\)th moment, and the low-dimensional hydrodynamic argument only needs the ODEs for \(p=1\) and \(p=2\).
\end{defn}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
\begin{theorem}[Effective long-range localization and Sak upper bound; quoted sufficient theorem]
For the Euclidean power-law kernels treated in the reference papers, with the
usual two-sided regularity assumptions and a non-trivial critical point, (CL)
holds in the range \(\alpha<1\). Together with the corresponding power-law
assumptions on \(J\) and the regularity inputs needed to pass from cutoff
localization to pointwise estimates, (CL) yields
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(x\leftrightarrow y)\pre \norm{x-y}^{-d+\alpha}.
\]
\end{theorem}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
The matching lower bound is obtained by separate arguments in the regimes
currently covered by the theory. Conversely, (CL) is known to fail in some
genuinely short-range regimes, in particular for $\alpha>d$ and with special
marginal consequences at $\alpha=d$; this is weaker than proving failure
throughout the entire expected short-range side of Sak's crossover.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
Assume \(d<3\alpha\) and that the model satisfies (wCL), together with the
standard cutoff two-point consequences used below. Let
\[
  M_r=
  \min\left\{n:
  \P_{\beta_c,r}\!\left(
    \max_x |K_x\cap B_r|\geq n
  \right)\leq e^{-1}\right\}
\]
