and define \(M_r^*\) in the same way under the full critical measure \(\P_{\beta_c}\). Thus \(M_r\) and \(M_r^*\) are the median scales for the largest cluster intersection with \(B_r\) in the cutoff and full models respectively. The conditional conclusions take the form
\begin{theorem}[Low-effective-dimensional long-range hyperscaling; conditional theorem]
Assume \(d<3\alpha\) and the effective long-range localization hypotheses
used above, in particular (wCL). Then
\[
  M_r\asymp M_r^*\asymp r^{(d+\alpha)/2},
  \qquad
  \mathbb E_{\beta_c}|K\cap B_r|\asymp r^\alpha,
\]
and
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)
  \asymp
  n^{-(d-\alpha)/(d+\alpha)}.
\]
\end{theorem}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
There is also a useful hydrodynamic formulation. In the cutoff model, let $M_r$ be the median or typical value of the largest cutoff cluster intersected with a radius-$r$ box. The natural direct-merge scale is
\[
  r^{(d+\alpha)/2},
\]
because two clusters of this size in neighbouring boxes connect through bulk long edges with probability of order one:
\[
  r^{-d-\alpha}|A||B|\approx 1.
\]
\begin{defn}[Hydrodynamic condition]
The cutoff model satisfies the hydrodynamic condition if
\[
  M_r=o(r^{(d+\alpha)/2}).
\]
\end{defn}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
\begin{prop}[Failure of hydrodynamics below \(3\alpha\)]
Assume \(d<3\alpha\), (wCL), the cutoff first-moment bounds
\[
  m_1(r)=\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|\asymp r^\alpha,
\]
and the spatial-average bound
\[
  \E_{\beta_c,r}|K\cap B_{Cr}|\pre r^\alpha
\]
for each fixed \(C<\infty\). Then the hydrodynamic condition cannot hold
eventually. More precisely, \(M_r\) is bounded below by a positive multiple
of \(r^{(d+\alpha)/2}\) on arbitrarily large scales, and the combination of
(wCL) and universal tightness upgrades this to the scale of the hyperscaling
theorem.
\end{prop}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
\begin{proof}
The proof is a good illustration of the logic of the course. Let
\[
  m_1(r)=\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|,
  \qquad
  m_2(r)=\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^2 .
\]
Russo's formula gives, for every integer \(p\geq1\),
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd r}\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|^p
  =
  \beta_c |J'(r)|
  \sum_{\ell=0}^{p-1}\binom p\ell
  \E_{\beta_c,r}\!\left[
    |K|^{\ell+1}
    \sum_{y\in B_r}
    \1_{\{y\notin K\}}|K_y|^{p-\ell}
  \right].
\]
For \(p=1,2\) this can be written as
\[
  m_1'(r)
  =
  \beta_c |J'(r)|\,|B_r|\,m_1(r)^2(1-\mathcal E_{1,r})
\]
and
\[
  m_2'(r)
  =
  3\beta_c |J'(r)|\,|B_r|\,m_1(r)m_2(r)(1-\mathcal E_{2,r}),
\]
where
\[
  \mathcal E_{1,r}
  =
  \frac{|B_r|m_1(r)^2-
  \E_r\!\left[
    |K|\sum_{y\in B_r}\1_{\{y\notin K\}}|K_y|
  \right]}
  {|B_r|m_1(r)^2}
\]
and
\[
  \mathcal E_{2,r}
  =
  \frac{|B_r|m_1(r)m_2(r)-
  \E_r\!\left[
    |K|\sum_{y\in B_r}\1_{\{y\notin K\}}|K_y|^2
  \right]}
  {|B_r|m_1(r)m_2(r)}.
\]
The same disjoint-cluster covariance estimate used in the high-dimensional
moment proof gives
\[
  0\leq \mathcal E_{1,r}
  \leq
  \frac{\E_r[|K|^2|K\cap B_r|]}
       {|B_r|m_1(r)^2}
\]
and
\[
  0\leq \mathcal E_{2,r}
  \leq
  \frac{\E_r[|K|^3|K\cap B_r|]}
       {|B_r|m_1(r)m_2(r)}.
\]
These are the exact error terms hidden behind the schematic statement that
the endpoint clusters should decouple.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
Assume now, for contradiction, that hydrodynamics holds eventually. By
(wCL), after choosing \(C\) large the first four full cutoff moments can be
replaced up to \(1+o(1)\) errors by the moments of \(|K\cap B_{Cr}|\). The
universal tightness estimate supplies, for fixed \(p,q\),
\[
  \E_r|K\cap B_{Cr}|^{p+q}
  \pre
  M_{Cr}^q\,\E_r|K\cap B_{Cr}|^p.
\]
Consequently
\[
  \E_r[|K|^2|K\cap B_r|]
  \pre
  \E_r|K\cap B_{Cr}|^3
  \pre
  M_{Cr}^2\,\E_r|K\cap B_{Cr}|
\]
and
\[
  \E_r[|K|^3|K\cap B_r|]
  \pre
  \E_r|K\cap B_{Cr}|^4
  \pre
  M_{Cr}^2\,\E_r|K\cap B_{Cr}|^2.
\]
Using the universal spatial-average bound
\(\E_{\beta_c,r}|K\cap B_{Cr}|\pre r^\alpha\), the lower bound
\(m_1(r)\suc r^\alpha\), and hydrodynamics
\(M_{Cr}=o(r^{(d+\alpha)/2})\), the first display gives
\[
  \mathcal E_{1,r}\to0.
\]
The first-moment ODE therefore reduces to
\[
  m_1'(r)\sim \beta_c r^{-\alpha-1}m_1(r)^2,
\]
and the elementary \(f'=Ar^{-\alpha-1}f^2\) lemma yields
\[
  m_1(r)\sim \frac{\alpha}{\beta_c}r^\alpha.
\]
The fourth-moment bound above gives, similarly,
\[
  \mathcal E_{2,r}
  \pre
  \frac{M_{Cr}^2}{|B_r|m_1(r)}
  \asymp
  \frac{M_{Cr}^2}{r^{d+\alpha}}
  \longrightarrow0.
\]
Substituting \(m_1(r)\sim(\alpha/\beta_c)r^\alpha\) into the second-moment
ODE gives
\[
  m_2'(r)\sim \frac{3\alpha}{r}m_2(r),
\]
so \(m_2\) is regularly varying of index \(3\alpha\), in particular
\[
  m_2(r)=r^{3\alpha+o(1)}.
\]

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
But (wCL) and universal tightness also give the direct upper bound
\[
  m_2(r)
  \leq
  2\E_r|K\cap B_{Cr}|^2
  \pre
  M_{Cr}\,\E_r|K\cap B_{Cr}|
  \pre
  r^{(d+\alpha)/2}r^\alpha .
\]
When \(d<3\alpha\), the exponent
\[
  \frac{d+\alpha}{2}+\alpha
\]
is strictly smaller than \(3\alpha\), contradicting regular variation of
index \(3\alpha\). Thus (wCL) and hydrodynamics cannot both hold below
\(3\alpha\).

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
Here is the finite-box estimate that universal tightness supplies. If
\[
  X_R=|K_o\cap B_R|,
  \qquad
  M_R=\operatorname{med}_{e^{-1}}\max_x |K_x\cap B_R|,
\]
then the single-cluster damping estimate gives, for each fixed \(q\geq1\),
\[
  \E_{\beta_c,r}[X_R^{p+q}]
  \pre_q
  M_R^q\,\E_{\beta_c,r}[X_R^p],
  \qquad p=1,2,
\]
uniformly in the cutoff parameter. Indeed, integrate the tail of
\(X_R^{p+q}\) dyadically above \(M_R\); every dyadic step above \(M_R\) costs
an exponential factor by universal tightness. This is the rigorous substitute
for saying that no single cluster in \(B_R\) is much larger than \(M_R\) on
the scales relevant to the moment calculation.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
The preceding contradiction first proves that hydrodynamics fails on an
unbounded sequence of scales. The upgrade to every large scale is a finitary
``bad interval'' argument. Since
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd r}\log m_2(r)
  =
  3\beta_c |J'(r)|\,|B_r|\,m_1(r)(1-\mathcal E_{2,r})
  \geq
  (1-o(1))(1-\mathcal E_{2,r})\frac{3\alpha}{r},
\]
and since the estimate above gives
\[
  \mathcal E_{2,r}
  \pre
  \frac{M_{Cr}^2}{r^{d+\alpha}},
\]
one can force \(m_2\) to grow almost like \(r^{3\alpha}\) on any interval on
which \(M_{Cr}\ll r^{(d+\alpha)/2}\).

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
Choose \(\delta>0\) small enough that
\[
  3(1-\delta)^2\alpha>\alpha+\frac{d+\alpha}{2}.
\]
The sequence failure of hydrodynamics gives arbitrarily large scales with
\(M_r\geq 2\delta r^{(d+\alpha)/2}\), after decreasing \(\delta\) if needed.
Suppose that \([r,R]\) is a maximal interval of bad scales, meaning that
\[
  M_s\leq \delta s^{(d+\alpha)/2}
  \qquad (r<s\leq R),
\]
while \(M_r\geq\delta r^{(d+\alpha)/2}\). On the shortened interval
\([r,R/C]\), the error estimate gives \(\mathcal E_{2,s}\leq \delta\), so
integration yields
\[
  \frac{m_2(R/C)}{m_2(r)}
  \suc
  \left(\frac{R/C}{r}\right)^{3(1-\delta)^2\alpha}.
\]
The definition of \(M_r\) and translation invariance give the lower moment
bound
\[
  m_2(r)\suc \frac{M_r^3}{r^d}
  \suc
  r^{\alpha+(d+\alpha)/2}.
\]
On the other hand, (wCL), universal tightness, and the already-known upper
bound on \(M_s\) give, at \(R/C\),
\[
  m_2(R/C)\pre (R/C)^{\alpha+(d+\alpha)/2}.
\]
Comparing the last three displays gives
\[
  \left(\frac{R/C}{r}\right)^{3(1-\delta)^2\alpha}
  \pre
  \left(\frac{R/C}{r}\right)^{\alpha+(d+\alpha)/2}.
\]
Because of the choice of \(\delta\), the ratio \(R/r\) is bounded by a
constant depending only on the model parameters. Thus bad intervals have
bounded logarithmic length. Every sufficiently large scale lies within a
bounded multiplicative factor of a good scale, and monotonicity of \(M_r\)
upgrades the subsequential lower bound to
\[
  M_r\suc r^{(d+\alpha)/2}
\]
for all large \(r\). This is why the low-dimensional theorem needs both
localization and universal tightness rather than just a single moment
estimate.
\end{proof}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
The low-dimensional conclusions include more than the volume tail. Under the effectively long-range hypotheses one obtains moment estimates for $|K\cap B_r|$, fractal dimension
\[
  d_f=\frac{d+\alpha}{2},
\]
and the tail exponent
\[
  \delta=\frac{d+\alpha}{d-\alpha}.
\]
In exponent language, a typical large cluster in a radius-$r$ box has volume $r^{(d+\alpha)/2}$, the probability that the origin belongs to such a cluster is $r^{-(d-\alpha)/2}$, and the identity
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq r^{(d+\alpha)/2})
  \asymp r^{-(d-\alpha)/2}
\]
is exactly the displayed value of $\delta$.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
\begin{lemma}[Mesoscopic negligibility; tail-extraction input]
In the cutoff model, small and medium clusters do not contribute a positive
fraction of the first moment once the correct largest-cluster scale has been
identified:
\[
  \E_{\beta_c,r}\!\left[
    |K|\wedge \delta r^{(d+\alpha)/2}
  \right]
  =
  o\!\left(\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|\right)
  \qquad\text{as }\delta\downarrow0,
\]
uniformly along large scales.
\end{lemma}

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
The proof is another use of the same finite-box technology, but it is useful
to record the differential mechanism. Write
\[
  T_m(r)=\E_{\beta_c,r}[|K|\wedge m].
\]
Russo's formula and the elementary inequality
\[
  a\bigl[(a+b)\wedge m-a\wedge m\bigr]
  \leq
  (a\wedge m)(b\wedge m)
\]
give the truncated first-moment inequality
\[
  T_m'(r)
  \leq
  \beta_c |J'(r)|\,|B_r|\,T_m(r)^2.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd r}\frac1{T_m(r)}
  \geq
  -\beta_c |J'(r)|\,|B_r|.
\]
After integration, this says that if \(T_m(r)\) is a fixed positive fraction
of \(m_1(r)\asymp r^\alpha\) at scale \(r\), then for every
\(\ell\leq \lambda r\), with \(\lambda\) small depending only on that
fraction,
\[
  T_m(\ell)\geq (1-o(1))\frac{\alpha}{\beta_c}\ell^\alpha.
\]
Thus persistent mesoscopic mass at scale \(r\) forces near-mean-field
truncated first moments on a whole interval of smaller scales.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
The second ingredient is a lower differential inequality for \(m_2\) in
terms of the same truncated moment. Under \(d<3\alpha\) and (wCL), the
low-dimensional moment estimates imply
\[
  m_2'(r)
  \geq
  3\beta_c |J'(r)|\,|B_r|
  \left(
    1-
    C\frac{m r^{(\alpha-d)/2}}{T_m(r)}
  \right)
  T_m(r)m_2(r).
\]
This comes from the usual second-moment Russo formula after replacing
\(|K_y|\) by \(|K_y|\wedge m\). The decoupled term gives
\(|B_r|T_m(r)m_2(r)\), while the collision error is bounded using
universal tightness and the already established low-dimensional moment
orders.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
Now suppose that for some \(\eps>0\) and arbitrarily small \(\delta\), the
set
\[
  \mathscr R(\eps,\delta)
  =
  \left\{
    r:\,
    \E_r\bigl[|K|\wedge \delta r^{(d+\alpha)/2}\bigr]
    \geq \eps r^\alpha
  \right\}
\]
contains long multiplicative intervals. On a slightly shrunken interval the
first truncated-moment inequality makes \(T_m(s)\) comparable to
\((\alpha/\beta_c)s^\alpha\), while choosing \(\delta\) small makes
\[
  C\frac{m s^{(\alpha-d)/2}}{T_m(s)}
\]
smaller than any prescribed constant. Hence on such an interval
\[
  \frac{\dd}{\dd s}\log m_2(s)
  \geq
  a\alpha s^{-1}
\]
for some
\[
  a>\frac{\alpha+(d+\alpha)/2}{\alpha}.
\]
Integrating would force \(m_2\) to grow faster than the proven
low-dimensional order
\[
  m_2(s)\asymp s^{\alpha+(d+\alpha)/2}.
\]
Thus the intervals contained in \(\mathscr R(\eps,\delta)\) have bounded
logarithmic length. Enlarging the scale by a bounded factor and using
monotonicity then gives
\[
  \E_{\beta_c,r}\!\left[
    |K|\wedge \delta r^{(d+\alpha)/2}
  \right]
  \leq
  \eps\,\E_{\beta_c,r}|K|
\]
after decreasing \(\delta\). This is the desired mesoscopic negligibility.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
Once mesoscopic negligibility is known, the volume-tail exponent follows
from the finite-box scale. A typical cluster contributing to
\(\E_{\beta_c}|K\cap B_r|\asymp r^\alpha\) has volume
\[
  r^{(d+\alpha)/2}.
\]
The probability that the origin belongs to such a cluster is therefore
\[
  \frac{\E_{\beta_c}|K\cap B_r|}
       {r^{(d+\alpha)/2}}
  \asymp
  r^{-(d-\alpha)/2}.
\]
Writing \(n=r^{(d+\alpha)/2}\) gives
\[
  \P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)
  \asymp
  n^{-(d-\alpha)/(d+\alpha)}.
\]
Mesoscopic negligibility is what justifies replacing this scale-by-scale
calculation by an actual tail asymptotic rather than merely a statement about
largest clusters in boxes.

chapter_title: Cutoff Renormalization and Effective Long-Range Behaviour
text:
\begin{corollary}[Low-dimensional long-range \(k\)-point bound; conditional on pointwise input]
If the pointwise two-point estimate
\[
  \mathbb P_{\beta_c}(x\leftrightarrow y)\asymp \norm{x-y}^{-d+\alpha}
\]
is available, the higher-point geometry developed in the chapter on continuum \(k\)-point functions gives
\[
  \tau_{\beta_c}(A)\asymp_{|A|} S(A)^{-(d-\alpha)/2}
\]
for finite sets $A$ in the effectively long-range low-dimensional regime. This closes the circle between the Mobius-covariant $k$-point heuristics and the long-range hyperscaling theory.
\end{corollary}

chapter_title: A Roadmap of the Proof Techniques
text: Let us close by summarizing the logical structure of the subject as developed in these notes. The basic definitions give the quantities of interest: $\tau$, $\chi$, $\theta$, arm probabilities, cluster-volume tails, and $k$-point functions. The first layer of proofs establishes robust inequalities among them. Sharpness identifies the subcritical and supercritical sides of the transition. Russo formulae turn parameter variation into pivotality. Harris-FKG gives positive association, and BK gives disjoint-occurrence bounds. Tree-graph inequalities then turn BK into moment and diagrammatic estimates.

chapter_title: A Roadmap of the Proof Techniques
A Roadmap of the Proof Techniques
text: The second layer turns inequalities into exponents under additional hypotheses. The triangle condition controls the reverse susceptibility differential inequality, giving $\chi_\beta\asymp(\beta_c-\beta)^{-1}$. Relative entropy and decision trees convert that susceptibility estimate into the critical volume tail and the supercritical density. OSSS gives universal derivative lower bounds through revealment, while intrinsic geometry turns volume-tail information into one-arm estimates. Universal tightness turns finite-volume cluster control into hyperscaling inequalities.

chapter_title: A Roadmap of the Proof Techniques
text:
For mean-field behaviour the proof map is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{triangle control}
&\Longrightarrow \chi_\beta'\suc \chi_\beta^2\\
&\Longrightarrow \chi_\beta\asymp(\beta_c-\beta)^{-1}\\
&\Longrightarrow \P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)\pre n^{-1/2}
    \text{ by entropy}\\
&\Longrightarrow \P_{\beta_c}(|K|\geq n)\asymp n^{-1/2}
    \text{ by integrated lower tails}\\
&\Longrightarrow \theta(\beta_c+\eps)\asymp\eps
    \text{ by entropy and sharpness}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For intrinsic geometry, the corresponding map is
\[
\text{volume tail upper bound}
\Longrightarrow
Q_{3r}^*\leq\P(|K|\geq n)+C(n/r)(Q_r^*)^2
\Longrightarrow
Q_r^*\pre r^{-1/(\delta-1)}.
\]
These implications are robust: they require transitivity, BK-type independence, and enough integrability, but not Euclidean geometry.

chapter_title: A Roadmap of the Proof Techniques
text:
For hyperscaling and low-dimensional constraints the map is different:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{universal tightness}
&\Longrightarrow \text{largest clusters have a stable typical scale}\\
&\Longrightarrow \text{moments of finite-box clusters are controlled}\\
&\Longrightarrow \text{hyperscaling inequalities}\\
&\Longrightarrow d_c\geq6\text{ for short-range percolation}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the geometry of boxes enters directly. This is why the same inequalities can prove mean-field behaviour above the upper critical dimension and rule it out below the upper critical dimension.

chapter_title: A Roadmap of the Proof Techniques
A Roadmap of the Proof Techniques
text:
The long-range dependency map is the most elaborate:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{sharpness and two-point control}
&\Longrightarrow \text{finite cutoff moments}\\
&\Longrightarrow \text{first-moment cutoff ODE}\\
&\Longrightarrow \E_{\beta_c,r}|K|\asymp r^\alpha\\
&\Longrightarrow \text{higher-moment ODE induction}\\
&\Longrightarrow \text{size-biased }N^2\text{ limit}\\
&\Longrightarrow \text{ghost-field singularity}\\
&\Longrightarrow \text{volume tail}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Spatial moments add the long-range/short-range distinction through the comparison of homogeneous exponent $2\alpha$ and forcing exponent $\alpha+2$. Effective long-range conditions then determine whether the cutoff scale is the true macroscopic scale. Finally, universal tightness and hydrodynamic arguments decide whether the high-dimensional ODE picture is self-consistent or contradicts the finite-box geometry.

chapter_title: A Roadmap of the Proof Techniques
text:
Thus the course has a single recurring pattern. One first identifies a robust inequality, then chooses the right regularized observable, then proves that error terms are negligible or else uses their non-negligibility to force a different scaling law. The same pattern appears in the triangle condition, in OSSS, in universal tightness, and in the cutoff renormalization for long-range percolation.
In low effective dimensions, (CL) or its localized moment consequences combine with universal tightness to rule out the hydrodynamic many-cluster picture and force the long-range hyperscaling exponents.
